Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 1:

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾

It is an address to all people: the believers, the People of the Book, and the polytheists, those who hear this verse from among those present at the time of its revelation, and those who come after them until the Day of Resurrection, so that they may receive the command to have taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) of Allah and khashyah (awe, fear) of Him, meaning fear of opposing what He commands them through His Messenger. The taqwa of each group is according to their condition: from being entangled in what Allah has forbidden and from neglecting what He has commanded, so that they may replace that with its opposite.

The first group of people to enter the address "O mankind" are the polytheists of Makkah, to the extent that it has been said the address is specifically for them. This also includes the polytheists of Madinah before they became pure of them. In expressing the Exalted Essence by the attribute of Lord (Rabb), in the form of a possessive added to the pronoun of those addressed, there is an indication that He deserves to be feared because of His greatness through being the Creator, and an indication of the worthiness of people to fear Him, because by the attribute of the management of lordship He commands and forbids only to safeguard the interests of people and to avert harms from them. Neither of these two matters is conveyed by any attribute other than that of Lord, rather than something like Creator or Master. Linking taqwa to the Essence of the Lord implies, by the implication of necessity (dalalat al-iqtida'), the meaning of guarding against opposing Him, or His punishment, or something similar, because taqwa is not related to the Essence itself but to an affair of it that is appropriate to the context. The first of His due taqwa is to declare Him free of imperfections, and at the forefront of that is to declare Him free of partners by believing in His oneness in divinity.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ is in the position of a cause (ʿillah) for the command to taqwa, as the emphatic particle (inna) used in a context of address where the listener has no doubt indicates. Causation implies that the convulsion of the Hour has an effect on the command to taqwa, namely that it is a time when the reward for taqwa and the punishment for disobedience will be realized, in a general manner which is detailed by what follows it in His words ﴿But the punishment of Allah is severe﴾ [al-Hajj: 2].

As for al-zalzalah (convulsion), its reality is a violent movement in a direction of the surface of the earth, resulting from the pressure of air currents located in the layers of the earth near its surface. It is among the terrifying earthly phenomena, which results in the collapse of buildings and may result in the swallowing of things into the interior of the earth.

As for al-sa'ah (the Hour): it is a term that has become predominant in the terminology of the Qur'an for the time of the annihilation of the world and the arrival at the world of the Resurrection in the Hereafter. Allah the Exalted says ﴿When the earth is shaken with its [final] earthquake﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1], up to His words ﴿On that Day, people will depart separated to be shown their deeds﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 6]. The idafah (construct phrase) of "zalzalat" to "al-sa'ah" carries the meaning of "in," i.e., the convulsion that occurs at the time of the arrival of the Hour. It is permissible that the convulsion be in this world or at the time of the Gathering. The apparent reading is to take "zalzalah" in its literal sense, and it occurs when the worldly realm approaches annihilation and the disruption of its order, so its attribution to the Hour is a true attribution, and the meaning of His words ﴿When the earth is shaken with its [final] earthquake﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1] and what follows applies. It is also permissible that "zalzalah" be a metaphor for the terrors and frightening events that will take place on the Day of Resurrection, for such events are described with the word "zalzalah." Allah the Exalted says ﴿and they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], meaning they were struck by calamities and harms, given His words before it ﴿Hardship and adversity touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. And in the supplication of the Prophet ﷺ against the confederates: "O Allah, defeat them and shake them."

The use of the word "shay'" (thing) is for the sake of magnifying the matter through its extreme indefiniteness, meaning the convulsion of the Hour cannot be known in its reality, and it is described as "a tremendous thing." This is one of the positions in which the word "shay'" is appropriately used, and it is what Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir drew attention to in Dala'il al-I'jaz, in a section on establishing the discussion of eloquence and fluency. We mentioned it at His words ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-'azim (tremendous): the massive, and here it is used metaphorically for the powerful and severe. The context indicates that it is severe in evil.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 2:

﴿On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed, and every pregnant woman will drop her burden, and you will see people as drunk, though they are not drunk, but the punishment of Allah is severe.﴾

The clause ﴿On the Day you see it﴾ and what follows is an explanation of the clause ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ [al-Hajj: 1], because what is mentioned in this clause clarifies the meaning of its being a tremendous thing, namely that it is tremendous in evil and in terror. The phrase ﴿On the Day you see it﴾ is connected to the verb (tadhhalu, "will be distracted"). Placing it before its governing verb serves to emphasize the timing of that Day and the expectation that every addressee will witness it. The original arrangement of the clause would be: "Every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed on the Day you see the convulsion of the Hour." The address is thus to everyone who is able to witness that convulsion. The pronoun of object in (taraunaha, "you see it") may refer to (zalzalah, "convulsion"), and "seeing" is used for its clear perception, which is like seeing visible things, since a convulsion is heard rather than seen. It may also refer to (al-sa'ah, "the Hour"), and seeing it means seeing what occurs in it of visible things, such as the gathering of people for the Resurrection and what follows it, and witnessing the horrors of punishment. The indicator of this is His saying ﴿every nursing mother will be distracted﴾, etc.

Page 189
Al-dhuhul (distraction) is forgetting something that by its nature should not be forgotten, while there is a factor that calls for remembering it; either because it is present, or because its knowledge is recent. It is forgotten only due to a great preoccupation with it. Thus the word "dhuhul" is mentioned here rather than "nisyan" (forgetting), because it is more indicative of the intensity of preoccupation. This was stated by our teacher al-Jidd al-Wazir, who said: The compassion of a mother for her son is stronger than the compassion of a father, so her compassion for the nursling is stronger than her compassion for others. All of this indicates, by way of a stronger implication, the distraction of other women and men. This kinaya (allusion) has yielded an indication of all the implications of the intensity of the terror; and it is not necessary in kinaya that all implications be stated explicitly, because the indication of kinaya is rational, not verbal. The feminine ta' marbuta was attached to the description (murdi'a, "nursing"), to indicate bringing the description closer to the meaning of the verb, for a verb whose action is not attributed to anyone other than a woman takes the sign of feminine gender, so that this approximation conveys that she is in the state of engaging in nursing, as one says: "She is nursing." Were it not for this subtle point, the apparent expectation would be to say: "kullu murdi'in" (every nursing [female]), because this attribute is specific to females, and so the ta' that originally serves to distinguish feminine from masculine to avoid confusion would not be needed with it. This is among the subtle questions of the grammarians of Kufa, and all have accepted it; Ibn Malik versified it in his Urjuza al-Kafiyya with his saying:

"Of the attributes specific to the female, the ta' is dispensed with, because the wording is explicit."

"Where the meaning of the verb intends the ta', add it, as in: 'she became nursing a child who was born.'"

The intended meaning is that this occurs to every nursing mother existing at the end of the days of this world. So the literal meaning is intended, and it does not require that the nursing actually be taking place. Thus the distraction of the nursing mother and the pregnant woman is expressed, and what is intended is the distraction of every person with a precious charge from their charge, by way of kinaya. The addition of the word "kull" (every) indicates that this distraction befalls every nursing mother, and it is not for only some of the nursing mothers, with the possibility of weakness in their memory. Then

Page 190
this kinaya implies a kinaya about generalizing this terror to all people, because the particularity of this meaning in this context is that it is most apparent in depicting the state of fright and panic, such that one who is in a state of extreme alertness is distracted, given the abundance of motives for alertness. That is because a woman, due to her intense compassion, frequently recalls what she is compassionate about; and a nursing mother is the most compassionate of women toward her nursling; and while engaged in nursing she is the furthest thing from distraction. So when she is distracted from her nursling in these circumstances, this indicates that the terror befalling her is a terror that breaks customary norms. This is among the excellent forms of kinaya for the intensity of that terror, because the implication that a nursing mother's distraction from her nursling results from intense terror necessarily implies the intensity of terror for others, by way of a stronger implication; so it is a implication of a second degree. This type of kinaya is called al-Iyma' (indication).

The (ma) in ﴿from what she nursed﴾ is a relative pronoun whose referent is the suckling infant. Its returning pronoun is elided, because it is a connected object pronoun governed by a verb, and the elision of its like is common. Using the relative pronoun with its clause to identify what she is distracted from, rather than saying "from her son," indicates that she is distracted from something that is right before her eyes while she is engaged in an action related to it, namely nursing, further intensifying the allusion to the intensity of terror. The phrase ﴿and every pregnant woman will drop her burden﴾ is likewise a kinaya, like His saying ﴿every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed﴾. Dropping a burden happens only due to the intense agitation of the pregnant woman's soul from extreme fright and fear, because the fetus is in a firm place.

Al-haml (burden) is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, by the indication of its connection to the verb (tada'u, "will drop"), i.e., she drops her fetus. The expression "dhat haml" (possessor of a burden) is used rather than "hamil" (pregnant), because it is what is customary in usage in most cases. So one does not say "imra'a hamil," but says "dhat haml"; God the Exalted said: ﴿And for those with burdens, their term is that they should lay down their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]; along with the alert implied in this idafa to the intense connection of the burden to the pregnant woman, indicating that her dropping it is due to a dreadful cause. The discussion of whether its sense is literal or a kinaya is like the discussion of ﴿every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed﴾. The address in (tara al-nas, "you see people") is to an unspecified addressee, namely everyone among the people who is able to see, so it is equivalent in meaning to the address in His saying (﴿On the Day you see it﴾). The singular was chosen here for variety, to avoid repeating the plural. The shift from the past tense to the present in His saying (wa tara, "and you see") is for bringing the state to mind and expressing wonder at it, like His saying ﴿then it stirs up clouds﴾ [al-Rum: 48] and His saying ﴿and he builds the ship﴾ [Hud: 38].

The majority read (sukara, "drunk") with a dammah on the unmarked sin and an alif after the kaf. Describing people with this is in the manner of the eloquent simile (tashbih baligh). His saying after it, ﴿though they are not drunk﴾, is an indicator that a simile is intended, and that upon it is built His saying after it, ﴿but the punishment of Allah is severe﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (sakra) in the pattern of (atsha, "thirsty") in both places. Sukara and sakra are plurals of sakran (drunk), which is one whose mind's perception is disturbed due to the effect of drinking wine; the analogical plural of it is sukara. As for sakra, it is treated as the plural of those who are foolish (nawka), because in intoxication there is disturbance of the mind. It has a parallel: the plural of kaslan (lazy) as kusala and kaslaa. The clause ﴿though they are not drunk﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from "people." The phrase (adhab Allah, "the punishment of Allah") encompasses His punishment in this world, which is the torment of fright and pain, and the torment of terror in the Hereafter through feeling the blaze of the Fire and being pushed by the angels of punishment. The clause ﴿though they are not drunk﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from (al-nas, "people").

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 3:

Page 192
﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.﴾
This is coordinated (ʿatf) with the sentence ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 1], meaning: the people are of two groups. One group complies with the command, so it fears Allah and dreads His punishment; and another group turns away from that and opposes it with false disputation concerning Allah, exalted is He, regarding His oneness, His attributes, and His messengership. This group are the leaders of polytheism and the chieftains of disbelief, because they are the ones who take up disputation, with their fallacies and sophistry, and with their eloquence and deception.

Restricting the reference to them is an indication that, were it not for their misguiding their people and their turning them away from following the religion, the common polytheists would have followed Islam, due to the clarity of its proof and its acceptance by the natural disposition (fitrah). It has been said: what is meant by ﴿one who disputes about Allah﴾ is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith or someone else, as will come. In that case, (min) in the relative sense is inclusive of a plurality, general to everyone to whom the relative clause applies.

Al-mujadalah (disputation) means contention and argumentation. The adverbial sense of the preposition (fi) is figurative, meaning: he disputes with a dispute that takes place concerning the matter of Allah. The dispute is described as "without knowledge," meaning a dispute mixed with the opposite of knowledge; the opposite of knowledge is ignorance. That is, a dispute arising from faulty reasoning and faulty thinking, so that one does not know what divinity requires of the attributes, such as oneness, knowledge, and doing whatever He wills.

Following the Shaytan (ittiba' al-shaytan) means submitting to his whispering, which one finds within oneself and which one received through habit, and acting upon it without hesitation or presenting it to reflection and reasoning. The word (kull) in His saying "every devil" is used in the sense of multiplicity, as will come soon at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and upon every lean camel﴾ [al-Hajj: 27] in this surah.

Page 193
It has already been discussed in the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And even if you brought to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-marid: an adjectival form (sifah mushabbahah) from maruda, with a damma on the ra', said of a task when one exceeds its bounds in it and reaches the extreme that surpasses what its practitioners are upon. It appears to be transformed from marada (with a fatha on the ra'), in the sense of maran, into the damma on the ra' to indicate that the description has become a disposition for him; so al-marid is an adjectival form, meaning: the one who is insolent in devilry.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 4:**

﴿It is decreed for him that whoever takes him as a guardian, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾

The clause ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْهِ أنَّهُ مَن تَوَلّاهُ﴾ through to its end is a second qualifier (ṣifa) of ﴿a rebellious devil﴾ (al-Hajj: 3). The pronoun in the genitive/oblique position is therefore referring to (shayṭān, devil). The same applies to the pronouns in ﴿أنَّهُ مَن تَوَلّاهُ فَأنَّهُ﴾. As for the two explicit pronouns in his saying ﴿يُضِلُّهُ ويَهْدِيهِ إلى عَذابِ السَّعِيرِ﴾, they refer to (man, the relative pronoun). That is: the devil misleads his follower away from the truth, and guides his follower to the punishment of the Blaze.

All ten canonical readings (al-qirā'āt al-'ashr) agree on reading (kutiba) with a ḍamma on the kāf, as a passive form (mabnī lil-nā'ib, in the passive voice). They also agree on the fatḥa of the two hamzas in his saying ﴿أنَّهُ مَن تَوَلّاهُ فَأنَّهُ يُضِلُّهُ﴾.

The verb "writing" (al-kitāba) is used metaphorically for establishment and necessity, meaning: it is necessary for him that he misleads his follower and directs him to the Blaze's punishment. The verb (kutiba 'alayhi), "it was written upon him," is applied to this necessity, meaning (wajiba 'alayhi), "it became obligatory for him." It is well known that when a covenant is meant to be carried out and not violated, it is written down in a document. Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza said:

*"Do desires undo what is in the scrolls?"*

[Page 194]

The pronoun in (annahu) refers to (shayṭān, devil), and it is not the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun of the matter, which is a dummy pronoun anticipating a following clause). This is because making it the pronoun of the matter does not suit the clause's position as the deputy subject (nā'ib fā'il) of (kutiba), since in that case it would be in the position of a verbal noun (ta'wīl maṣdar), and the pronoun of the matter requires a following clause. The two verbal nouns formed from his saying ﴿أنَّهُ مَن تَوَلّاهُ﴾ and his saying ﴿فَأنَّهُ يُضِلُّهُ﴾ are the deputy subject of the verb (kutiba) and are derived from it, marked by the conditional particle fa. That is: it was written upon him that he would mislead whoever took him as a guardian. (Al-tawallī) means taking a guardian (walī), that is, a helper (naṣīr), meaning whoever seeks help from him.

The word (man) is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) and not a conditional (shar̤iyya), because the meaning is an established statement and not a conditional dependent on a condition. It is the second subject (mubtada' thānī). The hidden pronoun in his saying (tawallāhu) refers to (man, the relative pronoun). The explicit object pronoun refers to (shayṭān, devil). That is: the one who takes the devil as a guardian, that devil misleads him.

The particle fa in his saying ﴿فَأنَّهُ يُضِلُّهُ﴾ is attached to the clause that functions as the predicate concerning (man, the relative pronoun). This makes the predicate clause concerning the relative pronoun resemble a conditional response (jawāb al-jazā'), since the relative pronoun resembles a conditional particle, in order to strengthen the statement. The verbal noun formed from his saying ﴿فَأنَّهُ يُضِلُّهُ ويَهْدِيهِ إلى عَذابِ السَّعِيرِ﴾ is in the estimation of a subject (mubtada'), which is the head of the clause functioning as the predicate concerning (man, the relative pronoun). The estimate is: his misleading of him and his guiding of him to the punishment of the Blaze. The predicate of this subject is implied, because it arises from the meaning of attributing the two verbs of misleading and guiding to the pronoun of the subject. The estimate is: both are established.

It is also permissible to make the fa in his saying ﴿فَأنَّهُ يُضِلُّهُ﴾ a fa of consequence (fā' al-tafrī'), and to make what follows it coordinated with ﴿مَن تَوَلّاهُ﴾, with the coordinated element being the intended object of the statement, as the consequence requires. The estimate is: it was written upon him that the misleading from him of his follower and the bringing of his follower to the punishment of the Blaze would follow. These are the two possible constructions of the verse's composition, and anything other than them is far-fetched.

Know that the composition in which the verse is arranged here does not follow the composition of His saying in surah Barā'a (al-Tawba): ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes God and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, to abide therein forever?﴾ (al-Tawba: 63)

[Page 195]

This is because the requirement of the verb of knowing (al-'ilm) differs from the requirement of the verb (kutiba). Therefore, in His saying ﴿مَن يُحادِدِ﴾ (al-Tawba: 63), (man) is necessarily conditional, and the discourse proceeds on the basis of the conditional, and the pronoun there in His saying (annahu) is the pronoun of the matter.

Since misguidance (al-ḍalāl) is well known in the sense of distance from good and righteousness, there was no need in this verse to mention the complement of the verb (yuḍilluhu) because the meaning is clear. The complement of the verb (yahdīhi) is mentioned, namely (ilā 'adhābi al-sa'īr, to the punishment of the Blaze), because its attachment to it is unusual, since the normal situation is that guidance is toward what benefits, not toward what harms and punishes.

In combining (yuḍilluhu wa yahdīhi, "misleads him and guides him"), there is the embellishment of antithesis (muḥassin al-ṭibāq bil-muḍādda), by the opposition of meanings. Among those included in this category is His saying ﴿Among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge﴾ (al-Hajj: 3), which has been counted as referring to al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, and it is said that the verse was revealed concerning him. He was very contentious; he would say: the angels are God's daughters, the Qur'an is the myths of the ancients, and God is unable to revive bodies that have decayed and become dust. Abū Jahl and Ubayy ibn Khalaf are also counted among them. As for one who says that the intended referent of His saying (man yujādilu, "one who disputes") is a specific individual, he has restricted the verse to that individual. There is no basis for such restriction, and it is nothing but restriction by the occasion of revelation (takhṣīṣ bil-sabab).

**[Page 196]**

Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 22, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop [of semen], then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make [it] clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whatever We will for a specified term. Then We bring you forth as infants, then [We let you grow] that you may reach your maturity. And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known.﴾

He repeated the address to mankind after having warned them of the convulsion of the Hour, and mentioned that among them are those who dispute about God without knowledge. So He repeated His address to them with an argument for the possibility of the Resurrection, and by analogy with something greater than it, which is the first creation. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Were We worn out by the first creation? Nay, they are in confusion about a new creation﴾ (Qaf 15). So the One who created man from nothing, brought him out of dust, then made him from water, then created him in wondrous stages, until He causes him to die, in the states of his body and in the states of his intellect and perception, is able to recreate him after his annihilation.

The entry of the polytheists at the very beginning of this address is more evident than their entry into the preceding address, because they are the ones who denied the Resurrection. So the purpose is to argue against them, and for this reason it has been said that the address here is specific to them. Their doubt about the Resurrection was framed with the conditional particle *in* (إنْ), even though their doubt was actual. This is to indicate that, since the situation is surrounded by proofs that nullify their doubt, it is treated as the situation of one whose doubt is not actual, as in His saying, ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you altogether because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ (al-Zukhruf 5). The sense of containment conveyed by *fi* (في, "in") is figurative: the attachment of doubt to them is likened to the enclosing of the container around the contained.

The clause ﴿indeed We created you from dust﴾ stands in the position of the answer to the condition, but its wording is not suitable to be the answer to this condition; rather it is the indication of the answer. The implied sense is: "Know," or "We will inform you," that it is possible, just as We created you from dust, like the crumbled remains to which bodies return after death. Or the implied sense is: "Look at the beginning of your creation, for indeed We created you from dust."

**[Page 197]**

That which was created from dust is the origin of the species, namely Adam, peace be upon him, and Eve. Then the capacity for reproduction was formed in Adam and his spouse, so creation came to be from the drop [of semen]; for this reason it is conjoined with *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then").

*Nutfah* (النُّطْفَةُ) is the name for a man's semen; it is of the pattern *fu'lah* in the sense of *maf'ul*, i.e., *mantuf* (poured out). *Al-natf* means dripping and pouring. *Alaqah* (العَلَقَةُ) is a piece of thick, soft clotted blood.

*Mudghah* (المُضْغَةُ) is a piece of flesh of the size that can be chewed. It is of the pattern *fi'lah* in the sense of *maf'ulah*, interpreted as "a quantity that is chewed." The *thumma* (ثُمَّ) by which the phrases ﴿then from a drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh﴾ are conjoined is a conjunction of distinct stages, so it indicates a real, genuine sequence in time.

The *min* (مِن, "from") repeated four times here is for origin, and its repetition is for emphasis. That man is created from a drop [of semen] is because it has been established in medical science that in the womb of the woman, during the period of menstruation, there is a part that is the place of the bodies prepared to form the embryo from them. This part of the womb is called in medical terminology *al-mabid* (المَبِيض, "the ovary"), with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *ba*, in the pattern of the noun of place, because it is the seat of very small eggs, which are very minute granules. These are, in the woman, in the position of the egg of the hen, or in the position of the granules of fish roe. They are enclosed in a delicate sphere like a sheath, called *al-huwaysilah* (الحُوَيْصِلَةُ), with a damma on the *ha*, in the diminutive form of *hawsalah*. It contains a fluid in which the egg swims. When the woman menstruates, the quantity of that fluid in which the egg swims increases, and this causes the sheath of the little sphere to burst. That fluid then begins to descend, carrying the egg swimming in it to a narrow canal called *buq Fallubiyus* (بُوقُ فُلُوبْيُوسَ, "the Fallopian tube"), named for its resemblance to a trumpet, and attributed to *Fallubiyus*, the name of its discoverer. It is the isthmus between the ovary and the uterus.

**[Page 198]**

When the man's water, which is the drop [of semen], descends into it after the flow of menstrual blood has ended, the egg is fertilized there, and its parts mix with the parts of the drop, which contains living spermatozoa. They remain with the egg moving for a period of seven days. During these days the egg undergoes development, taking shape by a kind of division, under the influence of a natural pressure. At the end of that period the egg reaches the uterus, and there it begins to take shape. After forty days the egg becomes a clot (*'alaqah*) the size of a large ant, its length from 12 to 14 millimeters. Then its shaping increases, and it becomes a small piece of flesh, which is what is called a lump (*mudghah*), its length three centimeters, in which the features of the face and nose appear very faintly, like lines. Then the shaping increases day by day until the embryo completes its term, and it then pushes toward coming out, which is birth.

His saying, ﴿formed and unformed﴾, is an adjective of *mudghah*. That is one of the developments of the lump, indicating the stages of the shaping of that lump: at first it is "unformed," meaning that the shape of creation does not yet appear in it. Then it becomes "formed," and what is meant is the shaping of the face and then of the limbs. For this reason, these two descriptions are not mentioned with the drop or the clot, since they do not have these two descriptions, unlike the lump. Since the lump has been placed among the beginnings of creation, it is established that both descriptions are necessarily attributes of the lump. Therefore, the interpretation of one who interprets "unformed" as "that whose creation was not completed, so it fell [as a miscarriage]" is not sound.

*Al-takhliq* (التَّخْلِيقُ) is a form that indicates the repetition of an action, i.e., creation after creation, i.e., shape after shape.

He placed the mention of "formed" before the mention of "unformed," contrary to the order in existence, because the "formed" is more directly relevant to the argument. He mentioned "unformed" after it, because it completes the proof and draws attention to the fact that its formation arose from non-existence. So both states are a proof of the power to originate, which is the purpose of the discourse. For this reason He followed it with His saying, ﴿that We may make [it] clear to you﴾, i.e., that We may manifest to you, if you reflect, a clear proof of the possibility of life after death.

The *lam* (لِ, "that") is for causation and is connected to what is implied in the answer of the condition, of a verb or the like, indicated by the clause ﴿indeed We created you from dust﴾ and so on. The implied verb is: "Know," or "We will inform you," or "Look."

The object of *linubayyina* (لِنُبَيِّنَ, "that We may make clear") is omitted so that the mind may go in its estimation in every direction that concerns explaining what is in these transformations of power and wisdom. That is, "that We may make clear to you Our power and Our wisdom." The clause ﴿and We settle﴾ (وَنُقِرُّ) is conjoined to the clause ﴿indeed We created you from dust﴾. He shifted from the past tense to the present tense to indicate the recalling of that state, because of its resemblance to the settling of bodies in graves and then their bringing forth from them by resurrection, as the infant comes out of the womb's resting place, though the durations of rest differ. Some embryos remain six months, and some remain longer than that, and this is what the general phrase ﴿for a specified term﴾ implies. The argument in all of this is that it is an origination after non-existence and an annihilation after existence, to make the possibility of the Resurrection clear by analogy and by contrast.

*Al-ajal* (الأجَلُ) is the fixed span set for completing some action, and what is meant here is the period of pregnancy.

*Al-musamma* (المُسَمّى) is the passive participle of *sammahu*, when one gives it a name. The term *musamma* is used metaphorically for what is specific and determined, to regulate matters that are not individually identified by a definite number or a reckoned time, by naming the thing with a feature of resemblance that distinguishes it from what resembles it.

**[Page 200]**

From this is the jurists' expression "the specified dower" (*al-mahr al-musamma*), i.e., the determined amount of a counted currency or a described item; and the notaries' phrase, "and he named for her such-and-such a dowry." For every child there is a term determined with God for its remaining in its mother's womb before its delivery. Most commonly it is completed in nine months and nine days, though the delivery may come sooner than that period due to some cause, and each is determined in the knowledge of God, exalted is He. This was discussed in His saying, ﴿for a specified term, then write it down﴾ (al-Baqarah 282), in Surah al-Baqarah.

He conjoined the clause ﴿then We bring you forth as infants﴾ with the particle *thumma* (ثُمَّ) to indicate the distance in rank, since bringing forth the embryo is the purpose; and His saying "as infants" (*tiflan*, طِفْلًا) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of ﴿We bring you forth﴾, meaning "in the condition of being infants." He used the singular *tiflan* because what is intended by it is the genus, so it is in the position of the plural.

The clause ﴿then [We let you grow] that you may reach your maturity﴾ (ثُمَّ لِتَبْلُغُوا أشُدَّكُمْ) is linked to the clause ﴿then We bring you forth as infants﴾ by the link of cause and effect; the *lam* is for causation, and what is caused is the verb ﴿We bring you forth as infants﴾. Since between infancy and the state of reaching maturity there are many stages, it is known that reaching maturity is the complete cause of the wisdom of bringing forth the infant. The stages before reaching maturity and after it have been indicated by His saying, ﴿and among you is he who is taken in death﴾ on the one hand, and ﴿and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age﴾ on the other. The *thumma* (ثُمَّ) in His saying ﴿then [We let you grow] that you may reach your maturity﴾ is an emphasis of the like of it in His saying ﴿then We bring you forth as infants﴾. This is what has become clear to me regarding the connection of this clause with what precedes it, though the exegetes have offered interpretations not free from objection, which al-Alusi has mentioned.

The reaching of maturity was made the cause because it is the strongest stage of man and the clearest manifestation of his gifts in body and intellect, and it is the most important aspect, as His saying after this indicates: ﴿so that he knows nothing after having known﴾. He thus made maturity (*al-ashudd*) as though it were the ultimate purpose of His shaping him.

*Al-ashudd* (الأشُدُّ) is the age of vigor and the gathering of powers. It was mentioned earlier in Surah Yusuf: ﴿When he reached his maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ (Yusuf 22). And it occurs in Surah al-Mu'min: ﴿then [We let you grow] that you may reach your maturity, then that you may become elders﴾ (Ghafir 67). There He conjoined the stage of old age to the stage of maturity, on the ground that old age is the goal of the living, because they love long life. That verse came in the context of favor, so the stage in which a person enjoys life is mentioned in it. It is not mentioned in the verse of Surah al-Hajj because it came in the context of argument for resurrection after non-existence, so it does not mention decline, and because those addressed by it are a specific group of polytheists who were in the stage of maturity; they were then warned, right after it, that among them were some who would be returned to the most abject age, which is the stage of old age, by His saying, ﴿and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age﴾. His saying ﴿and among you is he who is taken in death﴾ came as a parenthetical insertion, as an inductive survey of the stages that show the great power and wisdom of God, along with an indication that existence and non-existence intervene in the stages of man at the beginning and end, as the argument for resurrection requires. The meaning is: "And among you is he who dies before reaching some of the stages." As for death itself, it applies to every human being, not to some of them, and this was stated explicitly in Surah al-Mu'min: ﴿and among you is he who is taken in death before﴾ (Ghafir 67).

His saying ﴿and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age﴾ is the counterpart of His saying ﴿and among you is he who is taken in death﴾. He was silent about mentioning death after the most abject age, because it is known by way of the implication of the address (*lahn al-khitab*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 5 (part 2 of 2):

He made the loss of a person's knowledge at the most abject stage of life (ar-adhal al-'umur) a cause that leads to that stage, in the sense that it is a final cause (ʿillah ghāʾiyyah) of it. This is because it is among the things required by God's wisdom in the ordering of creation. So its occurrence is intended when a person is returned to the most abject stage of life, since the weakness of the bodily faculties entails the weakness of the intellectual faculties. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾ [Yasin: 68]. Thus al-khalq (creation) includes everything that belongs to the natural constitution and is not restricted to the body.

His words ﴿after knowledge﴾ mean: after he had known things before reaching the most abject stage of life. The "min" (from) that precedes "baʿda" (after) here is superfluous (mazīdah) for emphasis, according to the opinion of al-Akhfash and Ibn Malik, who do not restrict the superfluous "min" to the genitive of an indefinite noun following a negation or something similar. Alternatively, according to the majority (al-Jumhur), it is the "min" of origin (li-l-ibtidāʾ), and this origin is merely formal (ibtidāʾ ṣūrī), equivalent in meaning to emphasis. For this reason, "min" was not used in God's words ﴿so that he will know nothing after knowledge﴾ in Surat al-Nahl. The two verses have one meaning, so the use of "min" here is a variation (tafannun) within the context of the two lessons. The word "shayʾan" (anything) falls in a negative context and encompasses every item of knowledge, meaning that he acquires no new knowledge.

There are degrees of the weakness of the intellect according to how deeply a person sinks into the most abject stage of life. These reach the level where he completely loses the capacity to accept new knowledge. Before that there are varying degrees of weakness, such as forgetting things and confusion between known matters, and other such states.

﴿And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and brings forth every beautiful kind of growth﴾

This is a coordinate clause (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿Indeed, We created you from dust﴾. The address is to an unspecified audience, so it encompasses everyone who hears this speech.

[p. 203]

This is an elevation (irtiqāʾ) in the argument for resurrection after death, through analogical reasoning by example (qiyās al-tamthīl), since it is an argument based on a condition that is observed. For this reason it was introduced with the verb of seeing (fiʿl al-ruʾyah). This differs from the argument from the creation of man, whose origin is not observed. Therefore it was said concerning him ﴿Indeed, We created you from dust﴾, and so on. The point of the argument lies in His words ﴿but when We send down water upon it, it stirs﴾. It corresponds to His words in the first argument ﴿Indeed, We created you from dust﴾. Thus the lifelessness of the earth is equivalent to the death of a person, and its stirring, its swelling, and its bringing forth growth after that resembles revival after death.

Al-humūd (lifelessness) is close in meaning to al-khumūd. The lifelessness of the earth is its drying out and the disappearance of its vegetation, just as the lifelessness of a fire (humūd al-nār) is its extinguishing.

Al-ihtizāz (stirring) is movement upward. The stirring of the earth is a figurative depiction of the state in which its soil rises through the water, and the state in which its surface rises with the vegetation upon it, like one who stirs and moves upward.

Wa-rabat (and swelled): it acquired rubuww, with the "r" and the "b" both vowelled with a ḍammah, which is the increase of a thing. It is said: rabā yarbū rubuwwan. Here it is interpreted as the earth swelling from the splitting open of the plants and trees. Abu Jaʿfar (a Qur'anic reader) read ﴿wa-rabaʾat﴾ with a fatḥah on the hamzah after the "b", meaning it rose up (irtafaʿat). From this comes the saying "rabaʾa bi-nafsihi ʿan kadhā," meaning he elevated himself above such and such, in a figurative sense. It is a verb derived from the noun al-rabīʾah, which is the one who climbs a hill of the earth to look whether there is an enemy approaching them.

Al-zawj (kind/pair): it is a category of things. The name "zawj" was applied to it by analogy with the pair among animals, which is the male category and the female category, because each individual of one of the two categories pairs with an individual of the other category, becoming a pair. Each of them is called a zawj in this sense. Then the use of the term became common for one of the two categories, and then it was applied to every species and category, even if it is neither male nor female. Thus it is applied here to the species of plants.

Al-bahīj: that which is good to look at and delightful to the beholder. This description has been brought in as an embedded (idmāj) expression of divine favour (imtinān) in the midst of the argument, a favour through the beauty of the growing earth's appearance. For its being beautiful has no bearing on the argument, so it is pure favour, like His words ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6], and His words ﴿And We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5].

**[p. 205]**

This is a *fadhlaka* (summary recapitulation) of what has preceded, so the sentence is a *tadhyil* (concluding statement that sums up and confirms the preceding argument). The demonstrative ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ ("that") refers to what has preceded: the stages of human creation and its perishing, and the revival of the earth after its death and the sprouting of plants from it. The singular form of the address particle attached to the demonstrative (the *kaf* of *dhalika*) is used to address an unspecified addressee, following the pattern of His words ﴿And you see the earth lifeless﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. This is because attaching the demonstrative to the *kaf* of second-person singular address is the original form.

The prepositional phrase *bi-anna* ("because") is a predicate of the demonstrative, meaning: that occurred because Allah is the Truth, etc. The *bā'* (*bā'* of causation, *al-bā' al-sababiyya*) is causal. The meaning is: that human creation came about from dust and developed, and the sending down of water onto the lifeless earth and the sprouting of lush plants came about, because Allah is the true God, without any other. It is also permissible for the *bā'* to indicate association (*al-bā' al-mulābasa*), meaning that this creation and this lush growth were accompanied by the truth of Allah's divinity. This association is the association of evidence with what it proves. This reading is more elegant than taking the *bā'* to mean causation, and it is more comprehensive, because it includes the element of argument.

**[p. 205 continues]**

*Al-haqq* (the Truth) means what is established and beyond dispute, i.e., what truly exists. The restriction (*qasr*) here is *qasr idafi* (relative restriction), meaning: other than the things you worship, for they have no real existence. Allah says: ﴿They are only names you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. This argument is the foundation of the remaining proofs, because it refutes *shirk* (associating partners with Allah), which is the root of all the errors of its adherents, as Allah says: ﴿The postponement [of sacred months] is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawba: 37]. As for the remaining matters mentioned after His words ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾, they serve to demonstrate the possibility of resurrection.

The reason these five matters mentioned in this verse are connected to the circumstances of human creation and the revival of the earth is that those circumstances point to these five matters. This occurs either through the indication of the effect to its cause, with respect to Allah's existence and the confirmation of His power over everything, or through the indication of an analogy (*tamthil*) to what is analogized, and the occurrence of something indicates the possibility of its counterpart that has not yet occurred, with respect to Allah's reviving the dead, the coming of the Hour, and the resurrection. When the possibility of these things becomes clear, belief in their occurrence is affirmed, because nothing stood between them and belief in it except their assumption that it is impossible. Thus, the One who created humans from a prior non-existence is able to restore them after their dissolution, which came upon their existence, and this is even more fitting by way of reasoning.

Whoever created living beings after they had no life can certainly bring life into them, or into what remains of their traces, or create bodies similar to them and deposit their spirits in them, and this is even more fitting. When this is known, it becomes evident that the hour of this world's passing is certain to occur, by analogy with the non-existence of created things after their formation. And it becomes evident that Allah will restore them, by analogy with the bringing forth of offspring and the non-existence of their origin.

**[p. 206]**

The denial held by the polytheists concerning the occurrence of the Hour is treated as if it were non-existence, since it has no basis in any evidence. The form of negating the genus (*nafy al-jins*) in an explicit manner is a form of emphasis, because *la* (the negative particle of genus, *la al-nafiya li-l-jins*) in the context of negation has the same function as *inna* in the context of affirmation, and for this reason it operates on the same pattern in its grammatical effect.

The one meant by this verse is the same as the one meant by His saying earlier, ﴿And among people is one who argues about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil﴾ [22:3]. So the intended group is the stubborn and arrogant opponents who argue about God without knowledge after the warning of the Hour's quake has reached them. They likewise argue about God without knowledge after the proofs for the occurrence of the Resurrection have been made clear to them. What drives them to dispute about God when they hear the warning of the Hour is their lack of knowledge of what they are disputing and their following the whisperings of the devils. What drives them to dispute about God when the proofs for the Resurrection are clear is their lack of knowledge of what they are disputing, the absence of guidance, the absence of having received His law previously, arrogance against acknowledging proof, and love of misleading people from the path of God. This comes down to the meaning that their states differ, yet their possessors are one group, the group of polytheism and error. Among the pillars of this group are those counted in the interpretation of the first verse, such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

It has been said that the one meant in this verse by ﴿who argues about God﴾ is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and the mention of him is repeated to clarify the two conditions of his disputation. It has also been said that the one meant in this verse is Abu Jahl, just as it has been said that the one meant in the preceding verse is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith; so the verse is made specific by its occasion of revelation in the view of this speaker. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said that he is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. The meaning of his saying ﴿without knowledge﴾ was explained in the parallel of this verse. It has been said that what is meant by ﴿who argues about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil﴾ [22:3] are the imitators (al-muqallidun), with a kasra on the lam, from among the polytheists who follow what the lords of disbelief dictate to them. What is meant by ﴿who argues about God without knowledge or guidance﴾ are the imitated (al-muqallad), with a fatha on the lam, the leaders of disbelief.

Guidance (al-huda) is a verbal noun with the meaning of a noun in the genitive relation to its object, meaning "nor a guidance by which he is guided." This is the argument of an imitator when he is an imitator who is guided to the truth, like the followers of the messengers. This is below the rank of one who argues about God with knowledge. For this reason, mention of the former did not make mention of this one unnecessary.

The "clear Book" (al-kitab al-munir) refers to the books of the revealed laws, such as the Torah and the Gospel. This is like the way the People of the Book, before the coming of Islam, argued against the polytheists and the materialists (al-dahriyyun); it is argument with a clear Book.

"Clear" (al-munir) means that which makes the truth evident, likened to a lamp shining in the night.

The description of "Book" (kitab) with the attribute "clear" (munir) carries an allusion to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, since he would argue about Islam by comparing the clear Book of God with the book of the tales of Rustam and the book of the tales of Isfandiyar, which are dark and false.

Al-thany is the bending of a thing. It is said: "He turned the rein of his horse," when he twisted it to turn the head of the horse toward the direction he wished to face it. It is also used for inclining.

Al-'atf is the shoulder and the side. The phrase ﴿turning his side﴾ is a figure for arrogance and self-admiration. It is said: "He twisted his neck," when he turned away out of arrogance. This attribute fits the state of Abu Jahl, and therefore it has been said that he is the one meant here. The lam in His saying ﴿so that he may lead astray﴾ indicates the purpose of the argument; it is connected to "argues," meaning his aim in arguing is leading astray.

The path of God is the true religion.

[Page 209] His saying ﴿so that he may lead astray﴾ is with a damma on the ya, meaning that he leads people astray by his disputation. This disputant wants by his argument to make the common people imagine that Islam is false, so that they will not follow it. The singular pronoun in His saying "his side" and what is mentioned after it is in consideration of the wording of "one who" (man), although the meaning of those pronouns is plural.

The disgrace of this world (khizy al-dunya) is humiliation, and it is what befell them of killing on the Day of Badr and of killing and captivity after that. These are the ones who had not yet embraced Islam. The disgrace applies to what happened to Abu Jahl on the Day of Badr, when he was killed by the hands of two youths from the young men of the Ansar, who were the sons of 'Afra'. And [it applies to] 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud standing over his chest and slaughtering him, though in his greatness he never imagined that such three as these would come to his mind. The disgrace also applies to what befell al-Nadr ibn al-Harith of captivity on the Day of Badr and his being killed in patience (sabran) at a place called al-Uthayl near Madina, after the battle of Badr, as his sister Qutayla described him in her elegy for him, from an ode:

Patiently he is led to death, weary,
as a captive, bound, in chains.

Since this verse and its parallel that preceded it were revealed in Mecca without doubt, His saying ﴿for him in this world is disgrace﴾ is part of the reporting of the unseen, and it is one of the miracles of the Qur'an.

The making to taste of the punishment (idhaqat al-'adhab) is an imaginative representation (takhyil) for a metaphor by implication (al-makniyya). The clause ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ is a statement spoken by an omitted speaker, indicated by the structure of the speech, and it is a resumptive clause (mustaanifa); or it is in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the object in His saying "and We make him taste" (wa nudhiquhu).

[Page 210] "Sent forth" (qaddamat) means "sent ahead." He made his disbelief like a thing that he sent to the abode of recompense before he himself arrives there, so he finds it on the Day of Resurrection present, awaiting him. God says: ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾ [18:49]. The reference is to the punishment. The ba' is causal, and "ma" is a relative pronoun. Joined to the relative "ma" is His saying ﴿and that God is not at all unjust to the servants﴾, because it is in the interpretation of its verbal noun, meaning: and by the negation of God's injustice to the servants. That punishment is caused by these two matters, so its possessor deserves it, because it is the effect of God's justice, and He did not wrong him in what He made him taste.

The intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha) by its apparent meaning requires negation of severe injustice. The intended meaning is that injustice, as injustice, is a serious matter, so the intensive pattern was formed for it. Likewise, it is maintained in mentioning it wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. A group of later scholars have made it a habit to treat the intensification as relating to the negation rather than to the negated; but this is far-fetched.
