This describes another group among those who face the command to piety and the warning of the Hour: they neither remain unconvinced of the truth of the call of Islam, nor turn away from it entirely. Rather, they place themselves in a position of weighing their old religion against the religion of Islam. They accept the call of Islam and join its followers, and they watch what befalls them after entering Islam. If good comes to them as a result, they conclude that their old religion is not true, and that their gods have no power, for if they had power they would have avenged them for abandoning their worship. They believe that Islam is true. But if some evil of the worldly afflictions that arise in life, caused by ordinary causes, befalls them, they become angry with Islam and cast it off. They imagine that their gods have struck them with harm out of anger at their abandoning their worship, as God related about 'Ad when they said to their messenger: ﴿We say nothing except that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud: 54].

The worship in His words ﴿worships God on an edge﴾ means the worship of God alone, as evidenced by His words ﴿He calls, besides God, upon that which neither harms him nor benefits him﴾ [al-Hajj: 12]. It is apparent that the verse was revealed in Medina. In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And among the people is he who worships God on an edge﴾, he said: A man would come to Medina, and if his wife bore a boy and his mares foaled, he would say: "This is a good religion." But if his wife did not bear and his mares did not foal, he would say: "This is a bad religion."

In the narration of al-Hasan, it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, meaning the hypocrites from among those who had been polytheists, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. This is far-fetched, because those were concealing disbelief, so His words ﴿if good befalls him, he is reassured by it﴾ do not apply to them. Among those who may serve as an example of this group are the 'Uraniyyun, who embraced Islam and emigrated, but then found Medina unwholesome. The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to join the shepherd of the camels of charity outside Medina, so that they would drink of their milk and urine until they recovered. When they recovered, they killed the shepherd, drove off the camels, and fled. The Prophet (ﷺ) then sent pursuers after them until they caught up with them, and he ordered them to be executed, and they were killed.

In the hadith of the Muwatta': "A Bedouin embraced Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ), then he fell ill in Medina, so he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking to be released from his pledge, but he refused to release him. So he left Medina, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Medina is like a bellows: it expels its impurity and its goodness shines forth.'" He thus called him impurity, because he was not a firm believer.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) mentioned, on the authority of Muqatil, that a group from Asad and Ghatafan said: "We fear that God will not help Muhammad, and so the alliance between us and our allies among the Jews will be cut off, and they will not supply us with provisions." Then His words were revealed concerning them: ﴿Whoever thinks that God will never help him﴾ [al-Hajj: 15], and the verses that follow.

On the authority of al-Dahhak: the verse was revealed concerning those whose hearts were to be softened (al-mu'allafah qulubuhum), among whom were 'Uyayna ibn Hisn, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, and al-Abbas ibn Mirdas. They said: "We enter the religion of Muhammad; if we gain good, we will know that it is true, and if we gain otherwise, we will know that it is false." All of this arises from ignorance and from confusing worldly causes with otherworldly causes, and from treating coincidental concomitances as necessary connections. This is a great principle of the errors in matters of religion and matters of the world. And His words ﴿lost this world and the Hereafter﴾ are an excellent expression of this, since he cannot discern how to seek effects through their causes.

The "harf" of a thing is its edge and its side, whether it is elevated, like the edge of a mountain or a valley, or level, like the edge of a road. The word "harf" is also used for the flank of an army. Its plural is "tarf" on the pattern of "inab." Al-Firuzabadi said in al-Qamus: "It has no parallel except 'tall' and 'tilal.'"

His words ﴿worships God on an edge﴾ are an analogy for the state of one who wavers in his act of worship, intending to test its outcome by the condition of one who walks on the edge of a mountain or the edge of a valley, who is thus liable to slip down to its bottom and be overturned, i.e., to fall on his face.

The meaning of "iṭma'anna" is: he settled and became still in his place. Its verbal noun is "al-iṭmi'nan," and the noun of the verbal noun is "al-ṭuma'ninah." It was discussed in His words ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260] in Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning is: he remains steadfast in monotheism, rejoicing in the good that has befallen him. The steadfastness of such a person in faith makes him a believer once his wavering is removed, and the state of these people is close to the state of those whose hearts are to be softened.

"Al-inqilab" is the intransitive form of "qalabahu," meaning he overturned it, i.e., cast it into the opposite of its former condition, by making what was on top to be at the bottom, as a mold (al-qalib, with a fatha on the lam) is turned over. Thus "inqilab" is used in its literal sense, and the expression is an analogy. Our interpretation of "inqilab" here in this sense is what fits His words ﴿on his face﴾, i.e., he fell and was overturned onto it, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays: "He tumbles onto his chins among the trees of al-Kanahbal." And like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "This matter among the Quraysh will not be contested by anyone except that God will overturn him on his face." The particle of elevation ("'ala") is evident, and it also suits the analogy of the initial state of this person to the state of one who is on an edge. The term "inqilab" is frequently used to mean turning away from the direction one came toward to the direction from which one came, and this is a common metaphor, and the commentators interpreted it thus. But it is not appropriate to take it in that sense here, because for such a meaning one says "inqalaba 'ala 'aqibayhi" (he turned back on his heels), not "'ala wajhihi" (on his face), as God said: ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], since returning occurs only to a direction other than the direction of the face.

"Al-fitnah" is the disturbance of a situation and the anxiety of mind arising from the occurrence of an evil that cannot be repelled. It is the opposite of good.

The clause ﴿lost this world and the Hereafter﴾ is an inclusive apposition (badal al-ishtimal) of the clause ﴿turned over on his face﴾. The clause ﴿That is the manifest loss﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) between the clause ﴿turned over on his face﴾ and the clause ﴿He calls, besides God﴾ [al-Hajj: 12], which occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥal) relating to the pronoun in (inqalaba), meaning: he has fallen into polytheism.

"Al-khusran" is the loss of a part of the principal capital of trade. Thus the benefit of this world and the benefit of the Hereafter are compared to the capital of a merchant who strives to preserve it, because people desire to obtain it. Following this comparison, the attribution of loss to its owner is affirmed, and he is one of the synonyms of the capital of trade, which is the thing compared; thus the failure to gain the sought benefit is compared to the loss of capital.

The connection of the loss to "this world and the Hereafter" is by elision of a modifier; the estimated meaning is: he lost the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter. The loss of this world is due to the trial he suffered in it, and the loss of the Hereafter is due to his failure to benefit from its reward that he hoped for.

"Al-mubin" is that which contains within it what makes it clear to people that it is a loss, with the least reflection. The intended meaning is that it is a severe loss that cannot be concealed.

The use of the demonstrative (dhalika) serves to further distinguish the subject (musnad ilayhi) in the most complete distinction, to fix its meaning in minds. The pronoun "huwa" is a separating pronoun (ḍamir al-faṣl). The restriction derived from defining the predicate is an ascriptive restriction (qaṣr idda'i). It is claimed that the reality of manifest loss is confined to their loss. The purpose of the ascriptive restriction is to confirm the report and negate doubt about its occurrence. The separating pronoun reinforced the meaning of the restriction, and thus it served to strengthen the restricted predicate.

Surah 22, verse 12:

Page 215
﴿He calls, besides Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him. That is the far-reaching error.﴾

The clause ﴿He calls, besides Allah﴾ etc. is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in (inqalaba, "he turns back"). He placed harm before benefit in his saying ﴿that which does not harm him﴾, as a hint that he slipped away from Islam out of avoidance of harm, because he imagined that the harm that befell him was due to his Islam and due to the anger of the idols against him; so he returned to the worship of idols, reckoning that they would not harm him. In this hint there is a mockery of him, which becomes apparent through its being followed by the Exalted's saying ﴿and that which does not benefit him﴾, meaning: he is mistaken in calling upon the idols to remove harm from him so that he may benefit from their action. The meaning is: they do not do what repels harm nor what brings benefit.

The reference in His saying ﴿That is the error﴾ is to the calling (du'ā') understood from (yad'ū, "he calls").

What is said regarding the demonstrative pronoun, the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) and the restrictive construction (qaṣr) is like what preceded in His saying ﴿That is the manifest loss﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 11].

Al-ba'īd (the far-reaching): that which exceeds the known limit in the extent of error, i.e., it is the error to which no other error is comparable, because he worships what has no sufficiency at all.

This clause is in a position of a second circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). Its meaning is an escalation in exposing the misguidance of those who worship idols. Having already shown them that they worship what offers them no benefit, he went further and showed that they worship what contains harm.

[p. 216]

So the point of escalation is the content of the clause ﴿that which cannot harm him﴾ (Q. 22:12). It is as if it were said: "one who cannot harm him, but rather from whom harm will befall him." This is because worshipping idols harms the worshipper in this world, through turning to them when in need, so that his time is wasted in seeking what is not attained, and it harms him in the Hereafter, through being cast into the Fire.

Since the harm that comes from the idols is not harm arising from their own action, but rather harm that accompanies them, He established the harm through the mode of idafa (attribution to a pronoun, a possessive relation) and not through the mode of isnad (predication, attributing an action to an agent). Thus He said, ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾, and He did not say "who harms and does not benefit." This is because idafa is broader than isnad, so no contradiction arises between His saying ﴿that which cannot harm him﴾ (Q. 22:12) and His saying ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾.

His saying that its harm is "nearer" than its benefit is a kinaya (metonymy) for the harm being pure and unmixed, and for the absence of any benefit from it. This is because the nearer thing is attained before the distant one, so it follows that nothing accompanies it except harm.

The lām in His saying (لَمَن, "for whoever") is the lām al-ibtidā' (the inceptive lām, the emphatic lām of beginning). It serves to emphasize the content of the clause that follows it, so the lām al-ibtidā' conveys the emphasis that inna conveys. It has been fronted from its place, since its proper position is to enter upon a ṣila (relative clause) of the relative pronoun. The original would be: "he calls upon whoever whose harm is nearer than his benefit."

It is also permissible to consider the lām as entering upon the relative pronoun man, with the verb "yad'ū" (calls upon) being suspended from operating (ta'līq, suspension of the verb's government) because of the entry of the lām al-ibtidā', based on the correct view that ta'līq is not restricted to verbs of the heart (af'āl al-qulūb).

The clause ﴿an evil patron, and an evil companion﴾ (labi'sa al-mawlā wa-la-bi'sa al-'ashīr) is an expression of blame (inshā' dhamm) directed at the idols they call upon, stating that they are the worst of patrons and the worst of companions. This is because the nature of a patron (mawlā) is to bring benefit to his client, and the nature of a companion (ʿashīr) is to bring good to his associate. If this fails to occur from either of them only rarely, it is a reproach and a disgrace. But if it is consistently so from them, then that is the worst of patrons.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 14:

Page 217
﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.﴾
This is the counterpart of His saying ﴿And We will make him taste the punishment of the Blaze on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Hajj: 9] and His saying ﴿He has lost both this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]. So the sentence is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD). It mentions only the reward of the Hereafter for the believers, without mentioning their condition in this world, because that is of no importance to them nor in the view of the religion. The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the preceding discourse from His saying ﴿And among the people is he who disputes about Allah without knowledge﴾ [al-Hajj: 3] up to this point. It is an interjection (i'tiraD) between the sentences whose purpose is unified. It contains the sense of a general explanation (ta'lil ijmali) for the differing conditions of people in this world and the Hereafter. Allah's doing what He wills is the bringing into existence of the causes of the actions of His servants within the established order (sunnah nizam) of this world, and His making clear good and evil, and His arranging of reward and punishment. None encompasses the details of that except Allah, the Exalted.

**[Page 218]**

The placement of this verse is obscure, though its meaning is clear. Let us begin by explaining its placement, then explain its meaning, since there is a connection between the two.

It is possible that its placement is an inceptive resumption (*istīnāf ibtidā'ī*, a new sentence beginning a fresh topic), intended to mention a third group other than the two groups mentioned earlier, in His saying, ﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 3], and His saying, ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 11]. This third group consists of people who embraced Islam, were slow in seeing the victory of the Muslims, and so despaired of it. They were angered by their own haste to enter Islam without waiting. These are the hypocrites (*munāfiqūn*).

It is also possible that its placement is a concluding appendage (*tadhyīl*) to His saying, ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 11], after other sentences were inserted between that sentence and this one. In that case the meaning is: the group who worship Allah on an edge, and of whom He says, ﴿he has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 11], are people who think that Allah will not help them in this world or in the Hereafter if they remain upon Islam. As for their thinking that help is absent in this world, it is because they have despaired of help due to their impatience. As for the Hereafter, it is because they do not believe in resurrection. For this reason the verb (*lan yanṣuruhu*, "He will not help him") is linked with the prepositional phrase ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾, indicating that it is the object of the loss in His saying, ﴿he has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 11]. Indeed, the absence of help is a loss in this world, through the occurrence of its opposite, and in the Hereafter, through the impossibility of reward in the Hereafter according to their disbelieving belief. These are polytheists who are hesitant.

This possibility is strengthened by the change in the style of speech. It is not joined by the conjunction *wa* (and), as His saying, ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 11], was joined, and the phrase (*wa min al-nās*, "and among the people") is not repeated as it was in mentioning the two earlier groups. The intended purpose of the verse is then to threaten this group. Thus the expression for this group with His saying (*man kāna yaẓunn*, "whoever thinks") etc. is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (*iẓhār fī maqām al-iḍmār*), since the expected form would be to use a pronoun referring to that group, saying after His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 14]

**[Page 219]**

﴿So let him extend a rope to the sky﴾ etc., with the hidden pronoun in (*falyamdud*, "let him extend") referring back to ﴿one who worships Allah on an edge﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 11]. The shift from pronoun to explicit noun is for two reasons. The first is the distance of the antecedent. The second is to draw attention to the fact that his worship of Allah on an edge arises from his thinking that Allah will not help him in this world or the Hereafter if he insists on continuing to follow Islam, since he is not certain of the promise of victory for the Muslims. The pronoun of object in (*yanṣuruhu*) refers to ﴿one who worships Allah on an edge﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 11] under both possibilities. The noun (*al-samā'*, "the sky") is intended in its well-known meaning under both possibilities as well, following what al-Qurṭubī transmitted from Ibn Zayd (namely 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam) that he said, concerning His saying, ﴿So let him extend a rope to the sky﴾, "It is the well-known sky, meaning the canopy." The meaning is: let him stretch a rope upward to the sky, tied to it, then let him cut it, so that he falls from the sky and is torn into pieces, and his action does not avail him anything in removing his rage.

The object of (*yaqṭa'*, "let him cut") is omitted, as the context indicates it. The sense is: "then let him cut it," i.e., let him cut the means (*al-sabab*).

The imperative in His saying, ﴿So let him extend a rope to the sky﴾, is for incapacitation (*li-l-ta'jīz*), so it is known that making the answer depend on the fulfilment of a condition that will never occur, as in His saying, ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass beyond them﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 33].

As for drawing out the meaning of the verse from its construction, it is woven with wonderful concision. It likens the state of this group, who conceal disbelief and display Islam in rage, or whose state is one of hesitation between remaining among the Muslims and returning to the disbelievers, to the state of one enraged at what he has done. So it is said to them: "You must do what people like you do when rage has filled them and the paths of relief have become narrow for them. Extend a rope as far as a rope can reach, cling to it at the highest place, then cut it, and you will fall to the ground."

**[Page 220]**

This is mockery of them, in that they will find no sufficiency in any of their actions, and a warning that their trial in this world will continue along with loss in the Hereafter.

It is also possible that the verse refers to another group who embraced Islam during the time of Islam's weakness and were slow to see victory, so their hearts became constricted and Satanic thoughts occurred to them that they should abandon Islam and return to disbelief. Allah rebuked them and threatened them: if they are in despair of help in this world and doubtful about attaining the reward of the Hereafter, then their apostasy from Islam does not harm Allah or His Messenger, nor does it plot against the religion. And if they wish, let them choke themselves, and then see whether choking removes their rage. Perhaps these are among the hypocrites.

Thus the placement of the verse on this view is that of an inceptive resumption, to mention another group resembling the one who worships Allah on an edge. The connection is evident.

On this view it follows that the pronoun in ﴿Allah will help him﴾ refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is reported from Ibn 'Abbās, and it was chosen by al-Farrā' and al-Zajjāj. This entails, under all the possibilities, an allusive reminder to sincere believers not to despair of Allah's help in this world and the Hereafter, or in the Hereafter alone. Allah says, ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they pledged to Allah. Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow, and among them is he who awaits, and they have not altered in the least﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 23], ﴿That Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness and punish the hypocrites﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 24], and so on.

**[Page 221]**

The (*sabab*, "rope/means") is the rope. It was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿And their means of support were cut off from them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166], in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

Regarding (*al-qaṭ'*, "cutting"): it is said that it is applied to choking, because it cuts off the breath.

The (*mā*) is verbal-masdarial (*maṣdariyya*), i.e., (*ghayẓahu*, "his rage"). The interrogation with (*hal*) is denial (*inkārī*), and it suspends the verb (*falyanẓur*, "let him see") from acting. The seeing is of the heart. The action is called a plot (*kayd*) because it resembles a plot in that he does it in order to plot against the Muslims, in the ironic metaphorical sense (*isti'āra tahakkumiyya*), since he does not thereby plot against the Muslims but harms himself by it.

The majority read (*thumma li-yaqṭa'*, "then let him cut") with the lām of (*li-yaqṭa'*) sukūn-vowelled, being the lām of command. When it occurs at the beginning of a word, it is kasra-vowelled; when it occurs after a conjunction other than (*thumma*), it is sukūn-vowelled, as in ﴿And let there be among you a community﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 104]. When it occurs after (*thumma*), both forms are permitted. Ibn 'Āmir, Abū 'Amr, Warsh from Nāfi', Abū Ja'far, and Ruways from Ya'qūb read it with a kasra on the lām.

Since these verses included the clarification of the states of people in the face of the call of Islam, in a way that leaves no ambiguity after it, it was followed by a note of emphasis on this clarification. That clarification was likened to itself as a *kināya* (metonymy) for its reaching the utmost limit within its kind, such that nothing clearer than it can be found. The meaning is: "Like this sending down, We sent down the Qur'an as clear signs." Thus the sentence is conjoined to the sentences before it by *ʿaṭf gharaḍ ʿalā gharaḍ* (conjunction of one purpose upon another), and the connection is evident, so it is an *istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī* (an independent resumptive sentence). It is conjoined to the note of emphasis:

The *taʿlīl* (causal explanation) of its sending down in this manner is ﴿that Allah guides whom He wills﴾, i.e., by the Qur'an. The lam of causation is elided, and omitting the preposition before *anna* (that) is *muṭṭarid* (regular, consistent).

[Page 222]

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated others with God, indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed God is witness over all things.﴾

This is a summation (*fadhlakah*) of what came before. The preceding verses dealt with the conditions of those who hesitated to accept Islam, and this prompted the question of how the different communities stand in relation to one another across their various religions, and of which religion is the true one. Each nation claims that it is upon the truth and that others are upon falsehood, and they dispute about this. This verse therefore explains that the judgment between the people of the religions concerning what they dispute will take place on the Day of Resurrection, since arguments did not settle the matter for them in this world.

This statement, with its brevity, operates as a committing of the matter to God (*tafwid*). Such an expression can serve as an allusion (*kinaya*) to the speaker's affirmation of his own path and his condemnation of his opponent's path, because such a committing of the matter to God is not made except by one who is confident that he is upon the truth. It is like the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿For us are our deeds and for you your deeds. There is no argument between us and you. God will gather us, and to Him is the destination﴾ [al-Shura: 15]. This belongs to the category of indirect allusion (*kinaya ta'ridiyya*). The mention of the believers, the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians has already occurred in the verse of al-Baqarah and the verse of al-Ma'idah.

[Page 223]

This verse adds the mention of the Magians and the polytheists because the two preceding verses were in the context of explaining the excellence of monotheism (*tawhid*) and faith in God and the Last Day in every age and every nation. The mention of the Magians and the polytheists is added in this surah because this verse is directed toward explaining the committing of judgment to God regarding the disputes among the religious communities, and the Magians and the polytheists are not among the people of faith in God and the Last Day.

As for the Magians, they are a people of a religion that affirms two gods: a god of good and a god of evil. They are the people of Persia. Their religion branches into sects that return to these two principles. The oldest of the Magian sects was founded by Kayumarth, who was the first king of Persia in ancient times, believed to be before the time of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). For this reason he is also called by the title "Jal Shah," whose meaning is "king of the earth." However, this is not established on a scientifically verified basis. The era of Kayumarth was called "Zurvan," meaning eternity. Thus the origin of Magianism was the people of the religion called Zurvanism, which affirms two gods: Yazdan and Ahriman. They said: Yazdan existed alone in eternal being, and he was luminous, and he remained so for nine thousand and ninety years. Then a thought occurred to him: if an opponent were to arise for him, how would the matter be? From this thought there arose a new existent of darkness named Ahriman, who is the god of darkness, disposed toward evil and harm. Abu al-'Ala al-Ma'arri alluded to this in his *Luzumiyyat*, saying:

Some people said: their claim is false,
so fear God and do not make such claims.

Yazdan thought in his heedlessness,
and from his thought Ahriman was fashioned.

Between Ahriman and Yazdan there then arose enmity and war forever. Afterward, sects arose within this religion that were given names, and their teachings were close to one another.

[Page 224]

The most famous of them is the sect of Zarathustra, who appeared in the sixth century before the birth of Christ, and through him Magianism became well known. He named the god of good "Ahura Mazda," or "Ardmuzd," or "Hormuz," and named the god of evil "Ahriman." He made the god of good light and the god of evil darkness. Then he called people to worship fire as a manifestation of the god of good, which is light. He expanded the law of Magianism and composed for it a book which he named the "Zend-Avesta." Among the principles of his law is avoiding the worship of images. Then there appeared among the Magians the sect of Manichaeism (*al-Manawiyya*), attributed to Mani, who appeared in the time of Shapur ibn Ardashir, king of the Persians, between the years 238 and 271 CE. There also appeared among the Magians the sect of Mazdakism (*al-Mazdakiyya*), attributed to Mazdak, who appeared in the time of Qubad between the years 487 and 523 CE. It is a sect close to Manichaeism, and it is the last sect to have appeared in the development of Magianism before the Islamic conquest of the lands of Persia. Magianism bears some resemblance in its origin to polytheism, but it differs from it in prohibiting the worship of stones, and in that it has a book, so they resembled the People of the Book in this respect. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning them: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book," meaning in accepting the *jizya* (poll tax) from them without compelling them to embrace Islam, as polytheists are compelled to enter Islam. Some of this has already been mentioned at the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿God said, "Do not take two gods"﴾ [al-Nahl: 51] in Surat al-Nahl.

The particle *inna* is repeated at the beginning of the clause that serves as the predicate of the first *inna*, as a verbal emphasis (*tawkid lafzi*) of the predicate, because of the long separation between the subject of *inna* and its predicate. The predicate being a clause is a good emphasis because of this long separation. Earlier there occurred the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, indeed We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30] in Surat al-Kahf. When the separation is not long, emphasis by repeating *inna* is less good, as in the verse of Jarir:

Indeed the caliph, indeed God has clothed him
with the robe of a king, by which the seals are carried.

It is not good, when the subject of the clause that is the predicate of the first *inna* is a pronoun referring back to the first *inna*'s subject, as one says: "Indeed Zayd, indeed he is standing." Rather, there must be a difference so that the second emphasized element is other than the first, and then repeating the emphasized element is acceptable even if the first emphasized element was sufficient.

*Al-fasl* means judgment, that is, He will judge between them regarding what they differ about concerning the correctness of their religion.

The clause ﴿indeed God is witness over all things﴾ is a new independent statement (*istinaf ibtida'i*), to inform that God's knowledge encompasses their conditions, their disagreements, and the sound of their statements.

[Page 226]

This is a resumptive sentence (*jumla mustaʾnafa*, a sentence newly begun) introducing an argument for God's sole divinity (*infirād Allāh bil-ilāhiyya*). It is connected in meaning to His words ﴿He calls upon, besides God, that which neither harms him nor benefits him﴾ [22:12], up to His words ﴿Wretched is the protector and wretched is the companion﴾ [22:13], in the way that a proof is connected to what it is meant to establish. The indications of the conditions of all created things, rational and inanimate alike, bear witness to God's singularity in divinity. That indication also testifies to the falsehood of the claim of one who calls upon, besides God, that which neither harms nor benefits him. What lies between these two sentences is a digression (*istiṭrād*) and a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtirāḍ*).

The seeing (*al-ruʾya*) here is cognitive, meaning knowing. The address is to an unspecified audience.

The interrogation is one of denial (*istifhām inkārī*). It denies to the addressees that they know what the conditions of created things indicate about God's sole divinity. It is also permissible that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and that the interrogation is affirmative (*taqrīrī*), since the Prophet's ﷺ knowledge of this is established from Surah al-Ra'd and Surah al-Nahl. The meaning of this prostration has already been discussed in those two surahs.

Prostration (*al-sujūd*) has been used in both its literal sense (*ḥaqīqa*) and its figurative sense (*majāz*). This is sound, even though al-Zamakhshari rejected it. We have verified this in the ninth introduction (*al-muqaddima al-tāsiʿa*). The prostration attributed to many people is the true, literal prostration, for had that not been intended, there would have been no reason to qualify its attribution to "many of mankind" rather than to all of them. The reason for this division is that the prostration of non-human existents is nothing other than the indication of those existents that they are subjected to God's creation, so prostration is used metaphorically for the state of subjugation and submission. As for the indication of the human condition of servanthood to God, Most High, since the aversion of many people from prostrating to God has entered into it, and their engagement in prostration to idols, as is the state of the polytheists, the literal prostration of the latter overshadows the figurative prostration that indicates their servanthood to God. This is because direct observation is stronger than indication by condition. Thus prostration was not attributed to them in the way it was attributed to the rest of existents, even though it is present in their condition as it is in the condition of the other created things.

[Page 227]

The clause ﴿and many have deserved the punishment﴾ is a parenthetical insertion introduced by the conjunction *wāw*. The clause ﴿the punishment has become due upon him﴾ is a metonymy (*kināya*) for abandoning prostration to God, meaning: the punishment has become due upon them because they did not prostrate to God. God has decreed in His judgment that the polytheist deserves the punishment of the Fire. Thus those who associated partners with God and turned away from singling Him out in worship have had the punishment become due upon them, according to what God has decreed and warned them of.

The clause ﴿And whomever God humiliates, for him there is no honourer﴾ is a second parenthetical insertion introduced by *wāw*. The meaning is that God has humiliated them by making the punishment due to them, so they will find no one to honour them with victory or intercession.

The clause ﴿Indeed God does whatever He wills﴾ stands in the position of a causal justification for the two parenthetical clauses. This is because the presence of the emphasizing particle (*ḥarf al-tawkīd*) at the beginning of a sentence, when there is no denier, restricts the particle's function to conveying emphasis on the matter (*al-ihtimām*). From this arises the meaning of causation and justification, so *inna* takes the place of a particle of causation or reason. This is a place of prostration among the prostrations of the Qur'an, by the agreement of the jurists.

[Page 228]

Following the context of the surah, the connection of its verses, and their order of revelation, these verses were revealed in close connection with the verses before them. The sentence ﴿These two adversaries﴾ therefore falls in the position of an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question). The reason is that His saying ﴿and many deserve the punishment﴾ (Al-Hajj: 18) raises the question of someone asking about some details of the punishment that is due to many people who did not prostrate to God, so this sentence came to explain that. It is therefore an explanatory resumptive clause. The dual demonstrative ﴿these two﴾ refers to what is conveyed by God's saying ﴿and many people, and many deserve the punishment﴾ (Al-Hajj: 18), namely the division of those mentioned into two groups: people of monotheism and people of polytheism, as His saying ﴿and many people, and many deserve the punishment﴾ requires, since those people are two groups: a group that prostrates to God, and a group that prostrates to other than Him. The demonstration is thus directed at what is understood from the speech, by treating it as if it were seen with the eye, and many examples of this occur in speech.

*Al-ikhtisam* (mutual disputing) is a reflexive form (*if'tial*) derived from *al-khusumah*, which means arguing and disagreeing verbally. One says *khasamahu* and *ikhtasama*. It is one of the verbs that imply two sides, so no bare form of it is heard except when it is intended to mean prevailing in the dispute, since by that the agent becomes one party. His saying ﴿and do not be a disputant for the betrayers﴾ (An-Nisa: 105) has already been mentioned in Surah An-Nisa. The disputing of the two groups of believers and others is known to the listeners, and its clamour has filled the space. The statement that the two groups are "two adversaries" is therefore given not to convey new information, but as a preparation for the detail in His saying ﴿As for those who disbelieved, garments of fire will be cut for them﴾. So what is meant by this verse includes all believers and all their opponents in religion.

It is reported in the two Sahihs (of Bukhari and Muslim) from Abu Dharr that he used to swear that this verse ﴿These two adversaries, who dispute concerning their Lord﴾ was revealed concerning Hamzah and his two companions, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and 'Utbah ibn al-Harith, who fought in single combat at the Battle of Badr against Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah.

[Page 229]

In Sahih al-Bukhari it is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: "We are the first to kneel before the Most Merciful for the dispute on the Day of Resurrection." Qays ibn 'Ubad said: "It is concerning them that this verse was revealed: ﴿These two adversaries, who dispute concerning their Lord﴾." He said: "They are those who fought in single combat at the Battle of Badr: 'Ali, Hamzah, 'Ubaydah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah." There is nothing in 'Ali's statement that the verse was revealed on the day of Badr, but that addition is inserted into the words of Qays ibn 'Ubad. On this basis, this verse is Medinan, and so ﴿these two﴾ is a reference to two groups present in the minds of the addressees. The presence of the story of these two in their minds, which is so remarkable, was treated as if it were being witnessed, to the extent that the demonstrative pronoun designed for the witnessed was used to refer back to it. This usage occurs in the speech of eloquent writers. An example is the saying of al-Ahnaf ibn Qays: "I went out to help this man," meaning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, in the story of Siffin.

The more evident view is that Abu Dharr meant by the revelation of the verse concerning these people that those six men were the most prominent example and the most famous instance of this general meaning. So he expressed it with "revelation," meaning that they are among those intended by the meaning of the verse. Similar usage is common in the speech of earlier scholars. The disputing in the first sense is literal (*haqiqi*), while in the second sense the term "disputing" is applied to single combat figuratively by metonymy (*majaz mursal*, a figure where a related meaning is used), because disputing over religion is the cause of that combat.

The word *khasm* (adversary) is applied to one person and to a group when their dispute is one, as in His saying ﴿Has the news of the adversaries reached you, when they climbed over the wall into the sanctuary?﴾ (Sad: 21). Out of regard for the dual form of the word, the demonstrative designed for the dual, ﴿هَذانِ﴾ (*hadhani*, "these two"), was used, and out of regard for the number, the plural pronoun was used in His saying ﴿اخْتَصَمُوا﴾ (*ikhtasamu*, "they disputed") in ﴿they disputed concerning their Lord﴾. The meaning of ﴿in their Lord﴾ is "concerning His nature and attributes," so the speech contains an apparent ellipsis of a noun (*hadhf mudaf*, omission of a governed noun). Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read ﴿هَذانِ﴾ with a light *nun*, while Ibn Kathir read it with a doubled *nun*. Both are dialectal forms.

[Page 230]

*At-taqti'* (cutting into pieces) is an intensified form of cutting, which is separating some parts of a thing from the rest. The intended meaning is cutting a piece of cloth. This is because whoever wants to make a shirt or something similar cuts from the piece of cloth what suffices for the purpose. The form of intensification was used for the cutting to indicate speed in preparing this for them, so that garments of fire are made for them. Garments of fire are garments that burn the skin, and this is among the matters of the Hereafter.

*Al-hamim* is water of extreme heat.

*Al-isharu* means melting by fire or by the heat of the sun. One says *asharahu* and *sahharahu*. ﴿ما في بطونهم﴾ (*ma fi buṭūnihim*, "what is in their bellies") means their intestines, that is, it is intensely penetrating to their insides.

*Al-maqami'* is the plural of *miqma'ah*, with a kasra on the *mim*, in the pattern of an instrument noun for a tool of restraint. *Al-qam'* means restraining something with violence. *Al-miqma'ah* is a whip, meaning that they are struck with whips of iron. The meaning of ﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it, from distress, they will be returned into it﴾ is that, because of the intensity of what distresses them, that is, what prevents them from breathing, they try to get out, but they are returned into it, so they experience the pain of disappointment. And it is said to them: "Taste the punishment of the burning."

*Al-harid* is a great and widespread fire. This statement is a humiliation for them, since they already know that they will taste it.

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they were guided to the good of speech, and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.﴾

The apparent expectation was that this statement would be joined with the conjunction *wa* (and) to the sentence ﴿So those who disbelieved, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], because it is the counterpart of that sentence in the detailed explanation of the summary in ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], by saying: "And those who believe and do righteous deeds, Allah will admit them into gardens," and so on. But the discourse departs from that style to this arrangement, to draw the ears to this statement, since it comes as an independent beginning, opened with the particle of emphasis (inna) and crowned with the Name of Majesty (Allah). The eloquent speaker does not miss the recognition that this statement is a counterpart to the one before it, in the detailed explanation of the summary ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], describing the state of the believers in contrast with the state of those who disbelieved, in place, in clothing, and in the address of honour. So His saying ﴿Allah will admit those who believe﴾ and what follows corresponds to His saying ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, from distress, they will be returned into it﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. His saying ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. His saying ﴿and their clothing therein will be silk﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. His saying ﴿And they were guided to the good of speech﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22], for that is of the wicked speech.

Al-tahliyah (adornment) means placing ornaments on the parts of the body. One says *hallāhu*, meaning he dressed him in ornaments, like *jalbaba* (to dress in a jilbab).

Al-asawir is the plural of *aswira*, which is itself the plural of *siwar* (bracelet). The plural of a plural indicates abundance, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and will wear green garments﴾ [al-Kahf: 31], in Surat al-Kahf.

[p. 232]

The *min* in His saying *min asāwir* (with bracelets) is superfluous (*zā'ida*), for emphasis. Its rationale is that since men are not known to be adorned with bracelets, the report that they will be adorned with bracelets would be open to doubt as to whether the literal meaning is intended; so the emphatic particle is brought to convey the literal meaning. For this reason, *asāwir* is in the position of the second object of *yuḥallawna* (they will be adorned).

*Wa-lu'lu'an* (and pearls) was read by Nafi', Ya'qub, and 'Asim in the accusative, as a conjunction with the grammatical position (*maḥall*) of *asāwir*, meaning: they will be adorned with pearls, i.e., necklaces and the like. The rest read it in the genitive, as a conjunction with the wording (*lafẓ*). The meaning is: bracelets of gold and bracelets of pearls. It is written in the codex with an *alif* after the second *wāw* in this surah, so the genitive reading differs from the written codex. But recitation is transmission and narration, so following the orthography is not obligatory for one who transmits what differs from it. A similar word is written without an *alif* in Surat Fatir. Those who read it in the accusative also departed from the orthography of the codex, relying on their transmission. The sense of emphasis is the same in both readings, because the emphasis relates to the whole sentence, not specifically to the conjoined word, so there is no need to repeat the emphatic particle with the conjoined word.

Al-lu'lu' is pearl (*durr*). It is also called *jumān* and *jawhar*. It is white and yellow grains with a sheen, extracted from inside a snail-like aquatic animal, set within a shell of two valves closed around it, which it opens by a vital movement to absorb the water in which it swims. Its shell is called *ṣadaf*. A bead with a sheen is found inside the animal, varying in size, and in clarity and whiteness of colour. This animal is found in several seas: such as the Gulf (Persian Gulf, known as the Two Seas), the Gulf of Gabès, and the shore of the island of Djerba in Tunisia. The best and finest is that found in the Two Seas, where the Tigris and Euphrates rivers discharge. Skilled divers extract it [p. 233] from the bottom of the sea by diving. The diver, tied to a rope held by a man on the boat, dives, and after a moment sufficient for gathering, is hauled up.

The description of this appears in the words of al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas or al-A'sha:

*Lujjāna al-baḥrī jā'a bihā ghawwāṣuhā min luggat al-baḥr*
*Nawwaṣa al-nahārā al-mā'u ghāmiruhu wa rafīquhu bi'l-ghayb lā yadrī*

And Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said, describing a pearl:

*Fa-jā'a bihā mā shi'ta min laṭamiyya 'alā wajhihā mā'u al-Furāt yamūj*

It is also indicated by the verse in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿It is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh meat and extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾ [al-Nahl: 14].

Since adornment is other than clothing, the word for clothing is mentioned after *yuḥallawna* in the form of a noun, rather than *yalbasūna* (they will wear), so that the sense of permanence and continuity is conveyed; just as the form *yuḥallawna* indicates that adornment is renewed with various kinds and colours. From the generality of both forms, it is understood that the like of them is realized on the other side, so there is in the speech *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which one of two parallel elements is omitted and understood from the other). It is as if it were said: they will be adorned with them, and their adornment is of bracelets of gold, and their clothing therein is silk, which they will wear.

Al-ḥarīr (silk) is applied to what is woven from silk threads, as here. The original meaning of the name *ḥarīr* is the threads that a particular worm secretes from its saliva, wrapping them round itself layer upon layer, like a ball that is tightly bound, resembling the shape of a peanut, enclosing the worm like a nut. The worm remains in it for a period until it transforms into a moth with two wings, which pierces that cocoon and exits it. The threads are obtained from that cocoon by placing it in hot water at boiling point until its binding weakens because of the dissolution of the gummy saliva substance that holds it, and then they draw out a single long thread. From those threads, garments are woven [p. 234] that are extremely soft and lustrous. Silk garments are the finest garments in the world, both in ancient and modern times. Their earliest appearance was in the land of China, about five thousand years ago, where the mulberry tree abounds, because the silkworm does not produce silk except when its fodder is mulberry leaves, and it mostly builds its cocoons on mulberry branches. The people other than the Chinese did not know how to raise silkworms, so they obtained silk only by way of the land of Persia, brought by merchants, and therefore it was sold at high prices. Silk garments used to be sold for their weight in gold. Then the silkworm eggs from which the worms hatch were transferred to Constantinople in the time of the Emperor "Justinian," between the years 527 and 565 CE. Among the kinds of silk garments are *sundus* and *istabraq*, both of which were mentioned in Surat al-Kahf. Silk garments became known among the Romans around the early third century CE.

The meaning of ﴿And they were guided to the good of speech﴾ is that Allah guides them to words, that is, inspires them with good words that they say among themselves. Some of these are mentioned in His saying: ﴿Their call therein is "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein is "Peace," and the end of their call is "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Yunus: 10], and in His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the land, to settle in the Garden wherever we will. How excellent is the reward of the workers"﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. It is also possible that the meaning is that they are guided to places where they hear good words. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final home"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23]. This is more fitting as a contrast to what the people of the Fire hear in His saying: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22].

The clause ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*) at the end of the speech, and the *wāw* is for the parenthetical insertion. It is like a completion of the description of the goodness of their condition, due to the relevance of the mention of guidance in His saying ﴿And they were guided to the good of speech﴾. No counterpart to the content of this clause has preceded in relation to the states of the disbelievers. Its counterpart will come in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 25] up to His saying ﴿We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 25], and that is among the varieties of contrast (*muqābala*). The meaning is: they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy in the world, which is the religion of Islam; it is likened to a path because it leads to the pleasure of Allah.

Al-Ḥamīd is one of the Names of Allah, meaning the One who is much praised, so it is *fa'īl* in the sense of *maf'ūl*. The annexation of *ṣirāṭ* (path) to the Name Allah is to define which path it is. It is also possible that *al-Ḥamīd* is an adjective of *ṣirāṭ*, meaning the path praised by those who travel it. In that case the annexation of *ṣirāṭ* to it is the annexation of a noun to its adjective. The praiseworthy path is the path of the religion of Allah. In this sentence there is an allusion to the cause of meriting those blessings: that it is the prior guidance to the religion of Allah in the worldly life.

[p. 231]
