They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they were guided to the good of speech, and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.﴾

The apparent expectation was that this statement would be joined with the conjunction *wa* (and) to the sentence ﴿So those who disbelieved, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], because it is the counterpart of that sentence in the detailed explanation of the summary in ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], by saying: "And those who believe and do righteous deeds, Allah will admit them into gardens," and so on. But the discourse departs from that style to this arrangement, to draw the ears to this statement, since it comes as an independent beginning, opened with the particle of emphasis (inna) and crowned with the Name of Majesty (Allah). The eloquent speaker does not miss the recognition that this statement is a counterpart to the one before it, in the detailed explanation of the summary ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], describing the state of the believers in contrast with the state of those who disbelieved, in place, in clothing, and in the address of honour. So His saying ﴿Allah will admit those who believe﴾ and what follows corresponds to His saying ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, from distress, they will be returned into it﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. His saying ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. His saying ﴿and their clothing therein will be silk﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. His saying ﴿And they were guided to the good of speech﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22], for that is of the wicked speech.

Al-tahliyah (adornment) means placing ornaments on the parts of the body. One says *hallāhu*, meaning he dressed him in ornaments, like *jalbaba* (to dress in a jilbab).

Al-asawir is the plural of *aswira*, which is itself the plural of *siwar* (bracelet). The plural of a plural indicates abundance, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and will wear green garments﴾ [al-Kahf: 31], in Surat al-Kahf.

[p. 232]

The *min* in His saying *min asāwir* (with bracelets) is superfluous (*zā'ida*), for emphasis. Its rationale is that since men are not known to be adorned with bracelets, the report that they will be adorned with bracelets would be open to doubt as to whether the literal meaning is intended; so the emphatic particle is brought to convey the literal meaning. For this reason, *asāwir* is in the position of the second object of *yuḥallawna* (they will be adorned).

*Wa-lu'lu'an* (and pearls) was read by Nafi', Ya'qub, and 'Asim in the accusative, as a conjunction with the grammatical position (*maḥall*) of *asāwir*, meaning: they will be adorned with pearls, i.e., necklaces and the like. The rest read it in the genitive, as a conjunction with the wording (*lafẓ*). The meaning is: bracelets of gold and bracelets of pearls. It is written in the codex with an *alif* after the second *wāw* in this surah, so the genitive reading differs from the written codex. But recitation is transmission and narration, so following the orthography is not obligatory for one who transmits what differs from it. A similar word is written without an *alif* in Surat Fatir. Those who read it in the accusative also departed from the orthography of the codex, relying on their transmission. The sense of emphasis is the same in both readings, because the emphasis relates to the whole sentence, not specifically to the conjoined word, so there is no need to repeat the emphatic particle with the conjoined word.

Al-lu'lu' is pearl (*durr*). It is also called *jumān* and *jawhar*. It is white and yellow grains with a sheen, extracted from inside a snail-like aquatic animal, set within a shell of two valves closed around it, which it opens by a vital movement to absorb the water in which it swims. Its shell is called *ṣadaf*. A bead with a sheen is found inside the animal, varying in size, and in clarity and whiteness of colour. This animal is found in several seas: such as the Gulf (Persian Gulf, known as the Two Seas), the Gulf of Gabès, and the shore of the island of Djerba in Tunisia. The best and finest is that found in the Two Seas, where the Tigris and Euphrates rivers discharge. Skilled divers extract it [p. 233] from the bottom of the sea by diving. The diver, tied to a rope held by a man on the boat, dives, and after a moment sufficient for gathering, is hauled up.

The description of this appears in the words of al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas or al-A'sha:

*Lujjāna al-baḥrī jā'a bihā ghawwāṣuhā min luggat al-baḥr*
*Nawwaṣa al-nahārā al-mā'u ghāmiruhu wa rafīquhu bi'l-ghayb lā yadrī*

And Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said, describing a pearl:

*Fa-jā'a bihā mā shi'ta min laṭamiyya 'alā wajhihā mā'u al-Furāt yamūj*

It is also indicated by the verse in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿It is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh meat and extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾ [al-Nahl: 14].

Since adornment is other than clothing, the word for clothing is mentioned after *yuḥallawna* in the form of a noun, rather than *yalbasūna* (they will wear), so that the sense of permanence and continuity is conveyed; just as the form *yuḥallawna* indicates that adornment is renewed with various kinds and colours. From the generality of both forms, it is understood that the like of them is realized on the other side, so there is in the speech *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which one of two parallel elements is omitted and understood from the other). It is as if it were said: they will be adorned with them, and their adornment is of bracelets of gold, and their clothing therein is silk, which they will wear.

Al-ḥarīr (silk) is applied to what is woven from silk threads, as here. The original meaning of the name *ḥarīr* is the threads that a particular worm secretes from its saliva, wrapping them round itself layer upon layer, like a ball that is tightly bound, resembling the shape of a peanut, enclosing the worm like a nut. The worm remains in it for a period until it transforms into a moth with two wings, which pierces that cocoon and exits it. The threads are obtained from that cocoon by placing it in hot water at boiling point until its binding weakens because of the dissolution of the gummy saliva substance that holds it, and then they draw out a single long thread. From those threads, garments are woven [p. 234] that are extremely soft and lustrous. Silk garments are the finest garments in the world, both in ancient and modern times. Their earliest appearance was in the land of China, about five thousand years ago, where the mulberry tree abounds, because the silkworm does not produce silk except when its fodder is mulberry leaves, and it mostly builds its cocoons on mulberry branches. The people other than the Chinese did not know how to raise silkworms, so they obtained silk only by way of the land of Persia, brought by merchants, and therefore it was sold at high prices. Silk garments used to be sold for their weight in gold. Then the silkworm eggs from which the worms hatch were transferred to Constantinople in the time of the Emperor "Justinian," between the years 527 and 565 CE. Among the kinds of silk garments are *sundus* and *istabraq*, both of which were mentioned in Surat al-Kahf. Silk garments became known among the Romans around the early third century CE.

The meaning of ﴿And they were guided to the good of speech﴾ is that Allah guides them to words, that is, inspires them with good words that they say among themselves. Some of these are mentioned in His saying: ﴿Their call therein is "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein is "Peace," and the end of their call is "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Yunus: 10], and in His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the land, to settle in the Garden wherever we will. How excellent is the reward of the workers"﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. It is also possible that the meaning is that they are guided to places where they hear good words. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final home"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23]. This is more fitting as a contrast to what the people of the Fire hear in His saying: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22].

The clause ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*) at the end of the speech, and the *wāw* is for the parenthetical insertion. It is like a completion of the description of the goodness of their condition, due to the relevance of the mention of guidance in His saying ﴿And they were guided to the good of speech﴾. No counterpart to the content of this clause has preceded in relation to the states of the disbelievers. Its counterpart will come in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 25] up to His saying ﴿We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 25], and that is among the varieties of contrast (*muqābala*). The meaning is: they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy in the world, which is the religion of Islam; it is likened to a path because it leads to the pleasure of Allah.

Al-Ḥamīd is one of the Names of Allah, meaning the One who is much praised, so it is *fa'īl* in the sense of *maf'ūl*. The annexation of *ṣirāṭ* (path) to the Name Allah is to define which path it is. It is also possible that *al-Ḥamīd* is an adjective of *ṣirāṭ*, meaning the path praised by those who travel it. In that case the annexation of *ṣirāṭ* to it is the annexation of a noun to its adjective. The praiseworthy path is the path of the religion of Allah. In this sentence there is an allusion to the cause of meriting those blessings: that it is the prior guidance to the religion of Allah in the worldly life.

[Page 236]

This is in contrast to His saying ﴿And they were guided to the good word and to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Hajj: 24], with respect to the states of the polytheists. For His saying about them does not have a counterpart among the states mentioned in the verse ﴿Those who disbelieve, for them will be cut garments of fire﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], as has already been explained. So the position of this sentence is an explanatory resumption (al-istinaf al-bayani, a sentence that answers an implied question). The meaning is: just as the cause of the believers deserving that bliss was their following the path of God, so the cause of the polytheists deserving that punishment was their disbelief and their barring others from the path of God.

Within this, given its relation to what precedes it, there is also a graceful transition (takhallus) to what follows: the explanation of the right of the Muslims regarding the Sacred Mosque, the gravity of deviation (ilhad) within it, the honouring of it, and its being purified from becoming a refuge for polytheism, the filth of wrongdoing and transgression. The news is emphasised with the particle of emphasis for the sake of drawing attention to it. The verb (yasuddūna, "they bar") is in the present tense to indicate that this is repeated from them and is their habit, whether the people of Makkah or others, since the rest supported them in that barring and agreed with them. As for the past form in His saying ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾, it is because that action had become like a title for them, as in His saying ﴿God admits those who believe﴾ [al-Hajj: 14].

"The path of God" is Islam. So barring them from it is what brought about for them the punishment of the Fire, just as the believers' guidance to it brought them the bliss of Paradise.

Barring from the Sacred Mosque is included in barring from the path of God, but it is singled out for mention for the sake of giving it attention, and in order to move from it to honouring the Sacred Mosque, mentioning its construction, and the prescription of the Hajj to it from the time of Abraham. What is meant by their barring from the Sacred Mosque is a barring known to the Muslims at that time. Perhaps it is their preventing the Muslims from entering the Sacred Mosque and circumambulating the House. What is known of this is that after the Hijrah they prevented the Muslims from visiting the House. Abu Jahl said to Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, when he came to Makkah to perform the minor pilgrimage (umrah), and said to his companion Umayya ibn Khalaf: "Wait for me for an hour of the day, perhaps I may circumambulate the House." So while Sa'd was circumambulating, Abu Jahl came to him and recognised him. Abu Jahl said to him: "Are you circumambulating the Ka'bah? We have given you refuge, and you have been given shelter [or: you have been sheltered]," meaning the Muslims. Among that is what they did on the day of al-Hudaybiyah. It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning that. But I think the verse was revealed before that, whether it was revealed in Makkah or in Madinah.

[Page 237]

The description of the mosque in His saying ﴿which We made for the people﴾, and so on, is an indication of the reason for holding the polytheists accountable for barring others from it, because they opposed what God intended for it. For He made it for all people, who are equal in the right to worship in it: the one who stays in it (al-'akif), that is, the one who settles in the mosque, and the one from the desert (al-badi), that is, the one who is far from it when he enters it.

What is meant by al-'akif is the one who constantly remains in it in many states. It is a metonymy (kinaya) for the resident of Makkah, because the resident of Makkah frequently remains in the Sacred Mosque, as shown by its being contrasted with al-badi. So "remaining in the mosque" (al-'ukuf) is used figuratively for residing in Makkah, by a conventional relation of necessary association. In mentioning al-'ukuf there is an implicit reproach that they do not deserve any special privilege over others by living in Makkah, and that when they prevent those who come from outside Makkah from entering the Ka'bah, they have wronged them by monopolising Makkah.

The majority of readers read (sawā'un, "equal") in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and (al-'akifu fīhi, "the one who stays in it") as an agent that stands in place of the predicate, and the whole sentence is the second object of (ja'alnāhu, "We made it"). Hafs read it in the accusative, as the second object of (ja'alnāhu).

Al-'ukuf means constant staying. Al-badi means the resident of the desert.

His saying (sawā'un, "equal") does not specify in what respect they are equal. This is because it is clear that equality in it, in terms of its being a mosque, is only in the worship intended for it and what is attached to it, namely circumambulation, running between Safa and Marwah, and standing at 'Arafah. In the Mushaf (the written copy of the Qur'an) the word (al-bad) is written without a yā' at its end. Ibn Kathir read (al-badi) with the yā' retained, according to the usual rule, because it is definite, and the usual rule is to retain the yā' of a defective noun when it is made definite by the article. The reason it is written without a yā' in the Mushaf according to the people of this reading is that the yā' was treated like vowels and the long vowels in the middle of words, so they did not write it. Nafi' read it without a yā' in pausal position (waqf) and with the yā' in continuous speech (wasl).

[Page 238]

The reason it is written without a yā' according to this reading is that lightness was observed in the state of pause, since the normal practice of the orthography is to take account of the state of pause. The rest read it without a yā' in both states, continuous speech and pause. The reason for this is the intention of lightening, and there are many similar cases. There is no proof in this verse for the ruling on owning houses in Makkah, either affirmatively or negatively, because its context concerns the Sacred Mosque specifically and not anything else. What is attached to it, being part of its rites, is included: such as the place of running (al-Sa'y), the place of standing (al-Mawqif), the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), and the pillars of stoning (al-Jimar). The custom of the jurists has been to mention the question of owning houses in Makkah when mentioning this verse, by way of digression (istitrad).

There is no disagreement among the Muslims that people are equal in performing the rites at the Sacred Mosque and what follows it, except what the Law forbids, such as a menstruating woman circumambulating the Ka'bah.

As for the question of owning houses in Makkah, the jurists have three opinions:

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas and others said: whoever comes to Makkah for the Hajj may stay wherever he wishes among its houses, and the owner of the dwelling must give him shelter. The houses of Makkah were called "al-sawa'ib" (the free) during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may God be pleased with them both).

Malik and al-Shafi'i said: the houses of Makkah are owned by its people, and they have the right to refuse to house others, and they may rent them to people. Sharing is required only in cases of necessity. On this basis they interpreted what 'Umar used to do as an act of sharing. 'Umar bought the house of Safwan ibn Umayyah and made it a dwelling.

Abu Hanifa said: the houses of Makkah cannot be owned, and its people may not rent them out. It has been thought that the disagreement on this is based on the difference over whether Makkah was conquered by force ('anwatan) or by treaty (sulhan). But the truth is that there is no basis for this, because among those who say it was conquered by force are those who say the houses of Makkah can be owned. Malik ibn Anas holds that it was conquered by force, and holds that the ownership of its houses is valid. The reasoning is that the Prophet (ﷺ) left its people in their dwellings, so he would have granted them those houses as a grant, just as he granted its people release from captivity and from being taken as captives. The people of Makkah have continued to sell their houses to one another, and no scholar among the people of knowledge has objected to them.

The predicate of (inna alladhina kafaru, "indeed those who disbelieve") is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "We will make them taste a painful punishment," which is indicated by His saying in the following clause ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾. Since barring from the Sacred Mosque is deviation by wrongdoing, the clause ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾ is an appended conclusion (tadhyil) to the preceding clause, because of the generality contained in the conditional (man, "whoever").

Ilhad (deviation) is turning away from uprightness and the straight course of affairs. Wrongdoing (zulm) is applied to polytheism and to sins, because they are a wronging of the self. The preposition (bi-, "by") in (bi-ilhadin) is superfluous, for emphasis, like it in ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. That is: whoever intends deviation and distance from truth and uprightness, and that is their barring others from visiting it. The preposition (bi-) in (bi-zulmin, "by wrongdoing") indicates accompaniment. So the wrongdoing is polytheism, because the aim is to threaten the polytheists who were moved by polytheism to oppose the Muslims and to prevent them from visiting the Sacred Mosque. As for (min, "from") in His saying (min 'adhabin alimin, "from a painful punishment"), it is superfluous for emphasis according to the view of those who do not require that the superfluous (min) follow a negation or a prohibition. You may also make it partitive, meaning: We will make him taste a punishment from among painful punishments.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 26:

﴿And [mention] when We settled for Ibrahim the site of the House, [saying], "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate."﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) of one narrative upon another, joined to the sentence ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]. It is known from it that the sentence conjoined to it gives the reason: whoever deviates in the Sacred Mosque has, by his deviation therein, opposed what Allah intended by its purification when He commanded its construction. The transition from this to establishing the wrongdoing and ingratitude of the polytheists toward the blessing of Allah in establishing the Sacred Mosque and legislating the Hajj. The particle (idha) is a noun of time stripped of the sense of place, so it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, according to what is customary in such cases. The estimate is: "And remember when We settled," i.e., remember the time when We settled Ibrahim there, as in His saying, ﴿And [mention] when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will make upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], i.e., remember that great time. The greatness of it is known from the fact that the noun of time is added to a verbal sentence rather than to a verbal noun, so that it carries, by what the verb indicates of renewal, the sense of a present time.

And al-tabwiʾah (settling) means lodging. It has preceded in His saying, ﴿And thus We established Yusuf in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed﴾ [Yusuf: 56].

And al-makan is a plot of land and a place for being in it; it is a verb derived from al-kawn (being). So his settling Ibrahim in the place means permitting him to take it as a residence (mabaʾah), i.e., a station in which he builds a house. Thus by the mention of (makan) there occurs concision in the speech, as if it were said: "And when We gave him a place to take a house therein," and He said: "the site of the House," because this is a narrative of a well-known story among them, and its mention has preceded in what was revealed before this verse of the Qur'an. The lam in (li-Ibrahim) is the lam of cause, because (Ibrahim) is the first object of (bawwa'na), which is of the pattern of (aʿṭā), so the lam is like it in their saying: "I thanked you [li-ka]," i.e., she thanked you for your sake. In mentioning the lam in such a case there is a kind of care and honor. And (al-Bayt) is known and familiar at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an, so it was defined by the definite article of prior knowledge; had it not been for this subtlety, the mention of (makan) would be superfluous. The intent is that it be a shelter for religion, i.e., a place of devotion for the establishment of the rites of religion. It thus implicitly includes, in a general way, that it awaits instruction in religion; therefore it is followed by the explanatory particle (an), which occurs after a sentence containing the meaning of speech without its letters. The essence of religion was the negation of associating partners with Allah, so it is known that the House was made a sign of monotheism, such that whoever enters it is required not to be a polytheist. For this reason the Kaʿbah was the first house placed for mankind, for the proclamation of monotheism, as we explained at His saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾ [Al ʿImran: 96] in Surat Al ʿImran.

His saying, ﴿and purify My House﴾, indicates an implied statement which is shown by ﴿We settled for Ibrahim the site of the House﴾. The meaning: We commanded him to build the House in that place, and after he built it We said: "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House." The addition of the House to the Divine name (Allah) is an honoring of the House. And purification (tathhir) is to free it from every impurity: in meaning, such as polytheism, indecency, wronging people, and the spreading of blameworthy qualities; and in the physical sense, from filth and the like, i.e., prepare it pure for those who circumambulate it and those who stand therein.

Al-tawaf (circumambulation) is walking around the Kaʿbah, and it is an ancient worship from the time of Ibrahim, which Islam confirmed; the people of the Jahiliyyah used to circumambulate their idols just as they circumambulated the Kaʿbah.

By "those who stand" is meant those who supplicate facing the Kaʿbah, and from this the Station of Ibrahim (Maqam Ibrahim) was named, being the place of his standing for supplication; thus the place of clinging (al-multazam) became a place of supplication. Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl said:

"I have sought refuge in what Ibrahim sought refuge in, facing the Kaʿbah, standing."

And al-Rukkaʿ is the plural of rakiʿ (one who bows), and the pattern fuʿʿal commonly occurs as a plural of the active participle as an adjective when its final radical is sound, like ʿUdhhal and Suhhad.

And al-Sujud is the plural of sajid (one who prostrates), like al-Ruqud and al-Quʿud, and it is among the plurals of those adjectives that resemble the verbal nouns of their verbs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verses 27–28:

﴿And proclaim to mankind the Pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every deep mountain pass.﴾ ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves, and mention the name of Allah on known days over the beasts of livestock He has provided for them. So eat from them and feed the miserable, the poor.﴾

(And proclaim) is coordinated with ﴿And purify My House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26]. In it is an indication that among the honouring of the visitor is cleaning the dwelling, and that this occurs before the visitor's arrival at the place.

Al-ta'dhin (proclamation) is raising the voice to announce something. Its root is the doubled form of adhina, which means to hear; then it came to mean that news reached him, so from it came adhana, meaning to inform. The doubling of letters in adhdhin (proclaim) indicates repetition of the act, i.e., give abundant information about the matter; abundance is achieved by repetition and by raising the voice, which takes the place of repetition. Because it carries the meaning of informing, it is transitive to the second object by means of the preposition bi (with).

Al-nas (mankind) is general, encompassing all of humanity, i.e., everyone to whom it was possible for this to be conveyed.

Page 243
Al-hajj (the Pilgrimage) means intending the House of Allah. The word hajj became a proper designation by dominance for presence at the Sacred Mosque to perform the rites. Among the wisdoms of its legislation is receiving the creed of the Oneness of Allah through direct witnessing of the structure erected for that purpose, so that the meaning of monotheism becomes firmly rooted in souls, because souls have an inclination toward perceptible things, so that rational perception is strengthened by witnessing the perceptible. This is therefore a basis for the principle of influences upon those who pursue a beneficial purpose. In attaching the verb (ya'tunaka, they will come to you) to the second-person pronoun addressed to Ibrahim, there is an indication that he used to attend the season of the Hajj every year, conveying monotheism and the rules of the hanifiyya (primordial monotheistic faith) to the people. It is narrated that when Allah commanded him with this, Ibrahim ascended the mountain of Abu Qubays, placed his two fingers in his ears, and called out: "Indeed Allah has prescribed for you the Hajj, so perform the Hajj." That was the utmost of his capacity in complying with the command to proclaim. Ibrahim was a wanderer, so perhaps he would call out to the people in every place where he alighted.

The clause (ya'tunaka) is the answer to the imperative, making the proclamation a cause of their coming, in order to facilitate the Hajj for people. The answer to the imperative indicates that Allah guaranteed him the response to his call. His saying (rijalan, on foot) is a circumstantial state (hal) of the plural pronoun in (ya'tunaka). It is coordinated with it ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ by the conjunction waw of division, which carries the meaning of (aw, or), like the words of the Exalted ﴿matronly and virgin﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5], since the meaning of the coordination here, considering distribution, is between one on foot and one riding, for the rider is not on foot and nor the reverse. The intent is to encompass the conditions of those who come, in fulfilment of the promise of facilitating the coming alluded to, by making their coming an answer to the imperative, i.e., there will come to you those who have mounts and those who walk on their feet.

Page 244
Because this state is more striking, (rijalan) was placed first, and then after it ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ was mentioned as a completion of the generalization of conditions, since people's coming does not go beyond one of these two descriptions. (Rijalan) is the plural of rajil, which is the opposite of rakib (rider).

Al-dami (lean) means one with little flesh on the belly. It is said: damura, damurun, so he is dami', and a she-camel is also dami'. Leanness is among the desirable qualities of mounts and horses, because it helps them in travel and movement. So here dami' functions as a noun, as if he had said: "and on every mount." The word (kull, every) in ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ is used for abundance, i.e., and on many mounts. The word kull originally indicates the encompassing of the whole class of what it is attached to, and it is often used to mean a large quantity of what it is attached to, as in the words of the Exalted ﴿and she has been given of every thing﴾ [al-Naml: 23], meaning of the most of the things that the possessors of kingdom are given; and in the words of al-Nabigha:

By it every dhayyal and khansa'... graze toward every rajjaf of the sand, solitary

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verses 27–28:

﴿And proclaim to mankind the Pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every deep mountain pass.﴾ ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves, and mention the name of Allah on known days over the beasts of livestock He has provided for them. So eat from them and feed the miserable, the poor.﴾

(And proclaim) is coordinated with ﴿And purify My House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26]. In it is an indication that among the honouring of the visitor is cleaning the dwelling, and that this occurs before the visitor's arrival at the place.

Al-ta'dhin (proclamation) is raising the voice to announce something. Its root is the doubled form of adhina, which means to hear; then it came to mean that news reached him, so from it came adhana, meaning to inform. The doubling of letters in adhdhin (proclaim) indicates repetition of the act, i.e., give abundant information about the matter; abundance is achieved by repetition and by raising the voice, which takes the place of repetition. Because it carries the meaning of informing, it is transitive to the second object by means of the preposition bi (with).

Al-nas (mankind) is general, encompassing all of humanity, i.e., everyone to whom it was possible for this to be conveyed.

Page 243
Al-hajj (the Pilgrimage) means intending the House of Allah. The word hajj became a proper designation by dominance for presence at the Sacred Mosque to perform the rites. Among the wisdoms of its legislation is receiving the creed of the Oneness of Allah through direct witnessing of the structure erected for that purpose, so that the meaning of monotheism becomes firmly rooted in souls, because souls have an inclination toward perceptible things, so that rational perception is strengthened by witnessing the perceptible. This is therefore a basis for the principle of influences upon those who pursue a beneficial purpose. In attaching the verb (ya'tunaka, they will come to you) to the second-person pronoun addressed to Ibrahim, there is an indication that he used to attend the season of the Hajj every year, conveying monotheism and the rules of the hanifiyya (primordial monotheistic faith) to the people. It is narrated that when Allah commanded him with this, Ibrahim ascended the mountain of Abu Qubays, placed his two fingers in his ears, and called out: "Indeed Allah has prescribed for you the Hajj, so perform the Hajj." That was the utmost of his capacity in complying with the command to proclaim. Ibrahim was a wanderer, so perhaps he would call out to the people in every place where he alighted.

The clause (ya'tunaka) is the answer to the imperative, making the proclamation a cause of their coming, in order to facilitate the Hajj for people. The answer to the imperative indicates that Allah guaranteed him the response to his call. His saying (rijalan, on foot) is a circumstantial state (hal) of the plural pronoun in (ya'tunaka). It is coordinated with it ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ by the conjunction waw of division, which carries the meaning of (aw, or), like the words of the Exalted ﴿matronly and virgin﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5], since the meaning of the coordination here, considering distribution, is between one on foot and one riding, for the rider is not on foot and nor the reverse. The intent is to encompass the conditions of those who come, in fulfilment of the promise of facilitating the coming alluded to, by making their coming an answer to the imperative, i.e., there will come to you those who have mounts and those who walk on their feet.

This is part of what God addressed to Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Warsh, on the authority of Nafi', and Qunbul, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, along with Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr, read ﴿لِيَقْضُوا﴾ with a kasra on the lam. The rest read it with a sukun on the lam. Both are dialectal forms of the lam of command (lam al-amr) when it follows ﴿ثُمَّ﴾, as already mentioned earlier in His words ﴿ثُمَّ لْيَقْطَعْ﴾. Here ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ joins one sentence to another. It indicates a gradation in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), not a sequence in time. It therefore means that the sentence it introduces is more important to the purpose of the speech than the one before it. This is clear in the case of fulfilling vows and circumambulating the Ancient House, since these are two rites more important than sacrificing offerings. The phrase ﴿قَضَاءُ التَّفَثِ﴾ is to be understood as referring to something important, as we will explain.

Al-tafath (التَّفَثُ) is a word that occurs in the Qur'an, and the commentators disagreed about its intended meaning. The scholars of lexicography (ʿulamāʾ al-lugha, the study of Arabic vocabulary) also disagreed about its meaning, perhaps because they did not find it in the Arabic speech accepted as evidence. Al-Zajjaj said: the people of lexicography know tafath only from tafsir (exegesis), that is, from the statements of the commentators. On the authority of Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas:

[Page 249]

Tafath means the rites of the Hajj and all its actions. Ibn al-'Arabi said: if this is authentically transmitted from them, it would be decisive proof of comprehensive knowledge of the language. I say: al-Tabari narrated it from them through acceptable chains. Al-Jassas attributed it to Sa'id. Nifṭawayh and Qutrub said: tafath is filth and grime. Ibn Wahb narrated it from Malik ibn Anas, and Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi preferred it. Qutrub recited the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

They shaved their heads, but they did not shave tafath,
and they did not remove for them lice and nits.

It is possible that this verse is fabricated, because the leading lexicographers said that no poetry that can be used as evidence has come concerning the meaning of tafath. Nifṭawayh said: I asked a Bedouin Arab about the meaning of His words ﴿ثُمَّ لِيَقْضُوا تَفَثَهُمْ﴾, and he said: I do not interpret the Qur'an, but we say to a man, "What makes you tafath?", meaning, "What makes you filthy?"

From Abu 'Ubayda: tafath is cutting the nails, taking from the moustache, and everything that is forbidden to the one in ihram. 'Ikrima and Mujahid said something similar, though Mujahid sometimes added to that the stoning of the pillars (ramy al-jimar).

From the author of al-'Ayn, al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj: tafath is stoning, slaughtering, shaving, cutting the nails and moustache, and removing underarm hair. This is the view of al-Hasan, and it is also attributed to Malik ibn Anas. In my view, the verb ﴿لْيَقْضُوا﴾ indicates that tafath is an action of the Hajj, not filth, nor a nail, nor hair. This is supported by what was narrated above from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas. The use of ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ to join the command sentence to what precedes it also indicates gradation in rank, which requires that the sentence introduced by ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ be more important than what came before it. The actions of the Hajj are indeed the most important part of coming to Makkah. Therefore tafath is certainly the rites of the Hajj. This is the usage al-Hariri followed in his Makamat al-Makkiyya, where he said: "When I had, by God's help, completed the tafath, and made lawful the perfume and the sexual intercourse (al-rafath), I encountered the season of al-Khayf, in the fierce heat of summer."

[Page 250]

His words ﴿وَلْيُوفُوا نُذُورَهُمْ﴾ mean: if they had vowed actions beyond what the obligation of the Hajj requires, such as vowing an extra circumambulation, or i'tikaf (retreat) in the Sacred Mosque, or a rite of sacrifice, or feeding a poor person, or similar things.

Al-nadhr (النَّذْرُ) is the binding of oneself to an act of worship for God, which was not obligatory upon the one who binds himself to it, whether conditional on obtaining something desired or unconditional. By the vow, the act of worship that was bound becomes obligatory upon the one who vowed. The most common formula is: "For God upon me..." This verse is evidence that vowing was legislated in the law of Ibrahim. "'Umar vowed in the Jahiliyya to perform i'tikaf for a night in the Sacred Mosque, and he fulfilled it after embracing Islam," as is mentioned in the hadith. The majority read ﴿وَلْيُوفُوا﴾ with a damma on the yā' and a sukun on the wāw after it, the imperfect of awfā. Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿وَلْيُوَفُّوا﴾ with a shadda on the fā', and it has the same meaning as the unstressed reading, because both forms come from the verb wafā, which takes the hamza form and the doubled form. The address to Ibrahim ends with the command to circumambulate the House, indicating that they used to make the circumambulation of the House the last of the actions of the Hajj, which is called in Islam the ṭawāf al-ifāḍa (the circumambulation of return).

Al-ʿatīq (الْعَتِيقُ) means that which is freed and not owned by people. It is likened to the freed slave, in that no one has ownership over it. This contains an allusion to the polytheists, who used to prevent whomever they wished from entering it, to the extent that they made its door high without steps, so that only those they chose could enter, as is reported in the hadith of 'A'isha on the day of the conquest. al-Tirmidhi narrated with a good chain that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God named the House al-ʿatīq only because He freed it from the tyrants, so no tyrant ever prevailed over it." Know that these verses are a narration of what was in the time of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), so the rulings of the Hajj and the sacrifices in Islam are not derived from them.

[Page 251]

The majority read ﴿ثُمَّ لْيَقْضُوا - وَلْيُوفُوا - وَلْيَطَّوَّفُوا﴾ with a sukun on the lam of command in all of them. Ibn Dhakwan, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, read ﴿وَلِيُوفُوا - وَلِيَطَّوَّفُوا﴾ with a kasra on the lam in both. Ibn Hisham, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Warsh on the authority of Nafi', Qunbul on the authority of Ibn Kathir, and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub, read ﴿ثُمَّ لِيَقْضُوا﴾ with a kasra on the lam. The two readings were explained earlier at His words ﴿ثُمَّ لْيَقْطَعْ﴾. Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿وَلْيُوَفُّوا﴾ with a fatḥa on the wāw and a shadda on the fā', from the doubled form of wafā.

This is the commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 30:

﴿That [is so]. And whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah, it is better for him in the sight of his Lord.﴾

The demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) is used here to mark a separation between two statements, or between two aspects of one statement. Its purpose is to alert the listener to the importance of what will be mentioned after it. The demonstrative is intended as an alert, and this occurs where what follows cannot serve as a predicate of the demonstrative, so it is necessary to supply a predicate for it, meaning: "That is an explanation," or "a mention," and this is one of the methods of abrupt transition (iqtidab) in moving from one topic to another. The well-known form used in this construction is the word hadha, as in the words of the Exalted ﴿This [is so]. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil return.﴾ [Sad: 55], and in the verse of Zuhayr:

*Hadha, and he is not like the one who falters in his speech*
*amid the assembly when any speaker stands and speaks.*

In the verse, the demonstrative of the distant (ism al-ishara lil-b'id) is chosen to indicate the elevated rank of the matter, as a metaphor for the magnification of what precedes it. So the demonstrative is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate has been omitted because its supplied form is clear, i.e., "That is an explanation and the like." This is like a writer who presents a portion of his book on some topics, and then, when he wishes to enter into another topic, says: "Hadha, and [it was] such and such."

The clause "And whoever honours..." (wa man yu'annid ilakh) is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah) coordinated upon the clause ﴿And [mention] when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], as a coordination of one purpose upon another purpose. It is a transition to explaining what must be preserved of the hanifiyyah (the pure monotheistic faith), and an alert that Islam was built upon its foundation. The pronoun in (fa-huwa) refers to the honouring derived from the verb ﴿whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah﴾. The statement is directed to the Muslims, alerting them that Islam did not nullify the sanctity of those sacred rites, so the transition is from one purpose to another and from one addressee to another. The Muslims used to perform 'umrah and hajj before the obligation of hajj was imposed upon them, that is, before the conquest of Mecca.

Al-hurumat is the plural of hurmah (with two dammas): it is what must be respected.

Al-ihtiram (respect) is regarding a thing as sacred (dhu haram), a metaphor for not entering into it, meaning not violating it by opposing the command of Allah concerning it. Al-hurumat includes everything which Allah has enjoined to be magnified, so it includes all the rites of hajj. It is related from Zayd ibn Aslam: "The sacred things are five: the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred House, the Sacred Land, the Sacred Month, and the one in ihram as long as he is in ihram." So he restricted it to the entities rather than the acts. What appears to be the case is that al-hurumat includes the offerings (al-hada'ya), the garlands (al-qala'id), the Sacred Monument (al-mash'ar al-haram), and other acts of hajj, such as the ghusl at its places, and the shaving (halq) with its appointed times and rites.
