﴿Lawful for you are the grazing animals, except what is recited to you. So avoid the uncleanness of idols, and avoid the saying of falsehood, being hanifs for Allah, not associating anything with Him.﴾ [al-Hajj: 31]

When He had just mentioned the beast of cattle and the magnifying of the sacred things of Allah, He followed this with nullifying what the polytheists had forbidden upon themselves of cattle, such as the bahirah, the sa'ibah,

*Page 253*

the wasilah, and the ham, and some of what is in their bellies. This has been mentioned in Surat al-An'am. He excepted from it what is recited as forbidden in the Qur'an, which is what was mentioned in Surat al-An'am in His saying ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 145] and the verses that follow, and what was mentioned in Surat al-Nahl; both are Meccan and earlier. The present tense was used in His saying "except what is recited to you" so that it would include what was revealed of the Qur'an concerning this before the revelation of Surat al-Hajj, in that it was recited in the past and has not ceased to be recited, and it includes what may be revealed afterwards, such as His saying ﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah or sa'ibah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surat al-'Uqud.

The command to avoid idols is used to request continuity, as in His saying ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 136]. Upon this is built a parenthetical clause to make explicit the command to avoid what is not among the sacred things of Allah, namely the idols. Avoiding lying against Allah consists in their saying of some forbidden things, "this is lawful," such as blood and what is dedicated to other than Allah, and their saying of some things, "this is forbidden," such as the bahirah and the sa'ibah. Allah the Exalted said ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 116].

Al-rijs (uncleanness): its real meaning is filth and foulness. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿for indeed it is an abomination (rijs)﴾ in Surat al-An'am. The description of idols as rijs is because they are a spiritual uncleanness, since the belief in their divinity settling in souls is like the cleaving of filth to bodies, so applying rijs to them is an eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh). The (min) in His saying "min al-awthan" ("of idols") is explanatory (bayan) for the general term rijs, as it enters upon some of the nouns of specification (asma' al-tamyiz) to clarify what is meant by rijs here, not that the meaning of rijs is the very idols themselves; rather rijs is more general, and by it here is meant some of its kinds. This is the realisation of the meaning of the explanatory (bayaniyyah) "min."

*Page 254*

"Hunafa' lillah" (being hanifs for Allah) is a state (hal) from the pronoun in "ijtanibu" (avoid), meaning: if you avoid that, be hanifs for Allah. Hunafa' is the plural of hanif, which means one who is sincere to Allah in worship, i.e., that you be upon the religion of Abraham in truth. For this reason the meaning of "hunafa'" was made clearer by His saying "ghayra mushrikin bihi" (not associating anything with Him). This is like His saying ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [al-Nahl: 120]. The (ba') in "mushrikin bihi" is for accompaniment (musahabah) and concomitance (ma'iyyah), i.e., not associating anything alongside Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 31:

﴿Whoever associates partners with God, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind carried him off to a distant place.﴿

The prohibition against idols is followed by a depiction of the dreadful state of one who associates partners with God: by his association, his fate is brought to a state of decline, in which misguided ideas seize him and he despairs of salvation for as long as he remains a polytheist. It is a wonderful depiction, since it belongs to the kind of image that can be divided into its parts, each part being a separate comparison.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: It is possible that this comparison is of the composite and the divided kind, in that the state of the polytheist is depicted in the image of one who has fallen from the sky, and the birds seized him so that he was torn into pieces in their gullets, or the wind blew him violently until it hurled him into some far-off abyss. Even though it is divided, faith in its loftiness is likened to the sky; the one who abandoned faith and associated partners with God is likened to the one who fell from the sky; the desires that scatter his thoughts are likened to the birds that snatch; and Satan, who casts him into the valley of error, is likened to the wind that carries away and hurls him into some destructive chasm. End quote. He means that when the polytheist turns away from the natural faith, while it was within his capacity, it is as if he were in the sky and then fell from it, and the kinds of destruction seize him. It is not hidden from you that within the folds of this depiction there are many comparisons, and you will not lack the ability to extract them.

Al-Sahiq: the distant, so there is no escape for whoever lands in it. His saying ﴿or the wind carries him off﴾ is an alternative regarding the outcome of the comparison, like his saying ﴿or like a downpour from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. The verse indicates that disbelievers are of two kinds. One kind has a wavering and doubtful polytheism; this one is compared to him whom the birds snatch, for whenever one bird seizes a piece of him, another takes it from it, and likewise the wavering person, whenever a phantom appears to him, follows it and abandons what he was upon. The other kind is steadfast in disbelief and settled in it; this one is compared to him whom the wind casts into a deep valley. This implies that among the polytheists are those whose polytheism holds no hope of deliverance, like the one snatched by the birds, and among them are those whose polytheism may be rid of through repentance, but whose repentance is a distant matter, difficult to attain.

Al-khurur: falling; it was discussed in His saying ﴿the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 26] in Surat al-Nahl. And (takhattafahu) is the intensive form of khatifa. Al-khatf and al-khatafu: seizing something swiftly, whether on the earth or in the air; from it comes the snatching of the ball (takhattufu al-kurah). Al-huwiyy: the descent of something from a height to the ground. The ba' in (tahwi bihi) is for transitivity, like its use in: dhahaba bihi (he took him away).

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read (fatakhattafuhu) with a fatha on the kha' and a shadda on the ta' with fatha, the present tense of the intensive khattafa. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a sukun on the kha' and a fatha on the ta' unshaddened, the present tense of the simple khafila.

**Page 256**

﴿That, and whoever honours the rites of Allah—indeed, it is from the piety of hearts.﴾

(That) repeats its earlier counterpart.

Al-sha'a'ir (the rites) is the plural of sha'ira, meaning a clear sign or landmark, derived from al-shu'ur (awareness). Sha'a'ir Allah is a designation for the rites of Hajj. It is the plural of sha'ira in the sense of mush'ira, in the active participle form, i.e., "making aware," "marking out" by what Allah has specified. Thus the content of the clause "and whoever honours the rites of Allah" etc. is more specific than the content of the clause "and whoever honours the sacred things of Allah" [al-Hajj: 30]. Mentioning the more specific after the more general is for emphasis. Or it may be in the sense of something that makes one aware of them, so that sha'ira is on the pattern fa'ila in the sense of maf'ula, because it is made so that the observer becomes aware of it. Its mention has already occurred in His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the rites of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 158] in Surat al-Baqara. Thus, whatever Allah has commanded to be visited, or an action performed in it, is among the rites of Allah, i.e., of what Allah has made known to people, established and made famous. These are the landmarks of Hajj: the Ka'ba, al-Safa and al-Marwa, 'Arafa, al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and similar landmarks of Hajj. The term sha'ira is also applied to the camel of the offering, as He, the Exalted, said ﴿And the camels—We have made them for you among the rites of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 36], because they put a mark on them (shi'ar), and the shi'ar is the sign, by stabbing the right side of its hide until blood flows from it, so that it is a sign that it has been dedicated as an offering. So it is fa'ila in the sense of maf'ula, formed from ash'ara contrary to analogy. Accordingly, on the first interpretation, the clause "and whoever honours the rites of Allah" to its end is coordinated with the clause "and whoever honours the sacred things of Allah" [al-Hajj: 30] etc. And the rites of Allah are more specific than the sacred things of Allah, so the coordination of this clause is for the attention given to the rites.

**Page 257**

On the second interpretation of the rites, the clause "and whoever honours the rites of Allah" is coordinated with the clause ﴿and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the beast of cattle﴾ [al-Hajj: 28], singling it out for mention after the mention of the sacred things of Allah. The pronoun in (fa-innaha) refers to the rites of Allah that are honoured, so the meaning is: indeed, honouring them is from the piety of hearts. And His saying ﴿indeed, it is from the piety of hearts﴾ is the answer of the condition, and the link between the condition and its answer is the generality in His saying (hearts), for among the hearts are the hearts of those who honour the rites of Allah. So the estimate is: piety has indeed settled in his heart by honouring the rites, because it is from the piety of hearts; i.e., because honouring them is from the piety of hearts. The idafa of (piety) to (hearts) is because honouring the rites is a heartfelt conviction from which action arises.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 33:

﴿For you therein are benefits until a specified term; then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾

The clause ﴿For you therein are benefits﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the cattle in His words ﴿and the cattle have been made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 30]. What comes between them is parenthetical (i‘tirāḍāt), or it is a circumstantial clause referring to "the symbols of Allah" (sha‘ā’ir Allah) according to the second interpretation of "symbols." The predicate here is intended for a category of the cattle, namely the sacrificial animals (hadāyā, offerings brought to Makkah for sacrifice), as indicated by His words ﴿then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾. The address pronoun is directed to the believers.

Al-manāfi‘ (benefits) is the plural of manfa‘ah, which is the noun of benefit, namely the attainment of what is agreeable and advantageous. Making the benefits "in them" implies that they are a use of their distinctive qualities for what is sought from their kind before they become offerings (hady).

In this there is a legislative ruling permitting the use of the offerings in a way that does not destroy them. It is also a refutation of the polytheists, who, when they garlanded the offering and marked it, forbade its use: riding it, loading it, drinking its milk, and other things.

In al-Muwaṭṭa’ (the Muwatta’ of Imam Malik) it is related from Abu Hurayrah that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw a man driving a badanah (a camel designated for sacrifice) and said: 'Ride it.' He said: 'It is a badanah.' He said: 'Ride it.' He said: 'It is a badanah.' He said: 'Ride it, woe to you, the second or the third time.'"

The specified term (al-ajal al-musammā) is the time of its slaughter, which is one of the days of Mina. These are the "counted days" (al-ayyām al-ma‘dūdāt).

Al-maḥill, with a fatḥah on the mīm and a kasrah on the ḥā’, is a mīmī verbal noun from ḥalla, yaḥillu, meaning to arrive at a place and settle in it. It is a metaphor for the end of its matter, as one says "he reached the goal." The end of its matter is the slaughter (naḥr) or the cutting of its throat (dhabḥ). The particle ilā (to) denotes a figurative end, because they are not slaughtered in the Ka‘bah itself; rather, drawing near to Allah through them is by way of honouring the Ka‘bah, since the offerings were only legislated to complete the legislation of the Hajj (pilgrimage), and the Hajj is the intention of the House. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by mankind﴾ [Āl ‘Imrān: 97]. Thus the offerings belong to the Ka‘bah, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿an offering reaching the Ka‘bah﴾ [al-Mā’idah: 95], even though the Ka‘bah is not a place of slaughter. The places of slaughter are Mina, al-Marwah, and the mountain passes (fijāj) of Makkah, that is, its roads, according to the types of offerings. Its detailed explanation is in the Sunnah.

In His words ﴿then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾ there occurs radd al-‘ajuz ‘alā al-ṣadr (the rhetorical device of returning the end to the beginning), with reference to the starting point of these verses, which is His words ﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 26].

[Page 258]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 34:

Page 259
﴿And for every community We have appointed a rite (mansak), that they may mention the name of Allah over the beast of cattle He has provided for them. So your God is one God, so submit to Him.﴾
This is a conjunction with the clause ﴿Then its place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj: 33]. The "ummah" (community) here means the people of a religion who share in following it. The meaning is that the Muslims have one rite (mansak), which is the Ancient House, as was previously mentioned. The purpose of this is a rebuttal of the polytheists, who made for their idols rites resembling the rites of the Hajj, and made for them times (mawaqit) and places of sacrifice (madhabih), like al-Ghabghab, the place of sacrifice of al-'Uzza. So Allah the Exalted reminded them that He had appointed for every community only one rite (mansak) for drawing near to Allah the Exalted, who provided people with the cattle by which they draw near to Him. Therefore it is not right that a rite be appointed for other than Allah, because that which does not create the cattle by which one draws near, nor provides them to people, does not deserve to have a rite appointed for it for the offering of them. Thus the rites are not multiplied. The indefiniteness in His saying ﴿that they may mention the name of Allah﴾ and what more clearly indicates it is the consequence expressed by His saying ﴿so your God is one God﴾. The discourse implies following the rest of the communities, the people of the true religions. And (ʿalā) may be used for figurative elevation (al-istiʿlāʾ al-majāzī), connected to ﴿yadhkurū ism Allāh﴾ (that they may mention the name of Allah), with an omitted noun after (ʿalā), estimated as "ihdāʾ mā razaqahum" (the offering of what He provided them), meaning: at the offering of what He provided them, that is, slaughtering it or sacrificing it. It may also be that (ʿalā) carries the meaning of the lām of causation, and the meaning is: that they may mention the name of Allah for the sake of what He provided them of the beast of cattle.

Page 260
Upon this is built the singularity of divinity in His saying ﴿so your God is one God, so submit to Him﴾, meaning: since He has appointed for you one rite, He has thereby alerted you that He is one God, and if there were many gods, their laws would be different. This first consequence is a preparation for the consequence that follows it, which is the purpose, so there occurred in the composition a change by means of fronting and postponing. The original composition is: "So to Him submit," because your God is one God. The fronting of the prepositional phrase in ﴿so to Him submit﴾ is for restriction (hasr), meaning: submit to Him and not to other than Him. Islam (al-islam) is complete surrender (al-inqiyad al-tamm), which is sincerity (al-ikhlas) in obedience, meaning: do not devote yourselves except to Allah, that is, abandon all the rites that were established for other than Allah, and do not perform rites except at the rite that He appointed for you, as an allusion to rebuttal of the polytheists.

The majority (al-jumhur) read "mansakan" with a fatha on the sin, and Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the sin. On both readings it is a noun of place for the act of nusuk, which is slaughtering. However, on the reading of the majority it follows the analogical pattern, since its analogical form for a noun of place is with fatha, being from nasaka yansuku with a damma on the ʿayn in the present tense. As for the reading with kasra, it is a sama'i (transmitted, irregular) form, like masjid from sajada yasjudu. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "It seems that al-Kisa'i heard it from the Arabs."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 35:**

﴿And give good tidings to the humble (al-mukhbitin)﴾ [Al-Hajj: 34] ﴿those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and the patient in what befalls them, and those who establish the prayer, and from what We have provided them they spend﴾.

This is a parenthetical interjection within the enumeration of favours. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the bearers of these qualities are the Muslims.

*Al-mukhbit* (the humble one; one who is free of arrogance): the *mukhbit* is the one who is humble and in whom there is no arrogance. The original sense of *al-mukhbit* is one who travels the *khabt*, which is a low-lying place, the opposite of an ascending slope. Then the term was borrowed for the humble person, as if he had made himself travel into lowness. The intended meaning here is the believers, because humility is among their characteristics, just as arrogance is among the marks of the polytheists. The Exalted said: ﴿Thus does Allah seal every heart of an arrogant tyrant﴾ [Ghafir: 35].

*Al-wajal* means intense fear. It was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you"﴾ [Al-Hijr: 52], in Surah al-Hijr. He followed the description of *al-mukhbitin* with four qualities: the trembling of hearts at the mention of Allah, patience over harm suffered in His way, the establishment of the prayer, and spending. All four of these qualities are manifestations of humility. The intended meaning is not that one must combine all these qualities, since some believers do not find anything to spend from; rather, the intended meaning is one who does not neglect any one of them when it is possible to perform it.

By *spending* is meant spending on the needy, weak believers, because that is the practice of the humble. As for spending on the weak and on companions (for display or pride), that is something done by the arrogant among the Arabs, as was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿It has been prescribed for you that when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, a bequest to parents and relatives﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 180]. This is comparable to spending on the boon companions in drinking gatherings, and comparable to completing the *iysar* (the gambling arrows) at the places of gambling, as al-Nabigha said:

*Indeed I complete my arrows for them, and I give them the generous gifts, and I clothe the great dish with fat.*

By *patience* is meant patience over the harm that afflicts them in the cause of Islam. As for patience in wars and over the loss of loved ones, this is something in which the stout-hearted among the arrogant and the humble share. Much of that patience is an Islamic virtue when it is an adoption of the manners of Islam. The Exalted said: ﴿And give good tidings to the patient, who, when a calamity afflicts them, say, "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 155], and so on.

[Page 261]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 36:

﴿And the camels – We have made them for you among the symbols of Allah. In them there is good for you, so mention the name of Allah over them as they stand in ranks. Then when their sides have fallen (lifeless), eat from them and feed the contented and the beggar. Thus We have subjugated them for you, that you may be grateful.﴾

This is coordinated with the clause ﴿And for every community We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾ [al-Hajj: 34], meaning: We have appointed a rite of sacrifice (qurban) and offerings (hada'ya), and We have made the camels that are sent as offerings and by which one draws near to Allah among the symbols of Allah. The meaning is that Allah commanded the sacrifice of camels during the Hajj from the time of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and made it a compensation for what is permitted to be relaxed in the rites of Hajj. He commanded voluntary offering of them and promised great reward for them, so they received through this divine designation blessing, sanctity and inviolability, which joined them to the symbols of Allah. He thereby bestowed a favour upon the people through what the word (lakum, "for you") implies.

Al-budn is the plural of badanah (with a vowel on the ba' and sukun on the dal, i.e., badana). It is a large camel, great of body, and it is a noun derived from al-badanah, which means largeness of the body and fatness. Its verb is like karuma and nasara. The pattern badanah is not an adjective, but a noun derived from the root of the adjective. Its plural is budn. The analogical plural of this form would be with a damma on the dal, like khushub (plural of khashabah) and thumur (plural of thamarah), so the sukun on the dal is a common lightening. The name badanah came to be applied specifically to the camel designated for the hadi (offering).

In the Muwatta', from Abu Hurayrah: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a man driving a badanah, and he said: "Ride it." He said: "It is a badanah." He said: "Ride it." He said: "It is a badanah." He said: "Ride it, woe to you, on the second or third time."

So the man's saying, "It is a badanah," is definitively for the purpose of its being his offering for Hajj.

The placing of (al-budn) before its governing verb is for emphasis on it, to draw attention to its importance. The restriction to camels specifically is because they are the most excellent of offerings due to the abundance of their meat. Cows and sheep have been added to them by the evidence of the Sunnah. The name for all of these is hadi. The meaning of their being among the symbols of Allah is that Allah made them markers announcing the Hajj, and made for them a sanctity. This is the reason behind their naming the act of marking the sign by which the offering camel is known on its hide ish'ar (marking).

Malik said in the Muwatta': When 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar sent an offering from Madinah, he would garland it and mark it at Dhu al-Hulayfah, garlanding it before marking it... He would garland it with two sandals and mark it on the left side, with a stab in its hump. Thus ish'ar is a preparation for slaughter. He counted them among the sacred things in His saying ﴿Do not violate the symbols of Allah, nor the sacred month, nor the offering﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2] in Surat al-'Uqud.

The placing of (lakum) before the subject is so that the subject can be indefinite, its tanwin indicating glorification. The placing of (fiha) before its complement, which is (khayr), is for emphasis on what it contains and comprises of benefits.

Al-khayr means benefit: what accrues to people of benefit in this world, from the benefit of the poor from its meat, skins, coverings, sandals and garlands; what accrues to the offerers and their households of satiety from its meat on the day of sacrifice; and the good of the Hereafter, from the reward of the offerers and the reward of gratitude from those who give its meat to their Lord who has made them rich by it. From this it follows that people are commanded to mention the name of Allah over them at the time of slaughtering them.

Sawaffa is the plural of saffah. It is said: suffa when it is with others in a row, by being joined to it. Perhaps they used to line them up at the place of sacrifice on the day of sacrifice in Mina, since there was in Mina a site prepared for slaughter, which is the manhar. It has been reported in the hadith of Muslim from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah concerning the Farewell Pilgrimage, in which he said: "Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went to the manhar, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ slaughtered sixty-three camels with his own hand, stabbing them with a spear in his hand. Then he gave the spear to 'Ali, and he slaughtered what remained," meaning what was left, and they were one hundred camels. This indicates that they were gathered together and close to one another.

Sawaffa is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive in His saying (alayha, "over them"). The benefit of this state is mentioning the excellences of the sight of the camels, for the people making their camels stand in gathered and ordered rows, not scattered, adds majesty to their appearance. Close to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as if they were a structure joined firmly﴾ [al-Saff: 4].

The meaning of (wajabat) is fell, i.e., to the ground, and it is a metaphor for the departure of the soul by which movement is independent. The purpose of this timing is hastening to benefit from them, rushing toward the good that results from this in this world through feeding the poor and their owners eating from them, for it is recommended that the Hajj pilgrim's breakfast on the day of sacrifice be from his offering, and likewise the good that results from the reward of the Hereafter. The command in His saying (fa-kulu minha, "so eat from them") is general; it admits of obligation, permissibility and recommendation. The evidence against obligation is clear, because a person is not obligated to do what the motive for doing is already from his nature. Allah only intended to abolish what was among the people of the Jahiliyyah, namely the prohibition of the offerer eating from the meat of his offering, so the question remains whether it is purely permissible or recommended. The jurists differed regarding eating from the meat of obligatory offerings.

Malik said: eating from the meat of obligatory offerings is permitted. For him it is recommended, and one does not eat from the expiation for harm, the penalty for hunting, or the offering vowed for the poor. The proof for Malik is the explicit wording of the verse, for it is general except where evidence establishes its prohibition, namely the three things excepted. Abu Hanifah said: one eats from the offering of tamattu' and qiran, and does not eat from the obligatory offering that the pilgrim designated at his ihram. Al-Shafi'i said: one does not eat from the meat of offerings under any circumstance, relying on analogy: the offerer is obligated to remove the offering from his property, so how could he eat from it? So Ibn al-'Arabi reported. If this is the utmost of al-Shafi'i's argument, then it is an unpersuasive inference, and the wording of the Qur'an contradicts it, especially since the eating of the Prophet ﷺ and his companions from the meat of offerings is established by sound hadiths.

Ahmad said: one eats from the obligatory offerings except the penalty for hunting and the vowed offering.

As for the command in His saying ﴿and feed the contented and the beggar﴾, al-Shafi'i said: it is for obligation, and this is the most correct view. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the explicit view of Malik. I say: what is known from Malik's view is that if the offerer confined himself to something like his offering and did not give charity from it, he would be sinful.

Al-qani' is one who has the quality of qunu'; this is humble supplication. It is said: qana'a, in the pattern of sa'ala, qunu'an with a damma on the qaf, when he asked humbly.

As for qana'ah (contentment), its verb is of the pattern ta'iba, and the present tense is the same despite the difference of meaning. Among the finest things collected of such counterparts is what al-Khafaji recited:

The slave is free if he is content, and the free man is a slave if he is contented (with less).
So be content, and do not be covetous, for nothing disgraces but greed.

In al-Zamakhshari's Maqamat: O Abu al-Qasim, be content (iqna') with contentment (qana'ah), not with humble supplication (qunu'), you will be free of every giver and withholder.

In the Muwatta', in the Book of Hunting: Malik said: al-qani' is the poor person.

Al-mu'tarr is the active participle of i'tarra, when one presents himself for a gift, that is, without asking directly but by allusion, which is to come to the place of giving. It is said i'tarra when he presented himself. In the Muwatta', in the Book of Hunting: Malik said: I heard that al-mu'tarr is the visitor, meaning that it is from 'arra when he visited. The intended meaning is the visit of presenting oneself for a gift. This interpretation is better, and it is supported by the fact that He joined al-mu'tarr to al-qani' by conjunction, and the conjunction indicates difference; if they were of one meaning, one would not be conjoined to the other, just as in His saying ﴿and feed the distressed poor﴾ [al-Hajj: 28] it is not conjoined.

The clause ﴿Thus We have subjugated them for you﴾ is a resumptive clause for the purpose of favour, by what He created of creatures for the benefit of people. The sign indicating His will in this is that He subjugated them to people despite the weakness of man and the strength of those cattle: one man takes a number of them and drives them submissively, and they are pained by the marking and then by the stabbing. Had Allah not deposited in their nature this submission, they would not be less able than some wild animals which are weaker than them, which flee from man and are not subjugated to him.

His saying (thus, kadhalika) is like its counterparts, meaning: like that wondrous subjugation which you see, was their subjugation for you. The meaning of ﴿that you may be grateful﴾ is: We created them subjugated for you as an inducement for you to thank Allah by singling Him out in worship. This is an allusion against the polytheists, who placed polytheism in the position of gratitude.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 37:

Page 267
﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches God, but it is your piety that reaches Him.﴾
This sentence is in the position of a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the sentence ﴿Thus We have subjected them to you, so that you may give thanks.﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]. That is, it indicates that We subjected them to you so that you would give thanks to Me, that God does not benefit from any of their flesh or their blood at the time when you are able to benefit from them. So He does not desire from you, in this regard, anything except that you be mindful of Him (tuqa).

Al-nayl means attainment (al-isabah). It is said: nalahu, i.e., he reached it and arrived at it. It is also said in the sense of obtaining (ahraza), for it contains the meaning of attainment, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran: 92], and His saying ﴿and they plotted what they could not attain﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74]. The purpose of negating that their flesh and blood reach God is to nullify what the polytheists used to do of splashing blood on the slaughtering places and around the Ka'bah; they used to slaughter at al-Marwah. Al-Hasan said: "They used to smear themselves with the blood of the sacrificial offerings, and they used to cut the flesh of the offerings into pieces and set them up around the Ka'bah as an offering to God, Exalted is He," meaning in addition to what they gave to the needy. In His saying ﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches God, but it is your piety that reaches Him﴾ there is a hint that the shedding of blood and the cutting of flesh are not intended in themselves as acts of worship, but they are a means to benefit people through the offerings, since they are not benefited from through their flesh, skins and parts except by slaughtering or sacrificing, and that the purpose of their legislation is the benefit of the people who offer them and others.

As for those who offer them, their benefit is by eating from them on their day of festival, as the Prophet ﷺ said when prohibiting fasting on the Day of Sacrifice,

Page 268
"A day on which you eat of your rites (nusuk)," and this is a benefit to themselves and to their families, even if by storing some of it until they return to their own regions. As for others, the benefit is for one of the pilgrims who has no offering, by eating what those close to him and his companions give him, and the benefit of the needy among the people of the Haram by being satisfied, by taking provision from them, and by benefiting from their hides, their covers and their garlands. As His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿God has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of standing for the people, and the Sacred Month, and the offering and the garlands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97]. The question has repeatedly arisen whether, when the offerings exceed the need of the people of the season, with certainty or a probability close to certainty, as has been witnessed in the pilgrimage seasons, what remains of them alive should be sold and its price spent to relieve the needy, which is better than slaughtering them when no one desires them. And if the meats that were not cut up in time, and which exceed the needs of the needy, were preserved by a method that prevents their spoiling, so that they could be benefited from throughout the year, that would be more beneficial to the needy. The opinions of those among the jurists of this age who have undertaken to issue fatwas have wavered on the answer to this, and the statements of those who issued fatwas almost agreed that preserving them contradicts the worship of offering them.

As for me, what I see is that resorting to either of the two cases, namely selling or preserving what exceeds the needs of people during the days of the pilgrimage, so that the needy may benefit from them throughout their year, is more in accordance with the intent of the Lawgiver, avoiding the waste of what remains of them, observing the purpose of the Sharia of benefiting the needy and preserving wealth, while not leaving off slaughtering and sacrificing for the amount needed from them, which is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So mention the name of God over them while they stand in rows﴾ [al-Hajj: 36] and His saying ﴿Thus He has subjected them to you so that you may magnify God for having guided you﴾, combining the legal purposes.

Page 269
Another scenario arises, which is distributing the quantities sufficient for benefit over the three days of sacrifice, so that not all the offerings are slaughtered on the first day in pursuit of the virtue of hastening. For the piety that reaches God from those offerings is their being delivered for benefit. This is an analogy to the principle of preserving wealth, as they have stipulated in the case of selling a horse held in endowment (habs) when it suffers something that leads to its destruction or to the loss of its benefit, and in exchanging the yield of an endowment when it falls into ruin. The ruling on offerings is composed of both worship (ta'abbud) and causal reasoning (ta'lil). The meaning of causal reasoning in it is stronger. Its 'illah is the benefit of the Muslims, and the path to the 'illah is the implicit indication in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So eat from them and feed the contented one and the beggar﴾ [al-Hajj: 36].
Know that the supposition of drawing near to God by smearing with the blood of the sacrificial offerings, and of the one drawn near benefiting from that blood, is an ancient pagan belief. They used to cast away what they drew near with of meat and food, and would not let anyone eat it. The Greeks used to roast the meat of sacrifices on the fire until it became ash, imagining that the smell of roasting pleases the gods to whom the sacrifices are offered. The Egyptians used to throw food to the crocodiles in the Nile because they were sacred.

Al-Jumhur read (yanalu) and (yanaluhu) with a yā' at the beginning of both. Ya'qub read them with a tā' at the beginning, in consideration of what is permissible regarding the pronoun of a plural of non-rational beings. Perhaps they would throw pieces of meat, thinking them to be for God, so perhaps a needy person would reach them, or perhaps they would not notice them, and then the beasts of prey would eat them or they would spoil.

Piety includes mentioning God's name over them and giving some of them in charity to the needy. And (yanaluhu) is a mushakalah with the first (yanal), the word "nayl" being borrowed for the attachment of knowledge. The knowledge of God of their piety is likened to the arrival of the thing sent to God, a likeness whose aspect is attainment in each, and the mushakalah made it good.

Page 270
The (min) in His saying (minkum) is for origin (ibtida'iyyah). It is a reinforcement (tarshih) of the metaphor. For this reason He expressed it with the wording ﴿the piety from you﴾ rather than "your piety" or "piety" alone, even though the omitted alternative would be more concise, because this elaboration carries an additional meaning of eloquence.
* * *
﴿Thus He has subjected them to you so that you may magnify God for having guided you, and give good news to the doers of good.﴾
This is a repetition of the sentence ﴿Thus We have subjected them to you﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]. It is for building upon it the notice that praising God, the One who subjected them, is the essence of the thanks alluded to in the preceding verse, so the meaning of the two sentences became synonymous, and emphasis occurred. What is said regarding the sentence ﴿Thus He has subjected them to you so that you may magnify God﴾ is like what is said regarding its counterparts. As for His saying ﴿for having guided you﴾, the (ʿalā) in it is for figurative elevation, which carries the meaning of empowerment. That is, so that you may magnify God when you are empowered to slaughter them. The (mā) is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted along with its preposition. The estimate is: "for what He guided you to," i.e., of the livestock. The guidance to them is legislation regarding those times, so that people may benefit from them and the inhabitants of the Haram, whom God chose to be callers to monotheism, may be provided for, not departing from that place. The address is to the Muslims. The change of style is a deviation from the apparent requirement, by using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, to indicate that they have been guided and have acted upon the guidance, so they did good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 38:

[Page 271]
﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed. Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate.﴾

This is an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), answering a question that arises in the minds of the believers, stemming from His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and avert [others] from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 25], and so on. For He threatened the polytheists with a painful punishment for their hindering [people] from the way of Allah and from the Sacred Mosque. He gave glad tidings to the believers who are humble (al-mukhbitin) and who do good, with what immediately suggests the opposite of the threat against the polytheists, namely the reward of the Hereafter. The discourse on this was long, followed by what came after it, so the souls of the believers yearned (tashawwafat) to know the outcome of their affair in this world: Will they be granted victory over their enemies, or will all good be stored up for them until the Next Abode? So the context was fitting for Allah to reassure their souls that, just as He has prepared for them the bliss of the Hereafter, He is also their defender (mudafi') in this world and their helper. The object of (yudafi'u) is omitted because the context indicates it.

Thus the address is directed to the believers, and therefore its opening with the emphatic particle is either merely to confirm the report, or to treat as certain what is not in doubt, owing to the intensity of their longing for victory and their impatience for it. The expression by the relative pronoun (alladhina amanu), because of what it contains of faith, indicates the reason for constructing the statement this way: that Allah's defense of them is on account of their faith.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read the word (yudafi'u) with an alif after the dal, which conveys the intensity of the repelling. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read (yadfa'u) without an alif after the dal. The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate﴾ gives the reason for the defense by its being on behalf of those who believed: that Allah does not love the disbelieving treacherous ones,

[Page 272]
so for this reason He repels [harm] from the believers, warding off the harm of the disbelievers. In this there is an indication of the omitted object of (yudafi'u), namely: He defends against the treacherous disbelievers.

Al-Khawwan: one who is intensely treacherous. Al-Khawn, like al-khiyanah, is betrayal of a trust. By al-khawwan is meant the disbeliever, because disbelief is a betrayal of the covenant of Allah which He took from creatures, that they should affirm His oneness. He placed it in the natural disposition (fitrah) and conveyed it to people through the tongues of the messengers; thus that which He deposited in their natural disposition is brought to awareness.

Al-Kafur: one who is intensely ungrateful. The word (kull) in the context of negation conveys the generality of the negation of Allah's love from all disbelievers, since the context admits no other meaning. And it is not to be supposed from His saying (﴿does not love every treacherous one﴾) that He loves some of the treacherous ones, because the word (kull) is a fixed noun that does not imply an attribute, so there is no supposition that the negation is directed at the meaning of totality drawn from the word (kull). It is not like His saying, ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], which might suggest that negating the intensity of injustice does not entail negating slight injustice.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 39:

﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged. And indeed, Allah is capable of giving them victory.﴾

This sentence stands in apposition (badal al-ishtimal) to the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who believe﴾ [al-Hajj: 38], because Allah's defense of the people sometimes takes the form of permitting them to fight those whom Allah wills to repel from them. For when permission is given to them to fight, He has thereby taken on the responsibility of giving them victory.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read (أُذِنَ) (udhina, "permission was given") in the passive voice (bina' lil-na'ib, with the deputy of the subject). The rest read it in the active voice (bina' ila al-fa'il).

Page 273

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hafs and Abu Ja'far read (يُقاتَلُونَ) (yuqatalūna, "are fought against") with a fatha on the tā' (al-ta' al-fawqiyya) and in the passive voice (mabniyyan ila al-majhul). The rest read it with a kasra on the tā' and in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il). The phrase "those who are fought against" refers to the believers on both readings, because when they are fought against, they are also fighting. Fighting is used in a figurative sense, either through its root or through the past-tense form. On the reading with a fatha on the tā', the fighting intended is figurative killing, which is harm. As for the reading (yuqatilūna) with a kasra on the tā', the past-tense form is used figuratively to mean preparation and readiness, that is: permission was given to those who prepared themselves for fighting and awaited Allah's permission. This is because the polytheists were inflicting severe harm on the believers in Makkah, so the Muslims would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from among the beaten and wounded, complaining of their oppression. He would say to them: "Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight." When he emigrated, this verse was revealed after the Pledge of 'Aqaba, granting them permission to prepare to defend themselves. There had been no fighting before that, as is indicated by the words of Allah that follow it: ﴿Those who were expelled from their homes without right﴾ [al-Hajj: 40].

The preposition (ba') in (﴿بِأنَّهم ظُلِمُوا﴾, "because they have been wronged") I consider to be connected to (أُذِنَ) by virtue of its implying the sense of informing, that is: We informed them that they are wronged. This informing is a metonymy for permission to defend, because when you say to someone, "You are wronged," it is as if you have called upon him against his oppressor and reminded him of the obligation to defend. The indication of this is the phrase that follows it: ﴿And indeed, Allah is capable of giving them victory﴾. The phrase (﴿بِأنَّهم ظُلِمُوا﴾) serves as the deputy subject of (أُذِنَ) on the reading with a damma on the hamza, or as the object on the reading with a fatha on the hamza. The exegetes held that the ba' is causal (sababiyya) and that the thing permitted is omitted, indicated by the word (يُقاتَلُونَ), that is: permission was given to them to fight. This applies on both readings of (يُقاتَلُونَ). The interpretation I have adopted is more fitting and more elegant.

Page 274

The sentence ﴿And indeed, Allah is capable of giving them victory﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to the sentence ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against﴾, that is: permission was given to them for this, and they were reminded of Allah's power to grant them victory. This is a promise from Allah of victory, expressed in the manner of the speech of the Mighty and Powerful, by presenting the promise in the form of a statement that this is something certain in His knowledge, similar to the expressions "perhaps it will be such-and-such," or "we have some good," or the like, such that the one awaiting [the outcome] retains no doubt about attaining what he seeks.

The emphasis of this statement by a particle of emphasis (inna and the lam) serves to affirm it, or to imply a rebuke by treating them as if they were wavering about it, since they had been slow to see victory.

**[p. 275]**

﴿Those who were expelled from their homes without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah."﴾

This is a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for ﴿those who are fought against﴾. The attachment of this relative clause to them hints that "fighting" here means harm, and the greatest of that harm is expelling them from their homes, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And persecution is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191]. The phrase ﴿without right﴾ is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) referring to the pronoun in *ukhrijū* ("were expelled"). The meaning is: they were expelled while being characterized by the absence of a right that would have required their expulsion. A person has a right in his homeland and in living among his people. This right is established by *fiṭrah* (natural disposition), because it is part of human nature that one who grows up in a land and is born among a people is equal to all the people of that place in the right to dwell in their homeland and among their people, in the same way that it has been established for the majority of them in that place, whether by ancient upbringing or by conquest and dominance over its inhabitants. As ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said:

"Indeed, it is their land. They fought over it in the *jāhiliyyah* (pre-Islamic age) and embraced Islam upon it."

This right does not cease except by a cause established by the *sharīʿah* (divine law) or by customs that existed before the law. As Zuhayr said:

"The right has three ends: an oath, or a feud, or exile."

Among the laws of the sharīʿah is exile and banishment (*taghrīb* and *nafy*), and among the laws of the people of the *jāhiliyyah* is exile and disowning (*jalāʾ* and *khalʿ*). This happens only in response to an aggression that a person commits against his own people, for which they find no other means of deterrence. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah."﴾ Their belief in Allah does not lead to any aggression against others, since it is something confined to their souls, and declaring it verbally does not harm anyone else. Therefore, attacking them by expelling them from their homes for this reason is manifest injustice and the use of force to carry out that injustice.

The exception in His words ﴿except that they say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ is an exception from the generality of *ḥaqq* (right). Since what is meant by "right" is a right that requires expulsion, that is, a right held against them, this exception is used in the figure of *istiʿārah tahakkumiyyah* (ironic metaphor). That is: if there is any right against them, it is that they say, "Our Lord is Allah." From this is derived the emphasis on the absence of any right against them, by way of inferring what might be imagined to be a right against them. This is from the emphasis of a thing by means of something that seems to negate it. Among the rhetoricians this is called *taʾkīd al-madḥ bi-mā yushbih al-dhamm* (emphasizing praise by means of what resembles blame). Its example is the words of al-Nābighah:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords
are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

This verse was undoubtedly revealed in Medina.

* * *

**[p. 276]**

﴿And were it not that Allah repels some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned would surely have been demolished. And Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty.﴾

This is a *iʿtirāḍ* (parenthetical insertion) between the clause ﴿Permission has been given to those who are fought against…﴾ and His words ﴿those who, if We establish them in the land…﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 41]. When the clause ﴿Permission has been given to those who are fought against﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 39] contained permission for the Muslims to defend themselves against the polytheists, it was followed by an explanation of the wisdom behind this permission to defend, with an honoring of this defense and of those who undertake it, stating that it is a defense of the truth and of the religion from which all the people of the monotheistic religions benefit: the Jews, the Christians, and the Muslims. It is not a defense solely for the benefit of the Muslims.

The *wāw* in His words ﴿And were it not that Allah repels…﴾ up to the end is parenthetical and is called *wāw al-istiʾnāf* (the resumptive *wāw*). The purpose of this sentence is to give the reason for the content of the clause ﴿Permission has been given to those who are fought against…﴾.

The particle *lawlā* (were it not for) is a particle of *imtināʿ li-wujūd* (prevention of the consequent due to the existence of the condition). That is, it is a particle indicating that its consequent is negated because its condition exists; that is, when the content of its conditional clause is realized. Thus it requires two clauses. The meaning is: were it not for the people's defense of the places of worship of the Muslims, the polytheists would have prevailed and would have exceeded their bounds with regard to the Muslims, attacking what lies beside their lands from the other religious communities opposed to the community of polytheism, and they would have demolished their places of worship: monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques, belonging to the religions that oppose polytheism. Therefore, the mention of monasteries and churches is an *idmāj* (inclusion of related matters) so that they may pay attention to the support given to the Muslims. The definite article in *al-nās* (the people) is the definite article of prior reference (*ʿahd*), that is, the people who are fighting, namely the Muslims and the polytheists of Mecca.

It is also possible that what is meant is: were it not for what preceded Islam of Allah's permission to the nations of monotheism to fight the people of polytheism, as David fought Goliath, and as Solomon overcame the queen of Sheba, the polytheists would have obliterated the landmarks of monotheism, just as Nebuchadnezzar (*Bukhtanaṣr*) obliterated the Temple of Solomon. In that case this sentence is a *tadhyīl* (concluding addition) to the clause ﴿Permission has been given to those who are fought against because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 39]. That is: permission was given to the Muslims to fight just as it was given to the nations before them, so that the polytheists would not transgress against them, as they had transgressed against those before them when Allah had not permitted them to fight. In this case the definite article in *al-nās* is the definite article of the genus. The attribution of the *difāʿ* (defense) to Allah is a *isnād majāzī ʿaqlī* (figurative rational attribution), because it is permission given to people to repel attacks from their places of worship, so Allah's permission was the cause of the repelling. This urges the people of the religions to unite in resisting the people of polytheism.

Nāfiʿ, Abū Jaʿfar, and Yaʿqūb read *difāʿ* (with *alif*). The rest of the readers read *dafʿ* (without *alif*), with a *fatḥah* on the *dāl*. *Baʿḍahum* (some of them) is a *badal* (substitute) from *al-nās*, a substitute of part. *Bi-baʿḍin* (by means of some) is connected to *difāʿ*, and the *bāʾ* is the *bāʾ* of instrument.

*Al-hadm* means the collapse and toppling of a building.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Abū Jaʿfar read *lahudimat* with a light *dāl* (*lahudimat*). The rest read it with a doubled *dāl* (*lahuddimat*), for emphasis in the demolition, that is, *lahuddimat* as a demolition arising from rage, to the extent that they leave no trace of it.

*Al-ṣawāmiʿ* is the plural of *ṣawmaʿah*, on the pattern *fawʿalah*. It is a tall, elongated building that is ascended by stairs, with a room at its top. The monks used to take it for worship so that they would be remote from people's distractions. They used to light lamps in it to help them stay awake for worship and to illuminate the path for passers-by. For this reason the *ṣawmaʿah* was called a *manārah* (minaret). Imru' al-Qays said:

"It lights the darkness in the evening
like the beacon of an ascetic monk devoted to worship."

*Al-biyaʿ* is the plural of *biyaʿah*, with a *kasrah* on the *bāʾ* and a silent *yāʾ*, meaning the place of worship of the Christians. The origin of its derivation is not known. Perhaps it is an *muʿarrab* (Arabicized word) from another language.

*Al-ṣalawāt* is the plural of *ṣalāh*, and here it is meant as the synagogues of the Jews. It is an Arabicization of the word *Ṣalūthā*, with a *thāʾ* at its end followed by an *alif*. When it was Arabicized they replaced the *thāʾ* with a *tāʾ* and pluralized it in the same way.

It is related from Mujāhid, al-Jaḥdarī, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and Abū Rajāʾ that they read it here as *ṣalawāth* with a *thāʾ* at its end. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid read it as *Ṣilwīthā*, with a *kasrah* on the *ṣād*, a silent *lām*, a *kasrah* on the *wāw*, and a short *alif* after the *thāʾ*, that is the *thāʾ* (of *muthallathah*). As al-Qurṭubī said, this root has escaped the people of the language, and this is a remarkable oversight.

*Al-masājid* is the name for the place of prostration in every place of worship other than the three kinds mentioned before it at the time this verse was revealed. Accordingly, the verse was revealed at the beginning of the Muslims' emigration to Medina, when they built the Mosque of Qubāʾ and the Mosque of Medina.

The clause ﴿in which the name of Allah is much mentioned﴾ is a qualifier (*ṣifah*). It is generally the case that a qualifier that comes after a series of coordinated clauses refers to the thing qualified in all of those clauses. Therefore it has been said that the qualifier ﴿in which the name of Allah is mentioned﴾ refers to the monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques, all four mentioned before it, and they are the antecedent of the pronoun in *fīhā* (in them).

The benefit of this description is to hint that the reason for their demolition is that the name of Allah is much mentioned in them. That is, the names of the idols of the polytheists are not mentioned in them. When they expelled the Muslims without any cause other than that they mention the name of Allah, saying, "Our Lord is Allah," it is inevitable that, in order to erase the mention of Allah's name from their land, they demolish the places established for mentioning the name of Allah much, that is, without mentioning idols. Thus *al-kathrah* (much) is used to mean continuity, encompassing all times. In this there is a hint that these places have a religious benefit, which is the mention of Allah's name.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandād, one of the imams of the Mālikīs from the people of the late fourth century, said: "This verse includes the prohibition of demolishing the churches, synagogues, and fire-temples of the *dhimmīs* (protected non-Muslims)." End of quote.

I say: As for fire-temples, this verse does not include a prohibition against demolishing them, for the name of Allah is not mentioned in them. The prohibition of their demolition is rather the *ʿaqd al-dhimmah* (covenant of protection) that is concluded between their people and the Muslims. It has been said that the qualifier refers to particular mosques only.

The monasteries are mentioned first, before the others, because the monks' monasteries were more numerous in the lands of the Arabs than other places of worship, and they were more famous among them, because they used to be guided by their lights during their journeys and would take refuge in them. The mention of churches after them is by way of association, since they are the places of worship of the Christians, like the monasteries. As for the mention of synagogues after them, it is because the context was ready for mentioning them. The mosques are mentioned last because they are more general, and it is the nature of generality that the specific follows it, completing the benefit.

His words ﴿And Allah will surely support those who support Him﴾ are coordinated with the clause ﴿And were it not that Allah repels…﴾. That is, Allah commanded the Muslims to defend their religion, and guaranteed them victory in that defense, because by defending themselves they support the religion of Allah, as if they had supported Allah. For this reason He emphasized the sentence with the *lām* of oath and the *nūn* of emphasis. This sentence is a concluding addition (*tadhyīl*) to what precedes it, because of the generality it contains, which includes the Muslims whom the polytheists expelled. The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 74] is a rationale for the clause ﴿And Allah will surely support those who support Him﴾, that is, their victory was assured because their helper is capable of that by strength and might. Here *al-quwwah* (strength) is used to mean power, and *al-ʿizzah* (might) is used in its literal sense, because *al-ʿizzah* is *al-manaʿah* (invulnerability), that is, that no one other than its possessor can dominate its possessor.

**[p. 280]**

It is a substitute (*badal*) from ﴿those who were expelled from their homes without right﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. Thus, what is meant by ﴿those who, if We establish them in the land﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 41] is the emigrants. So it is praise for the emigrants and a testimony to them of the perfection of their religion. It is reported from ʿUthmān: "By Allah, this is praise before trial." That is, before testing. So it is among the reports of the unseen that Allah knew from their condition. The meaning of ﴿if We establish them in the land﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 41] is with the victory that We promised them in His words ﴿And indeed Allah is competent to give them victory﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 39].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 41:

﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, perform the prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.﴾

It is permissible that this be a substitute (badal) for the relative pronoun "man" (whoever) in His words (﴿whoever helps Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]). In that case the meaning is: every person from the generations of Muslims who supports the religion. That is, We will establish them through the promised victory if they support the religion of Allah. On both possibilities, the discourse is directed toward alerting them to give thanks for the blessing of victory by doing what Allah has commanded of the foundations of Islam, for by doing so their victory endures, the bond of their community remains intact, and their affairs are safe from disorder. If they deviate from that, they have neglected the guarantee of their victory, and their affair is left to Allah. As for the establishment of the prayer, it is because of what it indicates of upholding the religion and renewing its effect in souls. As for giving zakat, it is so that the individuals of the community are close to one another in the order of their livelihood. As for enjoining the ma'ruf (what is recognized as good) and forbidding the munkar (what is recognized as evil), it is for the implementation of the laws of Islam among the rest of the community, by their own initiative.

And al-tamkin (the establishing, empowering): its meaning is "strengthening" (al-tawthiq). Its root is the settling of a thing in a place, and it is used here in the sense of granting authority and possession. "Al-ard" (the land) is generic, meaning Allah grants them authority over some portion of the earth, so that this becomes their condition in what is their possession and what their hands have extended over.

Page 281

The words of the Exalted were already mentioned: ﴿And We have certainly established you upon the earth and made for you therein means of livelihood﴾ [al-A'raf: 10] in surah al-A'raf, and His words ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾ [Yusuf: 21] in surah Yusuf.

The meaning of al-ma'ruf is what is established among the matters of the religion. This may be either by it being recognized (ma'ruf) by the whole community, which is what is known of the religion by necessity, so all of the community equally knows that it is part of the religion; or by it being recognized by a group among them, which is the subtle rulings, so the ones whose task it is to know it, namely the scholars, are the ones who enjoin it, according to the differing levels of knowledge and the differing ranks of its scholars.

Al-munkar is that which by its nature is to be denied within the religion, that is, not to be accepted as being from the religion. This is every act that enters into the affairs of the community and the Shari'ah while contradicting it. From this it is known that what is intended by al-munkar is the acts that are sought to be introduced into the Shari'ah of the Muslims while contradicting it. Therefore, it does not include what people do in matters of their customs that fall within the sphere of the permissible (mubah), nor what they do in matters of their religion that are of the kind of religious practices, such as the acts that fall under general religious principles, and the acts legislated by way of qiyas (analogy) and the principles of the Shari'ah, which are among the fields of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) and deep understanding of the religion.

Forbidding the munkar leads back to enjoining the ma'ruf, and likewise enjoining the ma'ruf leads back to forbidding the munkar. The verse combined them only in consideration of what the souls of people first turn to when observing actions, and so that the ma'ruf would be an indication of denying the munkar, and vice versa, since things are distinguished by their opposites. The method of reasoning and argument has always included reasoning by contraries and inversions.

Page 282

﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs.﴾

This is a conjunction (atf) upon the clause ﴿Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 40], or upon the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Powerful, Mighty﴾ [al-Hajj: 74]. The final result is one, namely confirming that the victory will occur, because He who promised it is not prevented from fulfilling His promise by any obstacle. In it there is also a comforting of the emigrants (muhajirun), so that they do not consider the victory slow in coming.

Al-'aqibah: the last part of a thing and what follows the present. Its feminine form is due to considering the sense of a state, and through frequent usage it became a noun. In the hadith of Heraclius: "Then the outcome will be theirs" (thumma takunu lahumu al-'aqibah). The placing of the prepositional phrase first here is for emphasis and to alert that whatever belongs to Allah, He directs it however He wills.

**[p. 283]**

When he (Allah) censured the polytheists for their wrongdoings in matters of religion, namely their associating partners with Allah, their denial of the Resurrection, their turning people away from Islam and from the Sacred Mosque, and what is related to these in the purpose of the surah, which is the expulsion of the Prophet's people from it, he turned here to their misguidance in denying the Prophet (ﷺ). By this he intended to console the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to present them with examples of the nations whom Allah uprooted, and to warn them that they will meet the same fate.

﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud had already denied [their messengers] before them,﴾ ﴿and the people of Abraham and the people of Lot,﴾ ﴿and the companions of Madyan. And Moses was denied, but I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them; so how was My rejection?﴾

**[p. 284]**

The parallel of this verse, in its general and detailed forms, has occurred more than once before, in Surat Al 'Imran and elsewhere. The answer to the conditional clause is omitted, and it is indicated by his saying ﴿then the people of Noah ... had already denied [their messengers] before them﴾ and so on, since the implied meaning is: "There is no cause for wonder at their denial," or "There is no reproach upon you for your people's denial of you, for that is the custom of their like."

The people of Abraham were the Chaldeans. The companions of Madyan were the people of Shu'ayb. He did not refer to them as "the people of Shu'ayb" so that the word "qawm" (people) would not be repeated more than three times. He said "and Moses was denied" because those who denied him were the Copts, the people of Pharaoh, and his own people, the Children of Israel, did not deny him. His saying ﴿but I gave the disbelievers respite﴾ means "I gave them respite." He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun to indicate that the reason for granting them respite and then seizing them is disbelief in the messengers, which is an implicit warning to the polytheists of Quraysh.

The *akhdh* (seizing), in its literal sense, is the taking of what is not in one's hand, and it is used here metaphorically for power over them by imposing destruction after granting them respite. The reason for this metaphor is that granting respite resembles something being far from one who would grasp it, so the ending of that respite is likened to taking hold, and this is likened to God's seizing them at His side, because of the manifestation of His power over them after their threat. This seizing is known from other verses. The only exception is that no mention of the punishment or seizing of the people of Abraham preceded in the Qur'an, except that His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Anbiya' ﴿And they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:70] points to the evil outcome of their scheme. This verse is explicit in that, as we indicated there.

The reason for counting the people of Abraham here among the nations whom Allah seized, rather than the other verses in which the nations who were seized are mentioned, is that the people of Abraham bear a closer resemblance to the polytheists of Quraysh, in that they denied their messenger and harmed him, and forced him to leave his homeland: ﴿And he said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me"﴾ [al-Saffat 37:99]. So the mention of Quraysh's forcing the believers to leave their homeland, in His saying ﴿who were expelled from their homes without right﴾ [al-Hajj 22:40], is an appropriate parallel to the mention of the people of Abraham.

*Al-imla'* (granting respite) is leaving the one engaged in disobedience without hastening his punishment, delaying it until a later time, until he thinks that he has escaped, and then he is seized with the punishment.

The *fa'* in ﴿so I gave the disbelievers respite﴾ denotes sequence, indicating that the decree of their destruction was determined at the time of their denial, but it was postponed for them. This is a distributed sequence, so for each of these peoples there is a sequence of their respite. The seizing takes place after the respite with an interval, and therefore its verb is connected with the particle of interval. The clause ﴿so how was My rejection?﴾ is connected with *fa'* because the question should arise at the mention of that seizing. It is a rhetorical question of wonder, meaning: "Wonder at My rejection, how it came about." The aspect of wonder in it is that they were given calamity in exchange for blessing, death in exchange for life, and ruin in exchange for prosperity, so it is a lesson for others.

*Al-nakir* is the reproving denial of a change in the state in which the one being denounced finds himself. The *ya'* (of *nakiri*) with a kasra at its end indicates the omitted first-person pronoun, for lightness. The reason for choosing *nakir* in this verse, rather than punishment or the like, is that it came after the emphasis on forbidding *nukr* (what is denounced), to alert the Muslims that they should exert the utmost effort in changing what is reprehensible. For Allah punished what is reprehensible with the most severe punishment, so it is incumbent upon the believers to follow the example of Allah's action. The wise have said: wisdom is likeness to the Creator to the extent that human capacity can reach, and in this field the steeds of ambitions race one another.
