Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 45:

﴿So how many a town did We destroy while it was wrongdoing, so it lay in ruins over its roofs, and [how many] an abandoned well and a lofty palace.﴾

The mention of the phrase (﴿How many a town﴾) follows on from the phrase ﴿So how was My rejection?﴾ [al-Hajj: 44], and it is joined to it by the resultative fa' (fa' al-tafri'), with the sequence being one of mention, not of existence. This is because the granting of respite to many towns, and then seizing them after granting them respite, explains and clarifies the manner of Allah's rejection and His wrath against the wrongdoing towns. So it was fitting to mention the explanation directly after what is explained, using the resultative particle. Furthermore, what it contains of the noun indicates a great number, encompassing the peoples who were mentioned earlier in His words ﴿The people of Noah had denied before them﴾ [al-Hajj: 42] to the end of it, so it serves for that sentence as a concluding summary (tadhyil).

(Ka'ayyin) is a noun indicating the reporting of a large number. Its position in the sentence is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and what follows it is the predicate (khabar). The estimated meaning is: many towns We destroyed. The sentence (We destroyed them) is the predicate. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative case as the object of an omitted verb which is explained by (We destroyed them). The estimated meaning: We destroyed many towns, We destroyed them. The first view is the better, because it realises the initial position that (ka'ayyin) deserves, without any need to mention the sufficiency of formal initial position. On the first view, the sentence (We destroyed them) is in the genitive position as a qualifier of (town), and the sentence (﴿so it lay in ruins﴾) is conjoined to the sentence (We destroyed them). Its parallel has already been discussed in His words (﴿And how many a prophet﴾) [Al 'Imran: 146] in the surah of Al 'Imran.

The people of the cities whom Allah destroyed for their wrongdoing are many. Among them are those mentioned in the Qur'an, such as 'Ad and Thamud, and among them are those not mentioned, such as Tasm and Jadis, whose remains still exist in al-Yamama. The meaning of (﴿lay in ruins over its roofs﴾) is that no roof or wall remained in them. The phrase (﴿over its roofs﴾) is a second predicate regarding the pronoun in (fa-hiya). The meaning: it fell down over its roofs, i.e., its walls fell on top of its roofs.

Al-'Uruush is the plural of 'arsh, which is the roof. The explanation of a parallel to this verse has already been given at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town, and it was lying in ruins over its roofs﴾ [al-Baqara: 259] in the surah of al-Baqara.

Al-mu'attala is the one whose use has been rendered idle while it is fit for use. That is, it has water springing in it and water channels around it, but no one draws water from it because its people perished. The Muslims, on their march to Tabuk, found wells in the dwellings of Thamud, and the Prophet ﷺ forbade them to drink from them, except for one well, from which the she-camel of Salih (peace be upon him) drank.

Al-qasr: the dwelling built of stone, made in storeys.

Al-mashid: that which is built with shid, with a kasra on the shin and a sukun on the ya', which is gypsum (jiss). Building with stone is done with it because gypsum is harder than earth, so through its firm holding the stone that is bonded with it lasts a long time.

The lofty palaces, which are those left behind by the towns Allah destroyed, are many, such as the palace of Ghumdan in Yemen, the palaces of Thamud in al-Hijr, and the palaces of the Pharaohs in Upper Egypt. In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi it is said that this well and this palace are well known in Hadramawt. It is also said that it is the well of ar-Rass, which was in 'Adan and is called "Hadur" with a fatha on the ha'. Its people were a remnant of the believers in the messenger Salih (peace be upon him), and Salih was with them, but their affair ended in the worship of an idol. Allah sent to them Handhala ibn Safwan as a messenger, and he forbade them from worshipping the idol, so they killed him, and the well burst forth and they perished of thirst. He means that this town is one of the towns mentioned in this verse; otherwise the word (ka'ayyin) contradicts the intention of a specific town.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (﴿We destroyed them﴾) with the nun of majesty, while Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it (﴿I destroyed them﴾) with the ta' of the first person speaker.

[p. 288]

This is a consequence (*tafri'*) of the statement ﴿How many a town have We destroyed?﴾ [al-Hajj: 45] and what follows it. The interrogative is one of wonder at their condition, in failing to take a lesson from the fates of the nations that denied their prophets. The wonder applies both to those among them who travelled and saw some of those destroyed towns, and to those who did not travel. The travellers' habit is to tell those who stayed at home about the wonders they witnessed on their journeys, as His words ﴿or ears with which they hear﴾ indicate. So the intended object of the wonder is the condition of those who went about the earth. However, the interrogative was made to govern the negation of travel, because the travel of those travellers, since it did not yield them a lesson or a reminder, was treated as though it did not exist, and so the wonder was at its absence. The discourse therefore runs contrary to what the apparent sense requires. The *fa'* in ﴿so that they would have﴾ is causative and responsive, indicating that what follows it is caused by the travel. The meaning is: they did not travel in a way by which they would have hearts with which they understand, and ears with which they hear,

[p. 289]

that is, there is no possibility that they would have hearts and ears of this kind, because they did not travel on the earth. This is the rule for a response introduced by *fa'* after a negation: the *fa'* enters on what would be caused by the negated thing, were it affirmed. On this meaning al-Ma'arri said:

*It is said that travel brought him wealth; we say: Has it brought him a heart?*

Such is the nature of travel: it benefits the traveller in ways that residence in one's homeland does not, through acquaintance with the conditions of peoples, the distinctive features of lands, and the differences of customs. It benefits every person of resolve in matters that sharpen the force of his aim in what he pursues, and the greatest of these benefits is the lesson drawn from the causes of success and failure.

The word "hearts" is used for the faculties of reason by way of the figurative usage of the general relation (*al-majaz al-mursal*), since the heart is the source that pumps blood and the origin of life for the principal organs. Chief among them is the brain, which is the organ of reason. That is why He said ﴿with which they understand﴾. The actual instrument of reason is the brain, but the discourse first ran on the common usage of the language, and then was brought in its next phrase to the scientific reality, when He said ﴿with which they understand﴾. This indicates that the hearts are the reason.

Their reason is treated as if it were non-existent, just as their travel on the earth is treated as non-existent. As for the mention of ears, it is because ears are the instrument of hearing, and the traveller on the earth looks at the traces of nations and hears reports of their annihilation, so he infers from this the ordering of effects upon their causes. Moreover, most of those addressed, who are those who did not travel, have their share in receiving reports from the travellers, so that they come to know what the travellers knew, by a knowledge whose path is hearing reports.

In the mention of ears there is a sufficiency that dispenses with mentioning eyes, since it is known that the hearts which understand acquire their knowledge only through witnessing the traces of punishment and annihilation, as His words after this indicate: ﴿For it is not the eyes that are blind, but the hearts that are within the breasts are blind﴾.

[p. 290]

From the whole composition of the verse it results that they are like cattle: they have the instruments of inference, but their effects have ceased in them. ﴿So they have hearts with which they do not understand, and they have ears with which they do not hear, and they have eyes with which they do not see.﴾ This is like His saying: ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to what hears nothing but a call and a cry: deaf, dumb, blind; so they do not understand﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171].

The *fa'* in the clause ﴿For it is not the eyes that are blind﴾ is a consequence of the answer to the negation in His words ﴿so that they would have hearts with which they understand﴾, and it is a summation (*fadhlakah*) of the preceding discourse and a concluding appendage to it, with the generality contained in this clause.

The pronoun in His words ﴿For it﴾ is the pronoun of the matter and the case (*dhamir al-sha'n wa al-qissah*), meaning that the matter and the case is the content of the clause following the pronoun: ﴿it is not the eyes that are blind, but the hearts are blind﴾. That is, sight and hearing are pathways to the acquisition of knowledge of the things seen and heard, and what perceives these is the brain. If there is no reason in the brain, the one who sees is like the blind and the one who hears is like the deaf. The affliction in all of this is the derangement of reason.

The second blindness is used metaphorically (*isti'arah*) for the absence of perceiving the things seen by reason, while the faculty of sight is sound, because of its resemblance to physical blindness in the state that befalls its possessor. The definiteness in "the eyes," "the hearts," and "the breasts" is the definiteness of the genus, comprising the hearts of those spoken of and others. The plural is used in them with regard to their possessors.

The emphatic particle in His words ﴿For it is not the eyes that are blind﴾ is due to the strangeness of the ruling, not because it is something open to doubt.

[p. 291]

Most sentences that open with the pronoun of the matter are accompanied by an emphatic particle.

The restriction (*qasr*) derived from the negation and the adversative particle is an assertive restriction (*qasr idda'i*) for the sake of hyperbole, by treating the loss of the faculty of sight, which is called blindness, as though it were not blindness, and by treating the failure to be guided to the indications of things seen, while the faculty of sight is sound, as being blindness, in exaggeration of its deserving this name which has been borrowed for it. Thus the restriction serves as a nurturing (*tarshih*) of the metaphor. In this verse there are varieties of eloquence, rhetorical expression, and marvellous composition.

The phrase ﴿which are within the breasts﴾ is a qualifier of "the hearts," serving to emphasise the word "hearts." Its function is that of the description in His words ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38], and that of the restriction in His words ﴿they say with their mouths﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167]. It is for increasing confirmation and specification. Beyond emphasis, this qualifier also carries an implicit rebuke to the people spoken of: they did not benefit from their hearts, despite the closeness of those hearts to them, since the hearts are lodged in their breasts. This is like the saying of Umar ibn al-Khattab to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Now you are dearer to me than my own self that is between my two sides," for its being between his two sides requires that it be the dearest of things to him.

The commentary continues the discussion of the previous verse, the account of their denial, and they said: if Muhammad were truthful in his threat, he would hasten its fulfilment for us, so they would ask him to hasten the punishment's descent, mocking him,

[Page 291]

as Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or bring us a painful punishment"﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. He also said: ﴿And they say, "When is this victory, if you are truthful?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 28]. He mentioned this in this verse in connection with His saying (﴿So I gave respite to the disbelievers﴾), and so on. The verb (يَسْتَعْجِلُونَكَ, "they ask you to hasten") is related in the present tense to indicate that they repeated this, renewing their mockery and putting pressure on the Muslims.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, though the intended recipients of the message are them.

The preposition ba' in (بِالعَذابِ, "for the punishment") is supplementary (zā'idah), serving to emphasise the intensity of the act of hastening, as if it were said: they are eager to bring it on quickly. This was already discussed under His saying ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6] at the beginning of Surat al-Ra'd. Since their asking him to hasten it implied, by allusion, that they were certain it would not occur, Allah followed with His saying: ﴿But Allah will not fail His promise.﴾ That is, the punishment promised to them will certainly occur without doubt, because it is a promise from Allah, and Allah does not fail His promise. In this is reassurance (ta'nis) for the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, lest they grow impatient for it.

His saying ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ is coordinated with (عَطْفٌ) the sentence ﴿But Allah will not fail His promise﴾. Allah threatened them with punishment, and He is truthful in it, whether it be the punishment of this world or of the Hereafter. They were only asking for the punishment of this world, mockingly, and as a kinaya (an indirect expression) for their certainty that it would not occur, with one implication, and as an allusion to the non-occurrence of the punishment of the Hereafter, with two implications. So Allah answered them with a general refutation in His saying ﴿But Allah will not fail His promise﴾, and this was a source of firmness for the believers. Then He followed it with a warning that they would not escape the punishment of the Hereafter either, which is the severest punishment.

Thus His saying ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ is a statement used in the sense of an indirect allusion to the threat. This day is the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 292]

In the meaning of this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment, and were it not for a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them. And it will surely come to them suddenly while they do not perceive. They ask you to hasten the punishment, and indeed, Hell will encompass the disbelievers﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 53–54]. The intended meaning of His saying ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord﴾ to the end is not the shortening of the time before the punishment befalls them in this world, as most exegetes have followed, since that interpretation is not elegant. Moreover, this shortening is rendered unnecessary by His saying immediately after this: ﴿And how many a town did I give respite while it was wrongdoing, then I seized it﴾ [al-Hajj: 48].

The address in (تَعُدُّونَ, "you count") is to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. The majority of readers recited (تَعُدُّونَ) with the second-person ta' (taʿudduna). Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited (مِمّا يَعُدُّونَ, "of what they count") with the third-person ya' (yaʿudduna), meaning: of what the polytheists who are hastening the punishment count.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 48:

﴿How many a town did I give respite while it was wrongdoing, and then I seized it; and to Me is the final return.﴾

It is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause (﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]), or with the clause (﴿Allah will not fail His promise﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]), in view of the implication of their asking to hasten the punishment, which alludes to their despair of it because of its delay. So they are reminded that many nations were given respite and then the punishment befell them. The pattern of this verse is the pattern of His earlier words, ﴿So how many a town did We destroy while it was wrongdoing﴾ [al-Hajj: 45], and so on, except that the purpose of the first is the great number of nations that were destroyed, so that it would not be supposed, from the mention of the people of Nuh and those coordinated with them, that destruction did not extend beyond them. For this reason, only the destruction is mentioned there, not the respite. The purpose of this verse is to remind that the delay of the threat does not necessitate its annulment. For this reason, only the respite is mentioned here, followed by the seizing that is appropriate to the giving of respite (*imla'*), in that it is an entering into the grip after being far from it.

As for the clause ﴿So how many a town did We destroy﴾ [al-Hajj: 45] being coordinated with the particle *fa'* (then/so), and the clause ﴿How many a town did I give respite while it was wrongdoing﴾ being coordinated with *wa'* (and), the reason is that the first clause came as an apposition (*badal*) to the clause ﴿Then how was My rejection﴾ [al-Hajj: 44], so it was joined with *fa'*, the particle whose counterpart had entered the clause it replaces. As for this second clause, it is free of that, so it was coordinated with the original particle of coordination.

The clause (﴿And to Me is the final return﴾) is a concluding appendage (*tadhyil*), meaning: the return of all people is to Me. *Al-masir* is a mimi verbal noun (*masdar mimi*) of *sara* (to become/to return), meaning "returned," and it is a figurative return, meaning being within one's power. Placing the prepositional phrase first (*taqdim al-majrur*) signifies genuine restriction (*hasr haqiqi*), meaning that people return only to Allah. This implies that the return to Him is inevitable, and that is the intended purpose of the restriction, because restriction implies this all the more. So it is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the impossibility of escape.

[p. 293]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verses 49–51:

﴿Say, "O mankind, I am only to you a clear warner."﴾ ﴿So those who believe and do righteous deeds – for them is forgiveness and noble provision.﴾ ﴿But those who strive against Our verses, seeking to cause failure – those are the companions of Hellfire.﴾

This is a resumption after the preceding admonitions and warnings. Its opening with "Say" (qul) is for emphasis, and the opening of the speech with a call to "mankind" is to draw their minds to what follows. The addressees are the polytheists.

The purpose of addressing them is to inform them that their denial and mockery do not anger the Prophet (ﷺ) or deter him from conveying his message. In this there is a suppression of them, if they think that by their denial and mockery they will weary him so that he abandons his call. It also contains reassurance and consolation for the Prophet regarding what he encounters from them. The restriction of the Prophet to the attribute of warning is a restriction relative to a specific context, meaning: I do not seek to harm you, nor to gain your favor; whoever believes, it is for his own self, and whoever is blind, it is upon himself.

The nadhir (warner) is one who cautions against an evil that is anticipated.

In the fronting of the prepositional phrase "to you" (lakum), which indicates concern with warning them, there is an indication that they are on the brink of a great evil, and so they are deserving of the warning.

The mubin (clear) is one who is explicit and plain, meaning: clear in the warning, with nothing ambiguous and no flattery. Following the command to speak, there is a division of people in their reception of this warning, which the Messenger was commanded to convey, into one who believes and one who denies, in order to explain the state of both groups in this world and the Hereafter, as an encouragement toward the good state and a caution against the evil state. Thus Exalted God says: "So those who believe and do righteous deeds – for them..." to the end. This is a report from God Exalted, as the phrase "in Our verses" requires, and the sentence is parenthetical, introduced by the particle fa'.

Forgiveness (maghfirah) is the pardoning of what they committed of shirk and what follows from it of the laws of shirk, its misguidance and its corruptions. This forgiveness leads to the bliss of the Hereafter, so the meaning is that they succeed in the Hereafter.

Provision (rizq) is bounty. Describing it as noble (karim) comprises its abundance and its purity from what troubles it, as in God Exalted's saying: "For them is a reward never cut off" (Fussilat 41:8). That is Paradise.

Part of this provision is what they already have in this world: they enjoy the expansion of their hearts and their contentment with their Lord, and the greatest of it is what they will receive in the Hereafter.

"Those who strove" (alladhina sa'aw) are the group opposed to those who believe, so the meaning is: those who persisted in disbelief. Persistence is expressed by "striving against the verses," because it is more specific than disbelief, and this is the condition of the polytheists under discussion.

Sa'y (striving) is intense walking, and it is applied to intense eagerness in work, likening the eager worker to the one walking vigorously in that he exerts himself to reach a goal, as God Exalted says: "Then he turned away, striving (yas'a)..." (al-Nazi'at 79:22). The meaning is not that Pharaoh went out walking; rather, he devoted his effort to gathering the magicians to nullify the call of Musa. And God Exalted says: "And they strive in the land to cause corruption" (al-Ma'idah 5:33). The statement is a figurative image: the condition of their varied efforts in denying the Qur'an and seeking excuses to refute its proofs, from their saying "It is magic," "It is poetry," "It is the fables of the ancients," "He is a madman," and their confronting the Prophet (ﷺ) with disputes and contradictions, is likened to the condition of one hurrying along a path, competing with another to be the first to arrive.

Mu'jiz (one who frustrates) is the competitor who seeks to make his rival unable to reach the goal and unable to catch up with him. The form mufa'alah is used for it because each one seeks the other's inability to catch up. The meaning is: by their deeds they contend against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while not realizing that they are trying to overcome God. They thought they had attained their aim in this world, and they did not know the evil of the outcome that awaits them. The majority of readers recite (mu'ajizin) with an alif after the 'ain, while Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recite (mu'ajjizin) with a fatha on the 'ain and a doubled jim, meaning: those who try to frustrate God Exalted, while they do not know.

The introduction with the demonstrative in "Those are the companions of Hellfire" serves to draw attention to the fact that those spoken of deserve what follows the demonstrative as a judgment, because of the attributes mentioned before it; that is, they are the companions of Hellfire because they strove against Our verses, seeking to frustrate them. Among the best explanations of this verse is what is related in the authentic hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of me and of what God has sent me with is like a man who came to his people and said: 'O people, I have seen the army with my own eyes, and I am the naked warner. So, escape, escape!' A group of his people obeyed him, set off in the night, and departed at their leisure. But a group of them denied him, so they remained in their place, and the army came upon them at dawn, destroyed them and annihilated them. That is the likeness of me and the likeness of whoever obeys me and follows what I have brought, and the likeness of whoever disobeys me and denies what I have brought of the truth."

[Page 297]

﴿We never sent before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish. But Allah abolishes what Satan casts, then Allah establishes His verses. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease and whose hearts are hardened. Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension.﴾ ﴿And that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so that they believe in it and their hearts humble themselves to it. Indeed, Allah is guiding those who believe to a straight path.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence ﴿Say, O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you﴾ [al-Hajj 22:49], because when the preceding discourse led to strengthening the Prophet ﷺ and consoling him regarding what he met from his people of denial, [it showed that] this is the custom of the wrongdoing nations before them. This came after His saying ﴿And how many a city I have given respite while it was wrongdoing﴾ [al-Hajj 22:48], and [it showed] that his role is limited to warning: whoever believes is saved, and whoever disbelieves is destroyed. The intent is to move from that to the consolation and strengthening of him, [showing] that he met what his predecessors among the messengers and prophets (peace be upon them) met, and that none of them was spared from Satan's attempt to corrupt some of what they sought of guidance for their nations, and that they met from their peoples both deniers and believers, [in accordance with] Allah's sunnah (way) regarding His messengers (peace be upon them).

So His saying "from a messenger or prophet" is explicit in generality, and thus it indicates that this did not pass over any of the prophets and messengers. The coordination of "prophet" (nabī) with "messenger" (rasūl) indicates that "prophet" has a meaning other than the meaning of "messenger."

The rasūl (messenger) is a man sent by Allah to the people with a sharīʿah (revealed law). The nabī (prophet) is one to whom Allah revealed the reform of a people's affairs by bringing them to a prior sharīʿah, or by guiding them to what is established in all the sharīʿahs. Thus the nabī is more general than the rasūl, and this is the verified view.

Tamannā (wishing) is a well-known word. Its reality is seeking a thing whose attainment is difficult. Umniyyah is the thing wished for. Messengers and prophets only wish that all their people be righteous and guided. The exception (istithnāʾ) is from the generality of states that follow the generality of their possessors, namely "from a messenger or prophet." That is: We did not send them in any state except the state in which, when one of them wished a wish, Satan cast into it, etc. That is, in the state of the casting occurring at the time of the wish, because the wishes of the prophets are pure good, while Satan's habit is corruption and the nullification of good. The restriction derived from the negation and exception is a restriction of the qualified to a quality, and it is a relative restriction (qaṣr idāfī): that is, [it means] without our sending any of them in a state free from Satan's casting and his deceit.

The reality of ilqāʾ (casting) is throwing a thing from the hand. It is used here metaphorically for whispering and embellishing corruption, likening the embellishment to casting something from the hand among people. From this is His saying ﴿So the Samiri cast [it]﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 20:87], and His saying ﴿And they cast to them the word﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:86], and like His saying ﴿So I grasped a handful from the trace of the Messenger and cast it away﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 20:96], as we verified previously. The object of "cast" (alqā) is omitted, indicated by context, because Satan casts only evil and corruption. So attributing the wish to the prophets indicates that it is a wish for guidance and righteousness, and attributing the casting to Satan indicates that it is a casting of misguidance and corruption. The implied sense is: Satan introduced into the souls of the peoples misguidances that corrupt what the prophets said of guidance.

The meaning of Satan's casting into the wish of the prophet and messenger is the casting of what opposes it, like one who schemes and casts poison into butter. Satan's casting by his whispering is that he commands people to deny and disobey, and casts into the hearts of the leaders of disbelief slanders which they spread among their people. He promotes doubts by casting suspicions that divert the intellect's gaze from remembering the proof. Allah, exalted, renews the guidance and repeats the direction on the tongue of the prophet, and exposes Satan's whisperings and the evil of his deed by clear exposition, like His saying ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:27], and His saying ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fāṭir 35:6].

So Allah, by His guidance and His clarification, abolishes (yanskhu) what Satan casts, that is, He removes the doubts that Satan casts by Allah's clear exposition, and increases the verses of the call of His messengers in clarity. That is the establishing (iḥkām) of His verses, that is, their confirmation, the affirmation of their meaning, and their clarification in a way that leaves no doubt after it, except for one whose heart has been sealed with rust. The meaning of the decisive verses (al-āyāt al-muḥkamāt) has already been discussed in Āl ʿImrān.

Many exegetes (mufassirūn) interpreted "tamannā" as meaning "recited" (qaraʾa). The lexicographers followed them and mentioned a line of verse attributed to Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and they mentioned a story with weak narrations, which we will mention. In any case, the discussion regarding it and the discussion regarding the interpretation of tamannā in its well-known sense are the same. That is: when he recited to the people what was revealed to him, so that they would be guided by it, Satan cast into his umniyyah, that is, into his recitation; that is, he whispered to them in their souls what contradicts and negates it, by his whispering to people denial and turning away from reflection. So Satan's embellishment through his whispering to the disbelievers is likened to the non-compliance with the Prophet, [like] casting something in to mix it and corrupt it.

However, in my view there is great doubt regarding the correctness of applying the term umniyyah to recitation. Even though tamannā with the meaning of "recited" has occurred in a line attributed to Ḥassān ibn Thābit, if the narration of the line from Ḥassān is sound, with variation in its final hemistich:

*Tamannā Kitāba Allāhi awwala laylihi / tamannī Dāwūda al-Zabūra ʿalā mahal*

[He recited the Book of Allah at the start of his night, / as David recited the Psalms at leisure.]

Still, I do not think that recitation is called umniyyah.

It may also be that the meaning is: when the Prophet wished the guidance of his people, or was eager for that, and met obstinacy, and wished for their guidance by every means, Satan cast into the Prophet's soul the thought of despair of their guidance, so that the Prophet would cease from his eagerness, or so that it would weary him. These are thoughts that appear in the soul, but infallibility (ʿiṣmah) stands against them, so that thought does not remain long before it dissipates, and what the Messenger was commanded with, namely persistence in the call and eagerness for right guidance, becomes firmly established in his soul. In this case the meaning of the verse alludes to His saying ﴿And if their turning away is grievous to you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign — [you may do so]. But if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance, so do not be among the ignorant﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:35].

The "then" (thumma) in His saying ﴿then Allah establishes His verses﴾ is for sequence of rank (al-tartīb al-rutbī), because establishing the verses and confirming them is more important than abolishing what Satan casts. By establishing [the verses], guidance becomes clear, and what Satan casts becomes more abrogated.

The clause ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ is a parenthetical (iʿtirāḍ) clause.

The meaning of this verse: the prophets and messengers hope for the guidance of their people as far as they can, so they convey to them what is sent down to them from Allah, admonish them, and call them with wisdom and good argument, until they think their wish has succeeded and the people draw near to faith, as Allah related of the polytheists their saying: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger? He would have almost led us away from our gods, had we not been steadfast in adhering to them﴾ [al-Furqān 25:41]. Then Satan comes and continues to whisper into the souls of the disbelievers, so they turn back on their heels. These whisperings are of various kinds: reminding them of love for their gods, frightening them with the bad consequence of abandoning their religion, and similar types of misguidance related of them in the details of the Qur'an. So the people of misguidance cling to their religion and turn away from the call of their messengers. That is the steadfastness mentioned in His saying ﴿had we not been steadfast in adhering to them﴾ [al-Furqān 25:42], and His saying ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, saying: Walk on and be steadfast for your gods﴾ [Ṣād 38:6].

Whenever Satan corrupts the call of the messengers, Allah commands His messengers, and they return to guidance and repeat it. This is the cause of the repetition of similar admonitions in the Qur'an. Through that renewal, He abolishes what Satan cast, and the earlier verses are established.

So abolition (naskh) is removal, and establishment (iḥkām) is confirmation. In both clauses an element is omitted: that is, "its effects": what Satan casts abolishes its effects, and the effects of His verses are established.

The two lām particles in His saying "li-yajʿala" (that He may make) and "wa-li-yaʿlama" (and that He may know) are connected to the verb "yanskhu Allāhu" (Allah abolishes), because abolition necessitates something abrogated. In "yajʿalu" there is a pronoun referring to Allah in His saying "fa-yanskhu Allāhu."

Here, "jaʿl" (making) means the establishing of the system by which effects follow their causes, and the creation of differences in perceptive capacities and their levels of rank. The meaning is that Allah enabled Satan to do that action by the original nature of his creation, from the day He created in him the call to misguidance, and [He enabled] the abolition of what Satan casts through His messengers and His verses, so that from this there may be a trial of disbelieving misguidance and believing guidance, according to the differences in receptive capacities. This is like His saying ﴿He said: My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and mislead them all, except among them Your chosen servants.﴾ He said: ﴿This is a straight path to Me. Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them, except those who follow you among the deviators﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:39–42].

The lām in ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial﴾ is borrowed for the meaning of consequence (tarattub), like the lām in His saying ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:8]. It is used metaphorically for the meaning of subsequence, which properly should be expressed with the particle fāʾ. That is: there occurs, as a consequence of the abolition that Allah performed, the trial of those among the polytheists who are tried, by their turning away from reflecting on the proofs of the abolition of what Satan casts, and from listening to what Allah has established in His verses. Thus their disbelief continues and grows stronger.

As for the lām in ﴿And that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord﴾, it is on its original meaning of causation (taʿlīl): that is, He abolishes what Satan casts for the purpose that the believers may know that it is the truth, through the firm establishment of what the Messenger and the prophets wished for them of guidance, just as there results for them, through what Allah establishes of His verses, an increase of guidance in their hearts.

﴿Those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ are those who waver regarding accepting faith. ﴿And whose hearts are hardened﴾ are the disbelievers who are determined upon disbelief. Both groups are what is meant by "the wrongdoers" in His saying ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension﴾. Thus the mention of "the wrongdoers" is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, indicating that the cause of their being in extreme dissension is their wrongdoing; that is, their disbelief.

Shiqāq (dissension) is opposition and enmity.

Baʿīd (extreme) is used here in the sense of reaching a strong limit in its reality, likening the spread of the reality within it to the spread of distance in a far place, as in His saying ﴿So [He is] one of extensive supplication﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:51], that is, abundant and insistent supplication. The clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the coordinated clauses.

﴿Those who have been given knowledge﴾ are the believers, by the indication of its contrast with ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ [Muḥammad 47:20], and by His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is guiding those who believe to a straight path.﴾ So the meaning of "knowledge" is the revelation and the books given to the companions of the earlier messengers, for by them they become people of knowledge. The application of ﴿those who have been given knowledge﴾ to believers is repeated in the Qur'an. This is praise of the companions of the messengers, that they were given knowledge, namely the knowledge of religion which the messengers (upon them be blessings and peace) conveyed to them, for the light of prophethood shines in the hearts of those who accompany the Messenger. Therefore you find that one who accompanies the Messenger ﷺ may have been a coarse man before faith, and when he believes he becomes wise, like ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him. The Prophet ﷺ said: "My companions are like the stars: whichever of them you follow, you will be guided."

[Page 303]

The pronoun in "annahu al-haqq" refers back to the knowledge they were given, meaning: so that they may increase in certainty that the revelation they were given is the truth and nothing else, such as what Satan cast to them of doubt, misgivings and misguidance. Thus the restriction (qasr) derived from the definiteness of the two components is a restriction relative to a particular case (qasr idafi).

It is also permissible for the pronoun in "annahu" to refer back to what preceded, from His saying ﴿fa-yansakhu Allahu﴾ up to His saying ﴿thumma yuhkimu Allahu ayatihi﴾, meaning: what has been mentioned is the truth, like the saying of Ru'bah:

fīhā khuṭūṭun min sawādin wa-balaq ∗∗∗ ka-annahā fī al-jildi tawlīʿu al-bahaq

meaning: "as if what was mentioned..."

His saying ﴿fa-yu'minu bihi﴾ means: so that they increase in faith, or so that they believe in the abrogating and the muhkam just as they believed in the original.

Al-ikhbat means tranquility (al-itmi'nan) and humility (al-khushu'). It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿wa-bashshiri al-mukhbitin﴾ [al-Hajj: 34], meaning: that this settles in their hearts, like His saying ﴿qala bala wa-lakin liyatma'inna qalbi﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

With what you have received in the explanation of this verse of clear and evident coherence, independent in its indication and self-sufficient in its essence, free from artificial constructions and from the need for appended narratives, you see that the verse is far removed from what the fabricators and the weak transmitters in the sciences of the Sunnah attached to it, and what a group of exegetes accepted from them out of love for rare oddities without reflection or scrutiny, namely that the verse was revealed concerning a story related to Surat al-Najm. They were not satisfied with what they had corrupted of the meaning of this verse, until they went beyond this attachment to corrupting the meanings of Surat al-Najm. They mentioned in this regard reports from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Shihab, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak. The closest of them is a report from Ibn Shihab, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) sat in one of the assemblies of the Quraysh, many of whose people were Muslims and disbelievers, and he recited to them Surat al-Najm. When he reached His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 19], Satan cast between the listeners, right after that, the words: 'Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is to be hoped for.' The polytheists rejoiced that he had mentioned their gods favorably. There was at the end of that surah a prostration of recitation. When he prostrated at the end of the surah, everyone present of the Muslims and polytheists prostrated. The news spread that the Quraysh had embraced Islam, until it spread in the lands of Abyssinia. Thus some of the emigrants to Abyssinia, among them 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, returned to Madinah." And the Prophet (ﷺ) did not perceive that Satan had cast it. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) informed him, and he was grieved by that, so there was revealed His saying ﴿Wa-ma arsalna min qablika﴾, the verse, as consolation for him. This is a story which the hearer finds to be a handful upon a bundle, and which the expert does not pay attention to. It was only transmitted through feeble chains, and its ultimate is the mention of a story; none of its chains includes a companion's hearing of anything in the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ). Its chain to Ibn 'Abbas is a disputed chain. Moreover, on the day Surat al-Najm was revealed, Ibn 'Abbas was not attending the assemblies of the Prophet (ﷺ). These are solitary reports (akhbar ahad) which contradict the fundamental principles of the religion, because they contradict the principle of the infallibility of the Messenger (ﷺ), so there is no confusion for him in receiving the revelation. His saying ﴿Wa-ma yantiqu 'ani al-hawa﴾ [al-Najm: 3] suffices as a refutation of them. And in the knowledge of the King. Had the trustworthy transmitters narrated them, it would have been obligatory to reject them or interpret them, so how when they are weak and feeble? And how can it pass upon one with a grain of intellect that in a single speech there would be gathered a denunciation of the polytheists for their worship of idols, by His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [al-Najm: 19] up to His saying ﴿Allah has sent down no authority for them﴾ [al-Najm: 23], so that in the midst of that there occurs praise of them as the exalted cranes whose intercession is hoped for? Is this not speech in which part curses part?

The narrators have agreed that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the whole of Surat al-Najm, up to its end, ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship Him﴾ [al-Najm: 62], because they prostrated only when the Muslims prostrated. This indicates that they heard the whole surah, and between the verse ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19] and the end of the surah there are many verses refuting the idols and other objects of worship of the polytheists, and a great deal of discrediting of the beliefs of the polytheists. So how could it be valid that the polytheists prostrated for the sake of praise of their gods? If those reports are not false from their origin, then their interpretation is: that some of the polytheists found the mention of al-Lat and al-'Uzza an opportunity for interference, to fabricate words in praise of them, which are these words, and circulated them among the people to make their allies among the polytheists feel at ease and to cast doubt into the hearts of those weak in faith.

In al-Tibi's commentary on the Kashshaf, citing some historians: that the words of the "gharaniq" (i.e., these phrases) are among the fabrications of Ibn al-Ziba'ra. This is supported by what al-Tabari narrated from al-Dahhak: that the Prophet (ﷺ) had revealed to him the story of the gods of the Arabs, i.e., His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19] etc., so he began reciting: "al-Lat and al-'Uzza," meaning the verse containing this, and the people of Makkah heard the Prophet of Allah mentioning their gods, so they rejoiced and drew near to listen. Then Satan cast: "Those are the exalted cranes, from them the intercession is hoped for." For His saying "they drew near to listen, and Satan cast" etc. indicates that they did not hear the beginning of the surah nor its end, and that their devil cast those words. Perhaps Ibn al-Ziba'ra had an ability to imitate voices, and this ability is found in some people. I knew a youth of our peers who could imitate anyone's voice, such that the listener would think it was the voice of the one imitated. As for the composition of that story upon the report which is established that the polytheists prostrated at the end of Surat al-Najm when the Muslims prostrated, and that is transmitted in the Sahih, this is from the confusion of the compilers.

And likewise the composition of that story upon the verse of Surat al-Hajj. How far apart is the revelation of Surat al-Najm, which is among the early surahs revealed in Makkah, from the revelation of Surat al-Hajj, some of which was among the first revealed at Madinah and some of which was among the last revealed at Makkah. Likewise, linking that story to the story of the return of some of the emigrants from Abyssinia. How far apart is the period of the revelation of Surat al-Najm from the year of the return of those who returned from the emigrants to Abyssinia.

So the correct view: this rumor which was spread among the polytheists at the beginning of Islam is nothing but fabrications of the mockers, foolish of mind, from Makkah, such as Ibn al-Ziba'ra, and they targeted a verse in which al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are mentioned, and built upon it other words to spread sedition among the people. They singled out Surat al-Najm with this deceptive report because they had attended its recitation in the Masjid al-Haram and it had lodged in their minds, and sought to find an excuse for themselves among their people for their prostration in it, which Allah made a miracle for the Prophet (ﷺ). This artifice extended to establishing a meaning in the language: they claimed that (tamanna) means "recited," and al-umniyyah means "recitation," an assertion that is not trusted and for which there is no clear witness in the speech of the Arabs. They cited a verse of Hassan ibn Thabit in lamenting 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him):

tamanna kitaba Allahi awwala laylihi ∗∗∗ wa-akhirahu laqa himama al-maqadiri

It is possible that its meaning is: he wished to recite the Qur'an at the beginning of the night as was his custom, but he could not do so due to the disturbance of the besiegers against him, and they killed him at the end of the night. For this reason he made it a wish (tamanni), because he loved that but could not do it. Perhaps they recited it with another narration and it was taken as another witness, and perhaps they mistook the second narration for another verse. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention this meaning in al-Asas. We have already discussed this at His saying ﴿Among them are unlettered people who know not the Book except wishful fancies﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿Wa-inna Allaha la-hadi alladhina amanu ila sirat mustaqim﴾ is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and the waw is for interjection. "Those given knowledge" are the believers. Both attributes are combined for them, as in His saying ﴿Those who were given knowledge and faith said: "You have remained in the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection"﴾ [al-Rum: 56] in Surat al-Rum, and as in Surat Saba': ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [Saba': 6]. So the explicit mention of "those who believed" in place of the pronoun for "those given knowledge" is to praise them by the attribute of faith, and to indicate that their faith is the cause of their guidance. The opposite is His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. So what is meant by guidance in both verses is Allah's care in facilitating it; otherwise Allah guided both groups by the call and direction, and among them some were guided and among them some disbelieved.

In the Mushaf it is written "la-hadin" without a yā' after the dāl, following the pause-form... rather, considering the state of continuation (wasl), contrary to the usual practice. In pause, Ya'qub pronounces the yā', unlike the rest.

Thus the nabī is more general than the rasūl, and this is the verified view.

The clause ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ is a parenthetical (iʿtirāḍ) clause.

The meaning of this verse: the prophets and messengers hope for the guidance of their people as far as they can, so they convey to them what is sent down to them from Allah, admonish them, and call them with wisdom and good argument, until they think their wish has succeeded and the people draw near to faith, as Allah related of the polytheists their saying: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger? He would have almost led us away from our gods, had we not been steadfast in adhering to them﴾ [al-Furqān 25:41]. Then Satan comes and continues to whisper into the souls of the disbelievers, so they turn back on their heels. These whisperings are of various kinds: reminding them of love for their gods, frightening them with the bad consequence of abandoning their religion, and similar types of misguidance related of them in the details of the Qur'an. So the people of misguidance cling to their religion and turn away from the call of their messengers. That is the steadfastness mentioned in His saying ﴿had we not been steadfast in adhering to them﴾ [al-Furqān 25:42], and His saying ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, saying: Walk on and be steadfast for your gods﴾ [Ṣād 38:6].

Whenever Satan corrupts the call of the messengers, Allah commands His messengers, and they return to guidance and repeat it. This is the cause of the repetition of similar admonitions in the Qur'an. Through that renewal, He abolishes what Satan cast, and the earlier verses are established.

So abolition (naskh) is removal, and establishment (iḥkām) is confirmation. In both clauses an element is omitted: that is, "its effects": what Satan casts abolishes its effects, and the effects of His verses are established.

The two lām particles in His saying "li-yajʿala" (that He may make) and "wa-li-yaʿlama" (and that He may know) are connected to the verb "yanskhu Allāhu" (Allah abolishes), because abolition necessitates something abrogated. In "yajʿalu" there is a pronoun referring to Allah in His saying "fa-yanskhu Allāhu."

Here, "jaʿl" (making) means the establishing of the system by which effects follow their causes, and the creation of differences in perceptive capacities and their levels of rank. The meaning is that Allah enabled Satan to do that action by the original nature of his creation, from the day He created in him the call to misguidance, and [He enabled] the abolition of what Satan casts through His messengers and His verses, so that from this there may be a trial of disbelieving misguidance and believing guidance, according to the differences in receptive capacities. This is like His saying ﴿He said: My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and mislead them all, except among them Your chosen servants.﴾ He said: ﴿This is a straight path to Me. Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them, except those who follow you among the deviators﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:39–42].

The lām in ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial﴾ is borrowed for the meaning of consequence (tarattub), like the lām in His saying ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:8]. It is used metaphorically for the meaning of subsequence, which properly should be expressed with the particle fāʾ. That is: there occurs, as a consequence of the abolition that Allah performed, the trial of those among the polytheists who are tried, by their turning away from reflecting on the proofs of the abolition of what Satan casts, and from listening to what Allah has established in His verses. Thus their disbelief continues and grows stronger.

As for the lām in ﴿And that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord﴾, it is on its original meaning of causation (taʿlīl): that is, He abolishes what Satan casts for the purpose that the believers may know that it is the truth, through the firm establishment of what the Messenger and the prophets wished for them of guidance, just as there results for them, through what Allah establishes of His verses, an increase of guidance in their hearts.

﴿Those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ are those who waver regarding accepting faith. ﴿And whose hearts are hardened﴾ are the disbelievers who are determined upon disbelief. Both groups are what is meant by "the wrongdoers" in His saying ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension﴾. Thus the mention of "the wrongdoers" is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, indicating that the cause of their being in extreme dissension is their wrongdoing; that is, their disbelief.

Shiqāq (dissension) is opposition and enmity.

Baʿīd (extreme) is used here in the sense of reaching a strong limit in its reality, likening the spread of the reality within it to the spread of distance in a far place, as in His saying ﴿So [He is] one of extensive supplication﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:51], that is, abundant and insistent supplication. The clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the coordinated clauses.

﴿Those who have been given knowledge﴾ are the believers, by the indication of its contrast with ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ [Muḥammad 47:20], and by His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is guiding those who believe to a straight path.﴾ So the meaning of "knowledge" is the revelation and the books given to the companions of the earlier messengers, for by them they become people of knowledge. The application of ﴿those who have been given knowledge﴾ to believers is repeated in the Qur'an. This is praise of the companions of the messengers, that they were given knowledge, namely the knowledge of religion which the messengers (upon them be blessings and peace) conveyed to them, for the light of prophethood shines in the hearts of those who accompany the Messenger. Therefore you find that one who accompanies the Messenger ﷺ may have been a coarse man before faith, and when he believes he becomes wise, like ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him. The Prophet ﷺ said: "My companions are like the stars: whichever of them you follow, you will be guided."

[Page 303]

The pronoun in "annahu al-haqq" refers back to the knowledge they were given, meaning: so that they may increase in certainty that the revelation they were given is the truth and nothing else, such as what Satan cast to them of doubt, misgivings and misguidance. Thus the restriction (qasr) derived from the definiteness of the two components is a restriction relative to a particular case (qasr idafi).

It is also permissible for the pronoun in "annahu" to refer back to what preceded, from His saying ﴿fa-yansakhu Allahu﴾ up to His saying ﴿thumma yuhkimu Allahu ayatihi﴾, meaning: what has been mentioned is the truth, like the saying of Ru'bah:

fīhā khuṭūṭun min sawādin wa-balaq ∗∗∗ ka-annahā fī al-jildi tawlīʿu al-bahaq

meaning: "as if what was mentioned..."

His saying ﴿fa-yu'minu bihi﴾ means: so that they increase in faith, or so that they believe in the abrogating and the muhkam just as they believed in the original.

Al-ikhbat means tranquility (al-itmi'nan) and humility (al-khushu'). It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿wa-bashshiri al-mukhbitin﴾ [al-Hajj: 34], meaning: that this settles in their hearts, like His saying ﴿qala bala wa-lakin liyatma'inna qalbi﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

With what you have received in the explanation of this verse of clear and evident coherence, independent in its indication and self-sufficient in its essence, free from artificial constructions and from the need for appended narratives, you see that the verse is far removed from what the fabricators and the weak transmitters in the sciences of the Sunnah attached to it, and what a group of exegetes accepted from them out of love for rare oddities without reflection or scrutiny, namely that the verse was revealed concerning a story related to Surat al-Najm. They were not satisfied with what they had corrupted of the meaning of this verse, until they went beyond this attachment to corrupting the meanings of Surat al-Najm. They mentioned in this regard reports from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Shihab, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak. The closest of them is a report from Ibn Shihab, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) sat in one of the assemblies of the Quraysh, many of whose people were Muslims and disbelievers, and he recited to them Surat al-Najm. When he reached His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 19], Satan cast between the listeners, right after that, the words: 'Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is to be hoped for.' The polytheists rejoiced that he had mentioned their gods favorably. There was at the end of that surah a prostration of recitation. When he prostrated at the end of the surah, everyone present of the Muslims and polytheists prostrated. The news spread that the Quraysh had embraced Islam, until it spread in the lands of Abyssinia. Thus some of the emigrants to Abyssinia, among them 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, returned to Madinah." And the Prophet (ﷺ) did not perceive that Satan had cast it. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) informed him, and he was grieved by that, so there was revealed His saying ﴿Wa-ma arsalna min qablika﴾, the verse, as consolation for him. This is a story which the hearer finds to be a handful upon a bundle, and which the expert does not pay attention to. It was only transmitted through feeble chains, and its ultimate is the mention of a story; none of its chains includes a companion's hearing of anything in the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ). Its chain to Ibn 'Abbas is a disputed chain. Moreover, on the day Surat al-Najm was revealed, Ibn 'Abbas was not attending the assemblies of the Prophet (ﷺ). These are solitary reports (akhbar ahad) which contradict the fundamental principles of the religion, because they contradict the principle of the infallibility of the Messenger (ﷺ), so there is no confusion for him in receiving the revelation. His saying ﴿Wa-ma yantiqu 'ani al-hawa﴾ [al-Najm: 3] suffices as a refutation of them. And in the knowledge of the King. Had the trustworthy transmitters narrated them, it would have been obligatory to reject them or interpret them, so how when they are weak and feeble? And how can it pass upon one with a grain of intellect that in a single speech there would be gathered a denunciation of the polytheists for their worship of idols, by His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [al-Najm: 19] up to His saying ﴿Allah has sent down no authority for them﴾ [al-Najm: 23], so that in the midst of that there occurs praise of them as the exalted cranes whose intercession is hoped for? Is this not speech in which part curses part?

The narrators have agreed that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the whole of Surat al-Najm, up to its end, ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship Him﴾ [al-Najm: 62], because they prostrated only when the Muslims prostrated. This indicates that they heard the whole surah, and between the verse ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19] and the end of the surah there are many verses refuting the idols and other objects of worship of the polytheists, and a great deal of discrediting of the beliefs of the polytheists. So how could it be valid that the polytheists prostrated for the sake of praise of their gods? If those reports are not false from their origin, then their interpretation is: that some of the polytheists found the mention of al-Lat and al-'Uzza an opportunity for interference, to fabricate words in praise of them, which are these words, and circulated them among the people to make their allies among the polytheists feel at ease and to cast doubt into the hearts of those weak in faith.

In al-Tibi's commentary on the Kashshaf, citing some historians: that the words of the "gharaniq" (i.e., these phrases) are among the fabrications of Ibn al-Ziba'ra. This is supported by what al-Tabari narrated from al-Dahhak: that the Prophet (ﷺ) had revealed to him the story of the gods of the Arabs, i.e., His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19] etc., so he began reciting: "al-Lat and al-'Uzza," meaning the verse containing this, and the people of Makkah heard the Prophet of Allah mentioning their gods, so they rejoiced and drew near to listen. Then Satan cast: "Those are the exalted cranes, from them the intercession is hoped for." For His saying "they drew near to listen, and Satan cast" etc. indicates that they did not hear the beginning of the surah nor its end, and that their devil cast those words. Perhaps Ibn al-Ziba'ra had an ability to imitate voices, and this ability is found in some people. I knew a youth of our peers who could imitate anyone's voice, such that the listener would think it was the voice of the one imitated. As for the composition of that story upon the report which is established that the polytheists prostrated at the end of Surat al-Najm when the Muslims prostrated, and that is transmitted in the Sahih, this is from the confusion of the compilers.

And likewise the composition of that story upon the verse of Surat al-Hajj. How far apart is the revelation of Surat al-Najm, which is among the early surahs revealed in Makkah, from the revelation of Surat al-Hajj, some of which was among the first revealed at Madinah and some of which was among the last revealed at Makkah. Likewise, linking that story to the story of the return of some of the emigrants from Abyssinia. How far apart is the period of the revelation of Surat al-Najm from the year of the return of those who returned from the emigrants to Abyssinia.

So the correct view: this rumor which was spread among the polytheists at the beginning of Islam is nothing but fabrications of the mockers, foolish of mind, from Makkah, such as Ibn al-Ziba'ra, and they targeted a verse in which al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are mentioned, and built upon it other words to spread sedition among the people. They singled out Surat al-Najm with this deceptive report because they had attended its recitation in the Masjid al-Haram and it had lodged in their minds, and sought to find an excuse for themselves among their people for their prostration in it, which Allah made a miracle for the Prophet (ﷺ). This artifice extended to establishing a meaning in the language: they claimed that (tamanna) means "recited," and al-umniyyah means "recitation," an assertion that is not trusted and for which there is no clear witness in the speech of the Arabs. They cited a verse of Hassan ibn Thabit in lamenting 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him):

tamanna kitaba Allahi awwala laylihi ∗∗∗ wa-akhirahu laqa himama al-maqadiri

It is possible that its meaning is: he wished to recite the Qur'an at the beginning of the night as was his custom, but he could not do so due to the disturbance of the besiegers against him, and they killed him at the end of the night. For this reason he made it a wish (tamanni), because he loved that but could not do it. Perhaps they recited it with another narration and it was taken as another witness, and perhaps they mistook the second narration for another verse. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention this meaning in al-Asas. We have already discussed this at His saying ﴿Among them are unlettered people who know not the Book except wishful fancies﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿Wa-inna Allaha la-hadi alladhina amanu ila sirat mustaqim﴾ is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and the waw is for interjection. "Those given knowledge" are the believers. Both attributes are combined for them, as in His saying ﴿Those who were given knowledge and faith said: "You have remained in the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection"﴾ [al-Rum: 56] in Surat al-Rum, and as in Surat Saba': ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [Saba': 6]. So the explicit mention of "those who believed" in place of the pronoun for "those given knowledge" is to praise them by the attribute of faith, and to indicate that their faith is the cause of their guidance. The opposite is His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. So what is meant by guidance in both verses is Allah's care in facilitating it; otherwise Allah guided both groups by the call and direction, and among them some were guided and among them some disbelieved.

In the Mushaf it is written "la-hadin" without a yā' after the dāl, following the pause-form... rather, considering the state of continuation (wasl), contrary to the usual practice. In pause, Ya'qub pronounces the yā', unlike the rest.

[Page 297]

﴿We never sent before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish. But Allah abolishes what Satan casts, then Allah establishes His verses. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease and whose hearts are hardened. Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension.﴾ ﴿And that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so that they believe in it and their hearts humble themselves to it. Indeed, Allah is guiding those who believe to a straight path.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence ﴿Say, O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you﴾ [al-Hajj 22:49], because when the preceding discourse led to strengthening the Prophet ﷺ and consoling him regarding what he met from his people of denial, [it showed that] this is the custom of the wrongdoing nations before them. This came after His saying ﴿And how many a city I have given respite while it was wrongdoing﴾ [al-Hajj 22:48], and [it showed] that his role is limited to warning: whoever believes is saved, and whoever disbelieves is destroyed. The intent is to move from that to the consolation and strengthening of him, [showing] that he met what his predecessors among the messengers and prophets (peace be upon them) met, and that none of them was spared from Satan's attempt to corrupt some of what they sought of guidance for their nations, and that they met from their peoples both deniers and believers, [in accordance with] Allah's sunnah (way) regarding His messengers (peace be upon them).

So His saying "from a messenger or prophet" is explicit in generality, and thus it indicates that this did not pass over any of the prophets and messengers. The coordination of "prophet" (nabī) with "messenger" (rasūl) indicates that "prophet" has a meaning other than the meaning of "messenger."

The rasūl (messenger) is a man sent by Allah to the people with a sharīʿah (revealed law). The nabī (prophet) is one to whom Allah revealed the reform of a people's affairs by bringing them to a prior sharīʿah, or by guiding them to what is established in all the sharīʿahs. Thus the nabī is more general than the rasūl, and this is the verified view.

Tamannā (wishing) is a well-known word. Its reality is seeking a thing whose attainment is difficult. Umniyyah is the thing wished for. Messengers and prophets only wish that all their people be righteous and guided. The exception (istithnāʾ) is from the generality of states that follow the generality of their possessors, namely "from a messenger or prophet." That is: We did not send them in any state except the state in which, when one of them wished a wish, Satan cast into it, etc. That is, in the state of the casting occurring at the time of the wish, because the wishes of the prophets are pure good, while Satan's habit is corruption and the nullification of good. The restriction derived from the negation and exception is a restriction of the qualified to a quality, and it is a relative restriction (qaṣr idāfī): that is, [it means] without our sending any of them in a state free from Satan's casting and his deceit.

The reality of ilqāʾ (casting) is throwing a thing from the hand. It is used here metaphorically for whispering and embellishing corruption, likening the embellishment to casting something from the hand among people. From this is His saying ﴿So the Samiri cast [it]﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 20:87], and His saying ﴿And they cast to them the word﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:86], and like His saying ﴿So I grasped a handful from the trace of the Messenger and cast it away﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 20:96], as we verified previously. The object of "cast" (alqā) is omitted, indicated by context, because Satan casts only evil and corruption. So attributing the wish to the prophets indicates that it is a wish for guidance and righteousness, and attributing the casting to Satan indicates that it is a casting of misguidance and corruption. The implied sense is: Satan introduced into the souls of the peoples misguidances that corrupt what the prophets said of guidance.

The meaning of Satan's casting into the wish of the prophet and messenger is the casting of what opposes it, like one who schemes and casts poison into butter. Satan's casting by his whispering is that he commands people to deny and disobey, and casts into the hearts of the leaders of disbelief slanders which they spread among their people. He promotes doubts by casting suspicions that divert the intellect's gaze from remembering the proof. Allah, exalted, renews the guidance and repeats the direction on the tongue of the prophet, and exposes Satan's whisperings and the evil of his deed by clear exposition, like His saying ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:27], and His saying ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fāṭir 35:6].

So Allah, by His guidance and His clarification, abolishes (yanskhu) what Satan casts, that is, He removes the doubts that Satan casts by Allah's clear exposition, and increases the verses of the call of His messengers in clarity. That is the establishing (iḥkām) of His verses, that is, their confirmation, the affirmation of their meaning, and their clarification in a way that leaves no doubt after it, except for one whose heart has been sealed with rust. The meaning of the decisive verses (al-āyāt al-muḥkamāt) has already been discussed in Āl ʿImrān.

Many exegetes (mufassirūn) interpreted "tamannā" as meaning "recited" (qaraʾa). The lexicographers followed them and mentioned a line of verse attributed to Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and they mentioned a story with weak narrations, which we will mention. In any case, the discussion regarding it and the discussion regarding the interpretation of tamannā in its well-known sense are the same. That is: when he recited to the people what was revealed to him, so that they would be guided by it, Satan cast into his umniyyah, that is, into his recitation; that is, he whispered to them in their souls what contradicts and negates it, by his whispering to people denial and turning away from reflection. So Satan's embellishment through his whispering to the disbelievers is likened to the non-compliance with the Prophet, [like] casting something in to mix it and corrupt it.

However, in my view there is great doubt regarding the correctness of applying the term umniyyah to recitation. Even though tamannā with the meaning of "recited" has occurred in a line attributed to Ḥassān ibn Thābit, if the narration of the line from Ḥassān is sound, with variation in its final hemistich:

*Tamannā Kitāba Allāhi awwala laylihi / tamannī Dāwūda al-Zabūra ʿalā mahal*

[He recited the Book of Allah at the start of his night, / as David recited the Psalms at leisure.]

Still, I do not think that recitation is called umniyyah.

It may also be that the meaning is: when the Prophet wished the guidance of his people, or was eager for that, and met obstinacy, and wished for their guidance by every means, Satan cast into the Prophet's soul the thought of despair of their guidance, so that the Prophet would cease from his eagerness, or so that it would weary him. These are thoughts that appear in the soul, but infallibility (ʿiṣmah) stands against them, so that thought does not remain long before it dissipates, and what the Messenger was commanded with, namely persistence in the call and eagerness for right guidance, becomes firmly established in his soul. In this case the meaning of the verse alludes to His saying ﴿And if their turning away is grievous to you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign — [you may do so].
