﴿Those who have been given knowledge﴾ are the believers, by the indication of its contrast with ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ [Muḥammad 47:20], and by His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is guiding those who believe to a straight path.﴾ So the meaning of "knowledge" is the revelation and the books given to the companions of the earlier messengers, for by them they become people of knowledge. The application of ﴿those who have been given knowledge﴾ to believers is repeated in the Qur'an. This is praise of the companions of the messengers, that they were given knowledge, namely the knowledge of religion which the messengers (upon them be blessings and peace) conveyed to them, for the light of prophethood shines in the hearts of those who accompany the Messenger. Therefore you find that one who accompanies the Messenger ﷺ may have been a coarse man before faith, and when he believes he becomes wise, like ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him. The Prophet ﷺ said: "My companions are like the stars: whichever of them you follow, you will be guided."

[Page 303]

The pronoun in "annahu al-haqq" refers back to the knowledge they were given, meaning: so that they may increase in certainty that the revelation they were given is the truth and nothing else, such as what Satan cast to them of doubt, misgivings and misguidance. Thus the restriction (qasr) derived from the definiteness of the two components is a restriction relative to a particular case (qasr idafi).

It is also permissible for the pronoun in "annahu" to refer back to what preceded, from His saying ﴿fa-yansakhu Allahu﴾ up to His saying ﴿thumma yuhkimu Allahu ayatihi﴾, meaning: what has been mentioned is the truth, like the saying of Ru'bah:

fīhā khuṭūṭun min sawādin wa-balaq ∗∗∗ ka-annahā fī al-jildi tawlīʿu al-bahaq

meaning: "as if what was mentioned..."

His saying ﴿fa-yu'minu bihi﴾ means: so that they increase in faith, or so that they believe in the abrogating and the muhkam just as they believed in the original.

Al-ikhbat means tranquility (al-itmi'nan) and humility (al-khushu'). It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿wa-bashshiri al-mukhbitin﴾ [al-Hajj: 34], meaning: that this settles in their hearts, like His saying ﴿qala bala wa-lakin liyatma'inna qalbi﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

With what you have received in the explanation of this verse of clear and evident coherence, independent in its indication and self-sufficient in its essence, free from artificial constructions and from the need for appended narratives, you see that the verse is far removed from what the fabricators and the weak transmitters in the sciences of the Sunnah attached to it, and what a group of exegetes accepted from them out of love for rare oddities without reflection or scrutiny, namely that the verse was revealed concerning a story related to Surat al-Najm. They were not satisfied with what they had corrupted of the meaning of this verse, until they went beyond this attachment to corrupting the meanings of Surat al-Najm. They mentioned in this regard reports from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Shihab, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak. The closest of them is a report from Ibn Shihab, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) sat in one of the assemblies of the Quraysh, many of whose people were Muslims and disbelievers, and he recited to them Surat al-Najm. When he reached His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 19], Satan cast between the listeners, right after that, the words: 'Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is to be hoped for.' The polytheists rejoiced that he had mentioned their gods favorably. There was at the end of that surah a prostration of recitation. When he prostrated at the end of the surah, everyone present of the Muslims and polytheists prostrated. The news spread that the Quraysh had embraced Islam, until it spread in the lands of Abyssinia. Thus some of the emigrants to Abyssinia, among them 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, returned to Madinah." And the Prophet (ﷺ) did not perceive that Satan had cast it. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) informed him, and he was grieved by that, so there was revealed His saying ﴿Wa-ma arsalna min qablika﴾, the verse, as consolation for him. This is a story which the hearer finds to be a handful upon a bundle, and which the expert does not pay attention to. It was only transmitted through feeble chains, and its ultimate is the mention of a story; none of its chains includes a companion's hearing of anything in the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ). Its chain to Ibn 'Abbas is a disputed chain. Moreover, on the day Surat al-Najm was revealed, Ibn 'Abbas was not attending the assemblies of the Prophet (ﷺ). These are solitary reports (akhbar ahad) which contradict the fundamental principles of the religion, because they contradict the principle of the infallibility of the Messenger (ﷺ), so there is no confusion for him in receiving the revelation. His saying ﴿Wa-ma yantiqu 'ani al-hawa﴾ [al-Najm: 3] suffices as a refutation of them. And in the knowledge of the King. Had the trustworthy transmitters narrated them, it would have been obligatory to reject them or interpret them, so how when they are weak and feeble? And how can it pass upon one with a grain of intellect that in a single speech there would be gathered a denunciation of the polytheists for their worship of idols, by His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [al-Najm: 19] up to His saying ﴿Allah has sent down no authority for them﴾ [al-Najm: 23], so that in the midst of that there occurs praise of them as the exalted cranes whose intercession is hoped for? Is this not speech in which part curses part?

The narrators have agreed that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the whole of Surat al-Najm, up to its end, ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship Him﴾ [al-Najm: 62], because they prostrated only when the Muslims prostrated. This indicates that they heard the whole surah, and between the verse ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19] and the end of the surah there are many verses refuting the idols and other objects of worship of the polytheists, and a great deal of discrediting of the beliefs of the polytheists. So how could it be valid that the polytheists prostrated for the sake of praise of their gods? If those reports are not false from their origin, then their interpretation is: that some of the polytheists found the mention of al-Lat and al-'Uzza an opportunity for interference, to fabricate words in praise of them, which are these words, and circulated them among the people to make their allies among the polytheists feel at ease and to cast doubt into the hearts of those weak in faith.

In al-Tibi's commentary on the Kashshaf, citing some historians: that the words of the "gharaniq" (i.e., these phrases) are among the fabrications of Ibn al-Ziba'ra. This is supported by what al-Tabari narrated from al-Dahhak: that the Prophet (ﷺ) had revealed to him the story of the gods of the Arabs, i.e., His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19] etc., so he began reciting: "al-Lat and al-'Uzza," meaning the verse containing this, and the people of Makkah heard the Prophet of Allah mentioning their gods, so they rejoiced and drew near to listen. Then Satan cast: "Those are the exalted cranes, from them the intercession is hoped for." For His saying "they drew near to listen, and Satan cast" etc. indicates that they did not hear the beginning of the surah nor its end, and that their devil cast those words. Perhaps Ibn al-Ziba'ra had an ability to imitate voices, and this ability is found in some people. I knew a youth of our peers who could imitate anyone's voice, such that the listener would think it was the voice of the one imitated. As for the composition of that story upon the report which is established that the polytheists prostrated at the end of Surat al-Najm when the Muslims prostrated, and that is transmitted in the Sahih, this is from the confusion of the compilers.

And likewise the composition of that story upon the verse of Surat al-Hajj. How far apart is the revelation of Surat al-Najm, which is among the early surahs revealed in Makkah, from the revelation of Surat al-Hajj, some of which was among the first revealed at Madinah and some of which was among the last revealed at Makkah. Likewise, linking that story to the story of the return of some of the emigrants from Abyssinia. How far apart is the period of the revelation of Surat al-Najm from the year of the return of those who returned from the emigrants to Abyssinia.

So the correct view: this rumor which was spread among the polytheists at the beginning of Islam is nothing but fabrications of the mockers, foolish of mind, from Makkah, such as Ibn al-Ziba'ra, and they targeted a verse in which al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are mentioned, and built upon it other words to spread sedition among the people. They singled out Surat al-Najm with this deceptive report because they had attended its recitation in the Masjid al-Haram and it had lodged in their minds, and sought to find an excuse for themselves among their people for their prostration in it, which Allah made a miracle for the Prophet (ﷺ). This artifice extended to establishing a meaning in the language: they claimed that (tamanna) means "recited," and al-umniyyah means "recitation," an assertion that is not trusted and for which there is no clear witness in the speech of the Arabs. They cited a verse of Hassan ibn Thabit in lamenting 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him):

tamanna kitaba Allahi awwala laylihi ∗∗∗ wa-akhirahu laqa himama al-maqadiri

It is possible that its meaning is: he wished to recite the Qur'an at the beginning of the night as was his custom, but he could not do so due to the disturbance of the besiegers against him, and they killed him at the end of the night. For this reason he made it a wish (tamanni), because he loved that but could not do it. Perhaps they recited it with another narration and it was taken as another witness, and perhaps they mistook the second narration for another verse. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention this meaning in al-Asas. We have already discussed this at His saying ﴿Among them are unlettered people who know not the Book except wishful fancies﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿Wa-inna Allaha la-hadi alladhina amanu ila sirat mustaqim﴾ is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and the waw is for interjection. "Those given knowledge" are the believers. Both attributes are combined for them, as in His saying ﴿Those who were given knowledge and faith said: "You have remained in the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection"﴾ [al-Rum: 56] in Surat al-Rum, and as in Surat Saba': ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [Saba': 6]. So the explicit mention of "those who believed" in place of the pronoun for "those given knowledge" is to praise them by the attribute of faith, and to indicate that their faith is the cause of their guidance. The opposite is His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. So what is meant by guidance in both verses is Allah's care in facilitating it; otherwise Allah guided both groups by the call and direction, and among them some were guided and among them some disbelieved.

In the Mushaf it is written "la-hadin" without a yā' after the dāl, following the pause-form... rather, considering the state of continuation (wasl), contrary to the usual practice. In pause, Ya'qub pronounces the yā', unlike the rest.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 55:

﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day.﴾

When he related concerning those in whose hearts is a disease and those whose hearts are hardened, that what Satan casts forth for them of nullifying what the messengers brought would be a trial for them, he singled out in this verse the disbelievers concerning the Qur'an, after having included them generally along with the totality of disbelievers in the messengers. He specified that their doubt about what Muhammad ﷺ brought would persist, and that they would hesitate in embracing Islam, until a state arises in which they are cut off from it by the Hour coming upon them suddenly, or by a punishment coming upon them before the Hour.

So "those who disbelieve" here refers to the polytheists of the Arabs, by the indication of the present tense in the verb (lā yazāl, "will not cease") and the verb (ḥattā ta'tiyahum, "until it comes upon them"), which indicate the continuation of that in the future. For this reason a group of the exegetes said: the pronoun in ﴿in doubt about it﴾ refers to the Qur'an, as understood from the context. The more apparent view is that it refers to what the pronoun in ﴿that it is the truth from your Lord, so that they may believe in it﴾ [al-Hajj: 54] refers to.

And (al-sā'ah, "the Hour") is a proper name by predominance for the Day of Resurrection in the terminology of the Qur'an. And (al-yawm, "the day") here means the day of war. The use of the name "day" for the time of war has become widespread, and from it the famous wars of the Arabs were called "the Days of the Arabs" (ayyām al-'Arab).

And (al-'aqīm, "barren") is the woman who does not bear children; "barren" is used figuratively for "ill-omened," because they regard a woman who does not bear children as ill-omened. So the meaning is: a day comes upon them in which they will be utterly uprooted by slaughter. And this is a warning of the Day of Badr.

[p. 309]

The limit expressed in His words ﴿until the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾ (Al-Hajj: 55) indicates that this is the time when the doubt of those who disbelieved ends. This raised the question of what that ending of doubt looks like and what they will encounter when it ends. The context called for answering that question with the sentence ﴿Sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah; He will judge between them﴾, together with what follows it of detail. So it is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani, a clause that answers an implied question).

His words "on that Day" (yawma'idhin) have an omitted noun that the tanwin (nunation) replaces: "the Day when their doubt ends with the arrival of the Hour and the manifestation that what Allah promised them is the truth," or "the Day when the Hour comes upon them suddenly." The clause "He will judge between them" (yahkumu baynahum) is an inclusive apposition (ishtimal) of the clause "Sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah."

The judgment between them means the judgment concerning what they disputed: each group claimed that it was upon the truth and that its opponent was upon falsehood. This is indicated by His words ﴿so that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord﴾ (Al-Hajj: 54) and His words ﴿and those who disbelieve will continue in doubt about it﴾ (Al-Hajj: 55). The judgment may be by speech, or it may be by the appearance of the signs of truth to one group and the appearance of the signs of falsehood to the other. The judgment has been detailed by His words ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ (Al-Hajj: 50) and so on. This detail is a detail of the effect of the judgment, which indicates the detail of its essence; that is, this is Allah's judgment between them on that Day.

By "those who believed and did righteous deeds" is intended the whole category. Among them, those who emigrated in the way of Allah and were then killed or died are singled out for mention, to honour the emigration (hijrah). Because of it, its people are equal in the ranks of the Hereafter, whether they were killed in the way of Allah or died without fighting after emigrating from the land of disbelief.

[p. 310]

The definiteness in "sovereignty" (al-mulk) is the definiteness of the genus. The sentence ﴿Sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah﴾ indicates that the reality of sovereignty is restricted, on that Day, to being sovereignty belonging to Allah, as was mentioned earlier in His words "Praise belongs to Allah" (Al-Fatihah: 1); that is, there is no sovereignty for anyone other than Him on that Day.

The intended meaning of the speech is the clause "He will judge between them," since it is the substitute (badal). The clause ﴿Sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah﴾ was placed first as a preparation for it, so that the clarification by the substitute would come after the ambiguity in the substituted element.

The report about those who disbelieved opens with the demonstrative in His words ﴿then those, for them is a humiliating punishment﴾, to draw attention to the fact that they deserve the humiliating punishment because of their earlier description as disbelievers who denied the signs.

Al-muhin (humiliating) means that which causes humiliation; that is, for them is a punishment that includes what humiliates them, such as being struck with iron maces and the like.

The sentence ﴿then those, for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ is joined with the fa' (then) because of what the division (taqsim) contains of the sense of the particle of detail, which is (amma, as for). It is as if it were said: "As for those who disbelieved..." Because the reward of those who believed had been mentioned, the context prompted the question of one awaiting the contrast of the believers' reward with the punishment of the disbelievers, and that contrast is one of the places where the particle of detail is used.

Al-rizq (provision) is giving, and it is everything bestowed as a favour, whether material things or benefits. Describing it as hasan (good) indicates that it pleases them such that they seek nothing other than it, because nothing is better than it. The clause ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance which they will be pleased with﴾ is a substitute for the clause ﴿Allah will surely provide them with a good provision﴾; it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because the nobility of the dwelling is part of the goodness of the provision, indeed it is more delightful to people of high aspirations. For this reason the entrance is described by "which they will be pleased with" (yarduna-hu).

The clause ﴿And indeed Allah is the best of providers﴾ is placed as a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyyah) between the substitute and the substituted element. Its explicit meaning is praise of Allah, and its implicit meaning is an allusion that the provision Allah gives them is the best of provisions, because it comes from the best of providers. The clause is emphasised with the particle of emphasis (inna), its lam, and the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), to depict the greatness of Allah's provision. The clause ﴿And indeed Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil): He knows what they endured of hardships concerning their emigration from their homes, their families and their wealth, and He is Most Forbearing towards them regarding what they suffered, so He rewards them for what they bore for His sake. This verse shows the distinction of the emigrants in Islam.

Nafi' read mada-lan (مَدْخَلًا) with a fatha on the mim, as a noun of place from the unaugmented verb dakhala (دَخَلَ), since admitting (idkhal) implies entering. The rest read it with a damma on the mim, following the augmented verb in layudkhilannahum (لَيُدْخِلَنَّهُمُ), and it is also a noun of place for admitting.

The clause ﴿And indeed Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil): He knows what they endured of hardships concerning their emigration from their homes, their families and their wealth, and He is Most Forbearing towards them regarding what they suffered, so He rewards them for what they bore for His sake. This verse shows the distinction of the emigrants in Islam.

Nafi' read mada-lan (مَدْخَلًا) with a fatha on the mim, as a noun of place from the unaugmented verb dakhala (دَخَلَ), since admitting (idkhal) implies entering. The rest read it with a damma on the mim, following the augmented verb in layudkhilannahum (لَيُدْخِلَنَّهُمُ), and it is also a noun of place for admitting.

[p. 309]

The limit expressed in His words ﴿until the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾ (Al-Hajj: 55) indicates that this is the time when the doubt of those who disbelieved ends. This raised the question of what that ending of doubt looks like and what they will encounter when it ends. The context called for answering that question with the sentence ﴿Sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah; He will judge between them﴾, together with what follows it of detail. So it is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani, a clause that answers an implied question).

His words "on that Day" (yawma'idhin) have an omitted noun that the tanwin (nunation) replaces: "the Day when their doubt ends with the arrival of the Hour and the manifestation that what Allah promised them is the truth," or "the Day when the Hour comes upon them suddenly." The clause "He will judge between them" (yahkumu baynahum) is an inclusive apposition (ishtimal) of the clause "Sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah."

The judgment between them means the judgment concerning what they disputed: each group claimed that it was upon the truth and that its opponent was upon falsehood. This is indicated by His words ﴿so that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord﴾ (Al-Hajj: 54) and His words ﴿and those who disbelieve will continue in doubt about it﴾ (Al-Hajj: 55). The judgment may be by speech, or it may be by the appearance of the signs of truth to one group and the appearance of the signs of falsehood to the other. The judgment has been detailed by His words ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ (Al-Hajj: 50) and so on. This detail is a detail of the effect of the judgment, which indicates the detail of its essence; that is, this is Allah's judgment between them on that Day.

By "those who believed and did righteous deeds" is intended the whole category. Among them, those who emigrated in the way of Allah and were then killed or died are singled out for mention, to honour the emigration (hijrah). Because of it, its people are equal in the ranks of the Hereafter, whether they were killed in the way of Allah or died without fighting after emigrating from the land of disbelief.

[p. 310]

The definiteness in "sovereignty" (al-mulk) is the definiteness of the genus. The sentence ﴿Sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah﴾ indicates that the reality of sovereignty is restricted, on that Day, to being sovereignty belonging to Allah, as was mentioned earlier in His words "Praise belongs to Allah" (Al-Fatihah: 1); that is, there is no sovereignty for anyone other than Him on that Day.

The intended meaning of the speech is the clause "He will judge between them," since it is the substitute (badal). The clause ﴿Sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah﴾ was placed first as a preparation for it, so that the clarification by the substitute would come after the ambiguity in the substituted element.

The report about those who disbelieved opens with the demonstrative in His words ﴿then those, for them is a humiliating punishment﴾, to draw attention to the fact that they deserve the humiliating punishment because of their earlier description as disbelievers who denied the signs.

Al-muhin (humiliating) means that which causes humiliation; that is, for them is a punishment that includes what humiliates them, such as being struck with iron maces and the like.

The sentence ﴿then those, for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ is joined with the fa' (then) because of what the division (taqsim) contains of the sense of the particle of detail, which is (amma, as for). It is as if it were said: "As for those who disbelieved..." Because the reward of those who believed had been mentioned, the context prompted the question of one awaiting the contrast of the believers' reward with the punishment of the disbelievers, and that contrast is one of the places where the particle of detail is used.

Al-rizq (provision) is giving, and it is everything bestowed as a favour, whether material things or benefits. Describing it as hasan (good) indicates that it pleases them such that they seek nothing other than it, because nothing is better than it. The clause ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance which they will be pleased with﴾ is a substitute for the clause ﴿Allah will surely provide them with a good provision﴾; it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because the nobility of the dwelling is part of the goodness of the provision, indeed it is more delightful to people of high aspirations. For this reason the entrance is described by "which they will be pleased with" (yarduna-hu).

The clause ﴿And indeed Allah is the best of providers﴾ is placed as a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyyah) between the substitute and the substituted element. Its explicit meaning is praise of Allah, and its implicit meaning is an allusion that the provision Allah gives them is the best of provisions, because it comes from the best of providers. The clause is emphasised with the particle of emphasis (inna), its lam, and the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), to depict the greatness of Allah's provision. The clause ﴿And indeed Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil): He knows what they endured of hardships concerning their emigration from their homes, their families and their wealth, and He is Most Forbearing towards them regarding what they suffered, so He rewards them for what they bore for His sake. This verse shows the distinction of the emigrants in Islam.

Nafi' read mada-lan (مَدْخَلًا) with a fatha on the mim, as a noun of place from the unaugmented verb dakhala (دَخَلَ), since admitting (idkhal) implies entering. The rest read it with a damma on the mim, following the augmented verb in layudkhilannahum (لَيُدْخِلَنَّهُمُ), and it is also a noun of place for admitting.

**[Page 312]**

The demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") is used to separate the two statements, drawing the minds of the listeners to what is to follow, because what comes after it is not suitable to be a predicate of the demonstrative. A parallel to this was mentioned earlier, at His words ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah, it is better for him with his Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. The clause ﴿And whoever retaliates…﴾ and what follows it is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with the clause ﴿And those who emigrated in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 58].

The purpose of this is to prepare for jihad (striving, here armed struggle) and to promise the victory that was alluded to earlier in His words ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against because they have been wronged, and indeed Allah is competent to give them victory﴾ [al-Hajj: 39], up to His words ﴿And Allah will surely help those who help Him; indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]. That [earlier passage] came as an interjection in the midst of a reproach against the deniers' denial and their ingratitude for blessings. So the first purpose was completed through what it contained of shifts, and then the discourse returned to the purpose that had been briefly touched upon. Thus the speech here returns to the promise of Allah's help for the people who were transgressed against, just as He promised them that He would admit them into the Hereafter to an abode with which they would be content.

The demonstrative of separation is used to alert the listener to the importance of what follows. The referent of the relative *man* ("whoever") is general, in view of His earlier words ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39]. Thus it draws attention to the fact that the fighting that is permitted is retaliatory fighting in response to a prior aggression, as His words ﴿because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39] also indicate. The change from the plural style in His words ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against﴾ [al-Hajj: 39] to the singular style in His words ﴿And whoever retaliates﴾ indicates that the generality is intended. This makes the statement function as a universal rule (*qa'ida kulliyya*) for one of the divine laws (*sunan*) concerning nations.

Since the relative clause here uses the verb *'aqaba* ("to retaliate") while intending the complete generality of the relative clause to include those who were given permission because they had been wronged, the listener understands that the fighting permitted to them is retaliatory fighting for a prior injustice. In this there is a delimitation of the law of retribution: that it should be proportionate to the aggression that is being repaid, that is, not exceed it.

The aggression of the polytheists against the believers is called "retaliation" in His words ﴿with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾, because what drove the aggressors to aggression was the intention to punish [the believers] for their departure from the religion of polytheism and their rejection of the worship of their idols. It is known that this punishment was an injustice, by His words earlier, ﴿those who were expelled from their homes without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]. The meaning of ﴿with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾ is equivalence in kind. The polytheists harmed the Muslims and compelled them to leave their homeland. Their punishment for this is to expel whoever they can expel from that homeland. They could not do this except through jihad, because the polytheists were numerous and were protected by their city. So compelling whoever can be compelled to leave his homeland is either by fighting, which is complete expulsion, or by capture.

The *thumma* ("then") in His words ﴿and then is wronged﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾. The *thumma* here denotes a sequence of rank (*tarakhi rutbi*), since being wronged is more significant than retaliating with the like of what one suffered, as the one who initiates the injustice is the greater wrongdoer, as it is said: "The initiator is the greater wrongdoer." Thus the polytheists deserved to be punished, because they had transgressed against the Muslims.

The meaning of the verse is similar to the meaning of His words ﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths and planned to expel the Messenger, and they initiated [hostility] against you the first time?﴾ [al-Tawba: 13]. This was a legislation for the fundamentals of defending the "egg" (*al-bayḍa*, the core of the community). As for the verses that encourage pardon, this is not the context in which they were revealed; they pertain to the legislation for the dealings of the community with one another. Allah has affirmed for them His help, if they comply with what they were permitted and retaliate with the like of what they were afflicted with.

There are forced interpretations by the exegetes in explaining this verse, which reveal a bewilderment in reconciling its meanings.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ is a justification for limiting the permission for punishment to equivalence, as stated in His words ﴿And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾, rather than increasing the retaliation, even though the initiator is the greater wrongdoer. This is because Allah's pardon and forgiveness toward His creation, by His wisdom, require that He permit only punishment equal to the offense, since that is more fitting to the truth. It is related from Kisra that he was asked: "By what has your kingdom endured?" He said:

**[Page 313]**

"Because we punish according to the measure of the offense, not according to the measure of anger." Therefore, the mention of the two attributes ﴿Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ is not an allusion to encouraging pardon of the polytheists. It is also permissible that it be a justification for the promise of reward to the emigrants, following the justification in His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Forbearing﴾ [al-Hajj: 59], because the discourse continues concerning their situation.

[Page 315]

The demonstrative is not used here, as its counterpart before it was, to separate two statements. Rather, the reference is to the preceding statement, which indicates the guarantee of victory. Victory requires that one of two opposites prevail over the other and that the army be thrown into the battle against the other army. So God gave an example of this with the prevalence of the day's duration over the night's in part of the year, and the prevalence of the night's duration over the day's in another part. This is because the opposition between night and day, that is, darkness and light, is well known. Close to this is the metaphor of *al-taljīs* (concealment, or disguising) for thrusting oneself into war, in the words of al-Marrār al-Sulamī:

*"And a battalion I disguised with another battalion, until, when they were confused, I shook my hand over them."*

Thus the predicate of the demonstrative here is God's words ﴿because Allah causes the night to enter...﴾, and so on. It is also possible that the demonstrative is a repetition of its earlier counterpart, for the purpose of emphasizing it, since it is connected to it, because the clause ﴿because Allah causes the night to enter into the day﴾, and so on, is linked to the clause ﴿And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾ [al-Hajj: 60], and so on. For this reason it is correct to make ﴿because Allah causes the night to enter into the day﴾, and so on, dependent on God's words ﴿Allah will surely help him﴾ [al-Hajj: 60].

*Al-iylāj* (causing to enter) means inserting. It is used as an image for the concealment of the darkness of the night at the appearance of the light of the day, and vice versa, comparing that transformation to the insertion of one body into another body.

[Page 316]

Thus the *īlāj* of the night into the day is the covering of the light of the day over the darkness of the night. And the *īlāj* of the day into the night is the covering of the darkness of the night over what had been the light of the day. So the *mūlaj* (that which is made to enter) is that which is concealed. The *īlāj* of the night is its ending. The use of *īlāj* for this is a wonderful metaphor, because the shrinking of the darkness of the night occurs gradually, and likewise the shrinking of the light of the day occurs gradually. So this resembles the insertion of one thing into another, since it appears to enter it little by little.

The *bā'* (ب) is causal. That is: there is no wonder in the victory promised to the Muslims over the disbelievers despite the Muslims' small number, for the One who is able to make the day prevail over the night at one time, after their state had been the reverse at another time, is able to make the weak prevail over the strong. So the overall meaning becomes: that is because Allah is able to give them victory.

The combination of mentioning the night entering the day and the day entering the night indicates the alternation of the conditions of time, for the vanquished may become victorious and that victor may become vanquished. Along with this is an alert to the completeness of power, such that it relates to opposite acts and does not follow a single manner, unlike the power of human craftsmen. There is also an embedded (*idmāj*) reminder that the punishment which the polytheists were seeking to hasten is tied to the arrival of its appointed time, and the appointed time is nothing but the entry of night into day and day into night.

Mentioning night and day in this context also embeds a comparison of disbelief with night and Islam with day, because disbelief is an error of belief, so its adherent is like one who walks in darkness, and because faith is a light by which the truth and correct belief become manifest, so its adherent is like one who walks in daylight. In this there is an indication that the intended *īlāj* is the appearance of the day after the darkness of the night, that is, the manifestation of the true religion after the darkness of polytheism. For this reason the verse began with the *īlāj* of the night into the day, that is, the entering of the darkness of the night beneath the light of the day.

And His words ﴿and He causes the day to enter into the night﴾ are a completion (*tatmīm*) for showing the capacity of divine power. Earlier, in Surat Āl ʿImrān, we had ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 27]. The conjunction of ﴿and that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾ to the cause indicates God's knowledge of all conditions. So He gives victory to whoever supports Him, by His knowledge and wisdom, and He promises victory to whoever He knows will surely be His helper. Therefore nothing proceeds from Him except from wisdom.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 62:

﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they call upon besides Him is falsehood, and Allah is the Most High, the Great.﴾

The demonstrative "ذلك" (dhalika, "that") here repeats the demonstrative that preceded it, and for this reason it is not joined by a conjunction. It then gives another reason for the victory of the believers over the polytheists: Allah is the true Lord, who, whenever He wills something, does it and decrees it, so He gives victory to His allies. What the polytheists call upon besides Allah is falsehood, so they cannot give them victory, nor can they help themselves. This reading takes the "ب" (ba', "because of") in the phrase ﴿because Allah is the Truth﴾ to indicate causation (sababiyya), which is the interpretation of the commentators. It will come in Surat Luqman, in a parallel passage, that the more evident reading is to take the "ب" to indicate accompaniment (mulabasa), so that the conjunction of "وأن ما تدعون من دونه هو الباطل" (and that what you call upon besides Him is falsehood) fits smoothly.

"Al-Haqq" (the Truth) means that which corresponds to reality, that is, the true, derived from "haqqa al-shay'" when a thing is established. The meaning is that He is the Truth in divinity. The restriction (qasr) in this sentence, which is conveyed by the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), is a real restriction (qasr haqiqi).

As for the restriction in the phrase "وأن ما تدعون من دونه هو الباطل" (and that what you call upon besides Him is falsehood), which is conveyed by the separating pronoun, it is a claimed restriction (qasr idda'i), meaning that no other falsehood is taken into account, as though whatever else is not even falsehood. This is hyperbole in belittling their idols, because the context is one of polemic and threat. Otherwise, many of the idols and images of non-Arabs are also falsehood.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr (on the authority of 'Asim), and Abu Ja'far read "تدعون" (tad'una, "you call upon") with the second-person "ta'" (the turning of address, iltifat, to the polytheists), because the preceding speech, in which the third-person pronouns were used about them, is intended to make them hear, and to hint at the imminence of victory over them. The rest of the readers read it with the third-person "ya'" (yad'una), following the manner of the preceding speech.

The "ulluw" (exaltedness) of Allah is used metaphorically (musta'ar) for majesty and complete perfection.

"Al-Kibar" (greatness) is used metaphorically for complete power, that is, He is the Most High, the Great, unlike the idols that you worship, since they have no perfection nor power, by the evidence of observation.

**Verse 63:** ﴿Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green? Indeed, God is Subtle, All-Aware.﴾

This is a transition to reminding people of God's blessings upon them, in connection with what preceded it, namely His words ﴿That is because God causes the night to enter the day﴾ [al-Hajj: 61], and so on. The purpose is an indirect call to thank God for His blessings and not to worship anything besides Him, as indicated by the concluding statement (al-tadhyil) that follows the enumeration of these blessings, namely His words ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful﴾ [al-Hajj: 66], meaning the polytheist man. In all of this there is an embedded argument (idmaj al-istidlal) for His sole right to creation and governance, so He is the true Lord, deserving of worship. The connection (munasabah) is what has preceded, that God is the Truth and that what they call upon besides Him is falsehood. Therefore the sentence is a resumptive beginning (istinaf ibtida'i), a new start.

The address is to everyone who is capable of seeing, because the thing seen is well known.

The interrogative is a rhetorical denial (istifham inkari). The heedlessness of many people toward taking lesson from this blessing, and their failure to regard it as significant, has been placed in the position of not knowing it. So that non-knowledge is denied to the people who neglected gratitude and reflection. The verb that the denial questions has been stated with the particle (lam), which makes it refer to the past, and its complement has been stated in the past tense in His words ﴿sends down from the sky water﴾, which is likewise a past-tense sending down. In both of them the meaning of recurrence has not been considered, because the point of denying the non-knowledge of this is that it is a settled matter in the past that cannot plausibly be claimed to be unknown. And (tuṣbiḥu) means "becomes," since five of the sisters of (kāna) are used with the meaning of "became" (ṣāra).

The plant, which is the object of gratitude because it sustains the sustenance of people and animals, is expressed by mention of its green color, because that color is pleasing to the eyes. It is therefore also a cause for gratitude for the beauty of what God has created in visible form, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And for you in them there is beauty when you bring them home and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]. The outcome of the earth becoming green is expressed with the form (tuṣbiḥu mukhḍarrah), although that is a consequence of the verb ﴿sends down from the sky water﴾, which is in the past form, because by using the present form he intended to bring that wondrous, pleasing image vividly before the mind, and to convey that the effect of the sending down of rain persists from one time to another, just as you say: "So-and-so has bestowed a favor upon me, so I go out and come back thankful to him."

The verb (tuṣbiḥu) is a consequence of the verb (anzala), so it is affirmative in meaning. It is not a consequence of a negation or of an interrogative, which is why it was not put in the subjunctive after the particle fa, because the particle fa was not intended to answer a negation. The meaning is not: "Do you not see, so that the earth becomes green."

Sibawayh said: "I asked him, meaning al-Khalil, about ﴿Do you not see that God sends down from the sky water, and so the earth becomes green﴾, and he said: 'This is obligatory,' meaning the nominative (raf') is obligatory, and it serves as an alert, as though you had said: 'Do you hear? God sent down from the sky water, and so-and-so occurred.'" End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "If it were put in the accusative, it would give the opposite of the purpose, because its meaning, i.e., the statement, is the affirmation of greening, and with the accusative it would turn into a negation of greening. Its example is that you say to your companion: 'Do you not see that I have bestowed favors upon you, so that you give thanks?' If you put it in the accusative, you are negating his thanks and doubting his neglect of it; if you put it in the nominative, you are affirming thanks." And this and similar cases are what one who is known for knowledge should be keen to learn in the science of i'rab (grammatical parsing). End of quotation.

Al-mukhḍarrah is that whose color has become green. One says "ikhḍarra al-shay'," just as one says "iṣfarra al-thamar" and "iḥmarra" and "iswadda al-ufuq." The pattern (if'alla) is among those forms used to express the attribution of colors.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, God is Subtle, All-Aware﴾ serves as the reason (ta'lil) for the sending down, meaning He sent down the water on which the greening depends, because He is Subtle, that is, gentle toward His creatures, and because He is All-Aware of the arrangement of effects upon their causes.

[Page 318]

[Page 319]

The sentence is a second predicate of the Name of Majesty (Allah) in His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is Subtle, All-Aware﴾ [al-Hajj: 63]. It serves to draw attention to His exclusive possession of creation and of true sovereignty, so that it may be known from this that He alone deserves worship, and so that the claim of the polytheists that their idols are partners to Him in divinity is refuted, and their worship is redirected from their idols. The occasion (munasabah) is the mention of the sending down of rain and the growth of vegetation, and these are only part of what is in the heavens and what is on the earth.

The sentence was not conjoined (ʿatf) to the one before it, even though the two share the same purpose, because this sentence functions relative to the first as a concluding generalization (tadhyil) with a comprehensive universality that encompasses what the preceding sentence contained. It also does not contain a reminder of a blessing.

The sentence ﴿And indeed, Allah—He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to the sentence ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The fronting of the prepositional phrase (taqdim al-majrur) indicates restriction (qasr): meaning, to Him alone belongs that, not to other than Him, such as your idols, if the restriction is taken to be relative (idafi); or because the self-sufficiency of others and their praiseworthiness are not to be counted, if the restriction is taken to be claimed (idd'a'i). By the attribute of self-sufficiency (al-ghina) it is alerted that He does not depend on anything other than Himself. This is the meaning of self-sufficiency in His attributes, the Exalted: the absence of need, in His essence and His attributes, for any locus or for any determiner that assigns existence rather than non-existence, and the reverse. This is an alert that the dependence of idols on one who fashions them, on one who moves them from place to place, and on one who shakes off dust and filth from them, is evidence of the negation of divinity from them.

As for the description "the Praiseworthy" (al-Hamid), meaning "the one who is praised" (al-mahmud), it is frequently used, and its mention here is to pair with the attribute of self-sufficiency, because the Self-Sufficient bestows abundantly upon people, so they praise Him. The separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) conveys that He is the one exclusively characterized by self-sufficiency, not the idols, and that He is the one exclusively deserving of being praised, since the Arabs did not direct praise to other than Allah, the Exalted. He reinforced the restriction with the emphatic particle (harf al-tawkid) and the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') to affirm the attribution of the restriction to what is restricted, as in the saying of ʿAmr ibn Maʿd Yakrib: "Indeed, I am death." This emphasis is to treat their acknowledgment of His exclusive possession of self-sufficiency or praiseworthiness as though it were doubt or denial, because they did not act in accordance with the requirement of their knowledge when they worshipped other than Him, for only one who is characterized by self-sufficiency is worshipped.

[p. 320]

**[Page 321]**

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is on the earth, and the ship that runs upon the sea by His command, and He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission? Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to mankind.﴾

This is from the sequence (*nasaq*) of reminders of Allah's blessings, and it stands in the position of His saying: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green?﴾ [al-Hajj: 63]. It therefore belongs to the category of favour and argument. It is thus like a repetition made for a purpose, and for this reason the sentence is detached and not joined by a conjunction. This is a reminder of the blessing of the subjection of animals and other things. It also includes the incorporation (*idmaj*) of the argument for His sole right to subjection. The implied meaning is: "He is therefore the true Lord." The sentence ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is on the earth﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), like the sentence ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 63]. The address and the interrogation here are both as in the preceding verse.

*Taskhir* (subjection) means facilitating benefit without any obstacle, and it implies that benefit would otherwise be difficult. Its original sense is facilitating a benefit from something that is inclined to resist, such as the subjection of a servant, and the facilitation of the use of tame animals such as horses, camels, cattle, sheep and the like, by Allah placing in them the nature of fear of humans while preparing them to become accustomed to humans. Then the term was extended to the facilitation of benefit from things whose nature or condition would make benefit hard, were it not for what Allah inspired in humans of the means of overcoming them: by learning their laws, conditions, movements and times of appearance, and by contriving to take possession of them, such as hunting wild animals, diving for pearls and coral, the tools for digging and extracting minerals, shaping in the construction of ships and wheels, and assembling and smelting in the building of steamships, vessels and jewellery. It also includes guidance to controlling the conditions of the great created things, such as the sun, the moon, the stars, the rivers, the valleys, the winds, and night and day, insofar as those conditions appear on the face of the earth, and the countless things on the earth from which humans benefit. All of this falls within the meaning of subjection.

**[Page 322]**

The discussion of subjection has already been given earlier in this surah, and it has been given in Surat al-A'raf, Surat Ibrahim and elsewhere. Our discussion here adds further clarification of the meaning of subjection. The clause ﴿that runs upon the sea by His command﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) with respect to "the ship." This was singled out for mention because that running upon the sea is the manifestation of subjection, since, were it not for the inspiration to build it in its known form, its share of the sea would be drowning. His saying "by His command" refers to the command of creation (*amr al-takwin*), since He made the sea suitable to bear it, and He revealed to Nuh (peace be upon him) the knowledge of building it; then the inspiration of craftsmen continued in order to increase its perfection.

*Al-imsak* (holding back) means binding fast, and it is the opposite of letting fall. It is here, and in His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah holds back the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41], implicitly containing the meaning of prevention. Therefore a preposition is to be supplied to make the verb of holding back transitive after this implicit meaning, and "from" (*'an*) or "min" is to be understood. The connection between coupling the holding back of the sky with the subjection of what is on the earth and the subjection of the ship is that the holding back of the sky from falling upon the earth is a form of subjection, given the requirements of the greatness of the heavenly creatures for overpowering the earthly creatures and crushing them, were it not for what Allah has decreed for each kind of them of laws and systems that prevent any one of them from dominating another. This is as indicated by His saying ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each is floating in an orbit﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40]. Just as Allah has subjected to humans what appears on the face of the earth, among existing things, although many of them by their nature would destroy humans, so He has subjected to them the conditions that appear to people among the phenomena of the horizon, despite their number, vastness and distance, and despite the requirements of their being difficult to control; likewise He has subjected to the benefit of humans what is in the heavens, among existing things, by holding them back in an ordered manner bound to what Allah has decreed, as indicated by His saying ﴿except by His permission﴾, that is, His decree.

The word "the sky" (*al-sama'*) in His saying ﴿and He holds back the sky﴾ may mean what is opposite the earth in the usage of people, so that it is a comprehensive term for all the higher worlds, which we do not comprehend in knowledge, such as the wandering planets and what Allah knows of and reveals to people over successive times. Its falling upon the earth would then mean descent and collapse. The meaning would be that Allah, by the governance of His knowledge and power, has set for the sky a system that prevents it from descending upon the earth. Then His saying ﴿and He holds back the sky﴾ is a favour upon people, by their safety from what would corrupt their lives, and His saying ﴿except by His permission﴾ is a precaution, combining favour and warning. People would then be grateful, seeking more blessings, and fearful of the anger of their Lord, lest He permit some of the sky to fall upon the earth. The exception with His saying ﴿except by His permission﴾ has been found problematic, and it has been said in resolving the problem that its meaning is: "except on the Day of Resurrection, when Allah permits it to fall upon the earth." However, no report has come that the sky will collapse; rather what has been reported is that the sky will split and burst open. What we have said regarding it being a precaution resolves the problem, because a precaution is a hypothetical matter, and so the exception does not imply that the excepted thing occurs.

It is also possible that the word "the sky" means rain, as in the verse of Mu'awiyah ibn Malik:

*"When the rain descends upon the land of a people, we pasture under it, even if they are angry."*

And as in the saying of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani in the hadith of the Muwatta': "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in prayer at al-Hudaybiyah following a rain (*sama'*) that had fallen during the night." In that case the meaning of the verse is: Allah, by His decree, set for the descent of rain upon the earth measures, and He set its causes; and if the rain's descent upon the earth were to continue unabated, people would be harmed. So holding back its descent by regular continuity is a favour upon people, and setting the descent of rain at the time of its creation by Allah is also a blessing. This includes mention of two blessings: the blessing of the rain, and the blessing of safety from the overflowing of waters.

It is also possible that the word "sky" is used for all the higher existing things included in the word "sky," which is what is above the earth, so that the name is applied to what it contains, just as the word "earth" is applied to its inhabitants in His saying ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its extremities?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41]. So Allah holds back what is in the heavens of meteors, and of the spheres of ether and frost, from piercing the sphere of air; and He holds back what is in them of forces such as rain, hail, snow and lightning from falling upon the earth and striking it, except by Allah's permission, in what people are accustomed to having His permission for, such as the falling of rain, snow, lightning and meteors, and what they are not accustomed to, such as the falling of stars. Thus the place of ﴿and He holds back the sky﴾ after His saying ﴿and the ship that runs upon the sea by His command﴾ is like the place of His saying ﴿It is Allah who has subjected to you the sea, that the ship may run upon it by His command, and that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may be grateful. And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 12], in Surat al-Jathiyah. And in His saying ﴿except by His permission﴾ there is an incorporation (*idmaj*) of favour and warning, for among the permissions to fall upon the earth are some that are desired by people, and some that are disliked. This third interpretation is more comprehensive than the other two and more concise, and it is therefore more suitable to the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the Qur'an.

The exception in His saying ﴿except by His permission﴾ is an exception from the generality of the associated elements of the verb ﴿holds back﴾ and the circumstances of its object, which is the word "sky," according to its various interpretations. That is, He prevents what is in the sky from falling upon the earth in all its conditions, except for a fall accompanied by permission from Allah. This is what has become clear to me regarding the meaning of the verse.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that His saying ﴿except by His permission﴾ refers back to the holding back, because the speech implies, without need for a support, that is, it indicates by the implication (*dalalat al-iqtida'*) the supplying of this implied complement, taking from His saying ﴿without pillars that you can see﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2] and similar. So it is as if He meant: 'except by His permission, so He holds it back.'" End of quotation. He means that the particle of exception is an indicator of the omitted element.

*Al-idhn* (permission), in its reality, is a statement by which the doing of something is requested. Here it is used metaphorically for will and creation, and these two are the object of the will and power.

The verse has encompassed the three realms: the land, the sea and the air.

The place of the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to mankind﴾ is that of a reason (*ta'lil*) for the subjection and the holding back, in view of the exception, because in all of that there is mercy toward people through facilitating their benefits, within which is the removal of harm from them.

*Al-Ra'uf* is an intensive form derived from *ra'fah* (tenderness), or an attributive adjective of the stable type (*sifah mushabbahah*). It is an attribute that requires the averting of harm.

*Al-Rahim* is an attribute derived from mercy (*rahmah*). It is an attribute that requires the provision of benefit to one who needs it. The two attributes may follow one another, and combining them indicates what each attribute specifically entails and emphasises what they both share.

[Page 326]

﴿And it is He who gave you life, then causes you to die, then will give you life again﴾

After the argument for the Resurrection had been woven into the admonitions, the favours, and the reminders of blessings, the discussion of the Resurrection is resumed here in the manner of the conclusion of a syllogism (qiyas, a form of logical inference). The verse mentions the disbelievers' first life, about which there is no doubt, and their death, which they do not dispute. It thus becomes clear that after death there is another life, as was drawn from the previous proofs. This is the point of the argument. Accordingly, the clause ﴿And it is He who gave you life﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿and holds up the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 65], because the opening of this passage belongs to the enumeration of blessings. It was therefore fitting that it be coordinated with what precedes it, which contains both a favour and an argument.

* * *

﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil, a closing sentence that sums up the purpose) that gathers the aim of enumerating the blessings of the Benefactor, the great blessings which necessitate that He alone deserves gratitude, and that creation acknowledges His lordship (rububiyyah) and oneness.

The emphasis of the predicate with the particle ﴿inna﴾ ("indeed") is because they are treated as if they were deniers, that they are disbelievers. The definite article in ﴿al-insan﴾ ("man") is the definiteness of conventional comprehensiveness (al-istighraq al-ʿurfi), which indicates most individuals of the species, in the manner of the saying: "The commander gathered the goldsmiths," meaning the goldsmiths of his land, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So the magicians were assembled for an appointed day﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 38]. Most of the Arabs at that time denied the Resurrection. Alternatively, ﴿al-insan﴾ may refer specifically to the polytheist, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And man says: "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66].

The word ﴿kafur﴾ ("ungrateful") is an intensive form of ﴿kafir﴾ (disbeliever), because their disbelief was out of obstinacy and arrogance.

[Page 327]

It is also permissible that ﴿kafur﴾ be taken from the ingratitude for blessings (kufr al-niʿmah), in which case the intensiveness is considered in terms of the effects of heedlessness of gratitude. In that case the comprehensiveness is literal (haqiqi).

[Page 328 marker omitted; see below]

This is connected in meaning to His words, ﴿For every community We have appointed rites (manasik) for them to observe, so let them mention the name of God over the livestock He has provided for them﴾ [22:34], and what follows it. What separated the two statements was a digression that the context required, from His words, ﴿And give good tidings to the doers of good. Indeed, God defends those who believe﴾ [22:37], up to this point. So the discourse returned to the purpose stated in His words, ﴿For every community We have appointed rites﴾ [22:34], in order to build upon it His words, ﴿so let them not dispute with you about the matter﴾. This is an argument for the Oneness of God, drawn from the earlier religious laws, aimed at refuting the plurality of gods: God did not appoint for the people of any earlier religious community anything but one rite (mansak) by which they draw near to God, because the One who is drawn near to is one. The polytheists, however, made many rites. For each idol there was a house where animals were slaughtered, such as the ghabghab (a pit or basin for blood) for al-ʿUzzā. Al-Nābigha said:

*"And what was poured out on the altar-stones of flesh . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ."*

That is, of blood. His words, ﴿For every community We have appointed rites for them to observe, so let them mention the name of God over the livestock He has provided for them, for your God is one God, so submit to Him﴾ [22:34], as mentioned earlier, have pointed to this meaning.

Thus the sentence is a resumptive new statement (istinaf). The connection is evident, and for that reason the sentence is disjoined and not conjoined by a conjunction, as its earlier counterpart was.

[Page 329 marker omitted]

The word *mansak*, with a fatḥa on the *mīm* and a fatḥa on the *sīn*, is a noun of place from *nusuk*, which is vocalized with a ḍammah on both, as mentioned earlier. The root meaning of *nusuk* is worship, and it is also applied to sacrificial offering (qurbān). Here, therefore, *mansak* means the places of the Hajj, which differs from its meaning in the preceding verse, where it refers to the place of sacrificial offering. The pronoun in *nāsikūhu* is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, that is, *nāsikūna fīhi* (they perform rites in it).

In the *Muwaṭṭaʾ* (of Mālik): The Quraysh used to stand at the Sacred Monument (al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām) at Muzdalifah, at Quzaḥ, while the Arabs and others stood at ʿArafah. They would dispute, one party saying, "We are more correct," and the other saying, "We are more correct." So God, exalted is He, said, ﴿For every community We have appointed rites they perform﴾, and so on. In our view, and God knows best, this dispute was of this kind, and I have heard this from people of knowledge.

Al-Bājī said in *al-Muntaqā*: This is the view of Rabīʿah. This implies that the proponents of this interpretation hold that the verse was revealed after the obligation of Hajj had been enjoined in Islam and before the polytheists were prevented from it, that is, it was revealed in the year nine. The more apparent view is the opposite, as mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

From this argument it follows that they have no remaining proof with which to dispute with the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning monotheism, after the testimony of all the earlier religious communities. The prohibition, in its apparent form, is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), because what he was given of proofs is sufficient to cut off the disputation of his opponents. Thus the opponents are the real object of the prohibition. But since the cause of their prohibition is what the Messenger (ﷺ) possesses of proofs, the prohibition against their disputing with him was addressed to him, as if it were said: "Do not leave them anything with which they could dispute with you." This is of the type of the Arabic saying, "I will not find you doing such and such," meaning, "Do not do it, and I will (then) not find you (doing it)," so the speaker directs the prohibition to himself. The intended meaning is the prohibition of the listener from its causes, and it is a prohibition for another by way of kināyah (metonymy).

[Page 330 marker omitted]

Al-Zajjāj said: It is a prohibition addressed to the Messenger against disputing with them, because the form *mufāʿalah* (the reciprocal verbal pattern) requires the occurrence of the act from the side of both its agent and its object, so a prohibition of each of the two sides from it is valid. The verb is attributed here to the pronoun of the polytheists in order to intensify the prohibition against the Prophet's (ﷺ) disputing with them, like the affirmation of a thing by its proof. The essential meaning of this view is that it is a command to the Messenger to turn away from debating them after the proofs have been presented to them. The noun "the matter" (*al-amr*) here is general, intended as monotheism by context. It is also possible that the polytheists disputed about whether they were in error, by claiming that they were upon the religion of Abraham, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) had established the Hajj, which is among their rites, so they made this a pretext for claiming that they were upon the truth and the religion of Abraham. Thus His words, ﴿For every community We have appointed rites they perform﴾, were a disclosure of their confusion, showing that the Hajj is a true rite and a symbol of monotheism, and that whatever else there is, is false and an addition to it. So let them not dispute about the matter of the Hajj after this. This interpretation is the one that fits the coherence of the pronouns referring to the polytheists from what preceded up to His words, ﴿God has promised those who disbelieve the Fire, and wretched is the destination﴾ [22:72]. It also fits because part of this surah was revealed in Mecca at the end of the Prophet's (ﷺ) stay there, and part in Medina at the beginning of his stay there, so there was no dispute between the Prophet and the People of the Book at that time, and it is therefore remote to interpret the disputation as a dispute with the People of the Book.

His words, ﴿and invite to your Lord﴾, are coordinated with the clause ﴿so let them not dispute with you about the matter﴾. After the cessation of disputation over religion, it is a command to persist in the invitation and not to rest content with the manifestation of the proof, because obstinacy opposes conviction, and because persisting in the invitation has benefits for all people. The omission of the object of *udʿu* (invite) signifies generality.

[Page 331 marker omitted]

His words, ﴿indeed you are upon a straight guidance﴾, are a causal clause (taʿlīl) explaining the persistence in the invitation, and it stands in the place of the causal particle *fāʾ* (therefore), not as a refutation of doubt. The preposition *ʿalā* (upon) is used metaphorically to denote firm establishment in guidance.

The description of guidance as "straight" is an implicit metaphor (istiʿārah makniyyah). Guidance is likened to the road that leads to the desired goal, and it is alluded to by "straight," because the straight path delivers most swiftly. Thus the religion of Islam is the easiest of the laws in delivering to the psychological perfection which is the ultimate aim of religions. In this statement there is a reinforcement for the Prophet (ﷺ) and a renewal of his energy to bear the burdens of the invitation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verses 68–69:

﴿And if they argue with you, say: "Allah knows best what you do."﴾ ﴿Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which you used to differ.﴾

This is a coordination (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿So let them not dispute with you over the matter﴾ [al-Hajj: 67]. The meaning is: if it becomes clear that they are not persuaded by the proofs that end disputation, and they refuse anything but continued argument, out of mere contention and mockery, then say: "Allah knows best what you do." In His saying ﴿Allah knows best what you do﴾ there is an entrusting (tafwīḍ) of their affair to Allah, the Exalted. It is a metonymy (kināya) for ending the argument with them, and an integration (idmāj) with an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to threat and warning, expressed in words directed at them that suit what they display of seeking proof, and also suit what is in their souls of obstinate opposition, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So turn away from them and wait; indeed, they are waiting﴾ [al-Sajda: 30]. By "what they do" (mā yaʿmalūn) is meant what they do of kinds of opposition and argument based on falsehood, in order to refute the truth with it, and other things besides that.

Page 331

The clause ﴿Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a resumed statement (kalām mustaʾnaf), not part of what is said. It is therefore addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and not addressed to the polytheists, as indicated by His saying "between you." The intended purpose is to strengthen the Messenger and the believers. What they were differing about is what was expressed by "the matter" in His saying ﴿So let them not dispute with you over the matter﴾ [al-Hajj: 67].
