Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 70:

﴿Do you not know that Allah knows what is in the heaven and the earth? Indeed, that is in a Book. Indeed, that for Allah is easy.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (istina') serving to further confirm the assurance contained in His saying ﴿Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Hajj: 69]. That is: nothing escapes Him of your deeds, so He will recompense each person according to the account of his deed. The statement is thus a metonymy (kinaya) for the recompense of each person in a manner befitting him. And ﴿what is in the heaven and the earth﴾ includes what the polytheists do and what they used to dispute about.

The interrogative is either denunciatory (inkari) or affirmative (taqriri), meaning: you know that. This statement is also a metonymy for consolation (tasliya), that is: do not let your chest be constricted by what you encounter from them. The clause ﴿Indeed, that is in a Book﴾ explains the clause preceding it. That is: He knows what is in the heaven and the earth with a detailed knowledge that does not vary, because the nature of a Book is that increase and decrease do not reach it. The demonstrative ism al-isharah (the demonstrative noun) refers either to the deed in His saying ﴿Allah knows best what you do﴾ [al-Hajj: 68], or to (ma) in His saying ﴿concerning what you used to differ﴾ [al-Nahl: 92].

Page 332

The Book (kitab) is that by which all deeds are preserved: either by way of likening the complete preservation to writing, or literally, and it is permissible that Allah makes for this a book suited to unseen matters. The clause ﴿Indeed, that for Allah is easy﴾ explains the content of the interrogative concerning the recompense.

The demonstrative noun refers to the content of the interrogative in the sense of the metonymy, so its interpretation is by what has been mentioned. You may also make it an explanation of the clause ﴿He knows what is in the heaven and the earth﴾, the demonstrative noun then referring to the knowledge derived from the verb (ya'lamu), that is: Allah's knowledge of what is in the heaven and the earth belongs to Him, obtained without acquisition, because His knowledge is essential (dhati), requiring no study or inquiry. The fronting of the prepositional phrase over its governed element, which is (yasir), is for the sake of emphasis on mentioning it, to indicate its possibility on the side of Allah's knowledge, exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 71:

﴿And they worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that of which they have no knowledge. And for the wrongdoers there is no helper.﴾

It is permissible that the waw (wa) be a conjunctive particle (harf 'atf), and the sentence is then conjoined to the preceding sentence with what branches off from it, a conjunction of one purpose to another purpose.

It is also permissible that the waw be a waw of circumstance (wau al-hal), and the sentence after it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject pronoun in the word (jadalukā, "they disputed with you"). The meaning is: they disputed with you concerning the religion, persisting in worshipping that which does not deserve worship, after they had seen the proofs. The circumstantial clause contains a expression of wonder at their state, in their obstinacy and insistence.

The use of the present tense verb, which indicates renewal, on both interpretations is because the proofs that surround them, and those of which they were reminded in some of the preceding verses, are sufficient to make them desist from worshipping idols, were they seeking the truth.

The phrase "min dūni" (besides) indicates that they turn away from the worship of Allah, because the word "dūn," although it is a noun for distancing, may also apply to sharing between what is attributed to it and something else. So when "min" enters upon "dūn," it conveys the meaning of the beginning of the action from a side distant from what "dūn" is attributed to, and so it requires that the thing attributed is not a partner in the action. The reasoning for this is that, since their hearts were steeped in turning to the worship of idols and in incorporating them into the matters of their acts of devotion, even into the rites of the Hajj, for they placed idols among its rites, some of which they placed in the Ka'bah and some atop al-Safa and al-Marwah, they were made as those who wholly neglect the worship of Allah altogether.

Al-sultan means proof (al-hujjah). The "sent-down proof" is the divine command that came through His messengers and in His laws, meaning: they worship that for which they find no excuse for worshipping in the earlier laws. The utmost of their position is that they excused themselves by the precedence of their forefathers in worshipping their idols, and they did not claim that any prophet commanded his people to worship an idol, nor that any divine religion permitted the worship of idols.

﴿And that of which they have no knowledge﴾

That is, they have no firm conviction regarding it, because firm conviction does not arise except from evidence, and for falsehood it is impossible for evidence to be established. The mention of the absence of the legislative evidence before the absence of the rational evidence is because the legislative evidence is more important. The "mā" in His words ﴿And for the wrongdoers there is no helper﴾ is negating. The clause is conjoined to the clause ﴿they worship besides Allah﴾, meaning: they worship what has been mentioned, and they have no helper, so the worship of idols does not benefit them. The intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" is the polytheists being spoken of, and this is the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, to hint that the cause of their having no helper is their wrongdoing, that is, their disbelief. This also conveys that their worship of idols is in vain, because they worshipped them hoping for victory. By its generality it indicates that the idols do not help them, and so it dispenses with a third relative clause that would describe the idols, as if it were said: "and that which does not help them," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those you invoke besides Him are not able to help you﴾ [al-A'raf: 197].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 72:

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, you can recognize denial on the faces of those who disbelieve; they almost attack those who recite Our verses to them.﴾

This is conjoined to the clause ﴿and they worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Hajj: 71], to explain another of their crimes alongside the crime of idol worship. This is the crime of denying the Messenger and denying the Qur'an.

The "verses" (ayat) here are the Qur'an alone and not other miracles, based on His saying ﴿and when they are recited to them﴾ [Maryam: 73].

The "munkar" (that which is denounced) may be either the thing that sight and souls reject, so that here it is a noun, meaning the signs of their hatred, anger and determination toward evil; or it is a mimi verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī) meaning denial (inkar), like mukram meaning ikram. Both interpretations come back to the meaning that anger and rage appear on their faces when the Qur'an is recited to them and they are called to faith. This is a metonymy (kinayah) for their souls being filled with denial and rage, to the point that its effect exceeded their inner states and showed on their faces, as in His saying ﴿you recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 24], a metonymy for the abundance of their bliss and their excessive joy in it. Because of this metonymy, one departs from explicit statements such as: "their rage intensified," or "they almost burst with rage," and such as His saying ﴿their hearts deny, and they are arrogant﴾ [al-Nahl: 22].

Page 335
The restriction of the verses by the description "clear" (bayyinat) serves to magnify their denial of them, since there is nothing in them for which their deniers could be excused.

The address in His saying "you recognize" (ta'rifu) is to everyone who is fit to be addressed, as evidenced by His saying ﴿against those who recite Our verses to them﴾. The expression "those who disbelieve" (alladhina kafaru) is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun. The apparent construction would have been ﴿you recognize on the faces of those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., the faces of those who worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority. The apparent construction was departed from in order to record their disbelief against them, by implying that the cause of this is what they conceal of disbelief.

Al-saṭw means assault, i.e., they come close to attacking those who recite the verses to them, out of intense anger and rage at hearing the Qur'an.

"Those who recite" (alladhina yatlunna) may refer to the Prophet (ﷺ), by using a plural noun for the singular, as in His saying ﴿and the people of Noah when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37], i.e., they denied the Messenger.

It may also refer to those Muslims who recite the Qur'an to them, along with the Messenger. As for those among the believers who attacked them, they were perhaps not the same ones who recited the Qur'an to them, or the attack upon them occurred after the revelation of this verse, so there is no difficulty in the mention of the verb of approximation (yakadu).

The clause ﴿they almost attack﴾ is in the position of a substitute clause of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for the clause ﴿you recognize on the faces of those who disbelieve the denial﴾, because the intention to attack is among what the denial includes.

* * *

Page 336
﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire, which Allah has promised to those who disbelieve. And wretched is the destination.﴾

This is a fresh independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), indicating an increase in their rage, in that Allah commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to recite to them what indicates that they are heading to the Fire.

The connection with "fa" (then) arises from the appearance of the effect of denial on their faces, so the indications of their features were made to function like the indications of words. Upon this is based what is an answer to a statement, which increases their rage. It is also permissible that the connection is to the recitation derived from His saying ﴿and when Our verses are recited to them﴾, i.e., recite to them the verses warning of and clarifying their disbelief, and upon this is based their threat with the Fire.

The interrogative is used for seeking permission, and it is a mocking permission, since he had already informed them of it without waiting for their answer.

"Sharr" (worse) is a superlative noun, whose origin is ashharr. The hamza was frequently elided for lightness, as it was elided in khayr in the sense of akhyar. The indication by "dhalikum" (that) refers to what stirred their aversion and resentment, i.e., by that which is more harmful to you in your souls than what you heard which angered you; that is, if you are angry at what was recited to you of the verses, then increase in anger at this which I inform you of. His saying "the Fire" is the predicate of an omitted subject indicated by His saying ﴿worse than that﴾. The estimate is: "worse than that is the Fire."

Page 337
So the sentence is an explanatory fresh sentence (isti'naf bayani), i.e., if you ask about that which is worse, know that it is the Fire.

The clause "which Allah has promised" is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Fire," or it is a fresh sentence. The expression for them as "those who disbelieve" is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, i.e., Allah promised it to you for your disbelief.

"And wretched is the destination" means: wretched is their destination, it (the Fire). The definite article is a substitute for the genitive complement, so the clause is an expression of blame, conjoined to the circumstantial clause on the presumption of a verb of saying. It is also permissible that the definite article is generic, giving generality, i.e., wretched is the destination it is for whoever arrives at it; then the clause is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for the general ruling it contains concerning the addressees and others, and the "wa" is a parenthetical concluding "wa" (waw i'tiradiyyah tadhiliyyah).

[Page 338]

The verses of argument, admonition, and warning that this surah contains, which convince the mind that the God of mankind is One and that what is worshipped besides Him is false, are followed by a comprehensive parable describing the state of those deities and of their worshippers. The address "O mankind" (*yā ayyuhā al-nās*) is directed at the polytheists, since they are the intended target of the refutation and rebuke, as indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed, those you call upon﴾ according to the reading of the majority (*al-Jumhur*), who read *tad'ūna* with the second-person (*tā' al-khiṭāb*).

[Page 339]

Thus "mankind" here refers to the polytheists, which is the prevalent usage of the term in the Qur'an. It is also possible that "mankind" refers to all people, both Muslims and polytheists. The opening of the surah with "O mankind" and its closing with the same expression form a kind of *radd al-ʿajuz ʿalā al-ṣadr* (a rhetorical device in which the end echoes the beginning). What adds to its beauty is that the ending gathers what is in the beginning and what follows it, so that it serves as the conclusion of the argument, the summary of the sermon, and the essence of the lesson.

*Ḍarb al-mathal* (striking a parable) means mentioning and explaining it. The verb *ḍarb* is used metaphorically for speech and mention, by analogy with forcefully placing something, i.e., a parable has been put forth to you. Its meaning was explained earlier at His saying ﴿that He should not hesitate to strike any parable﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah. The verb *ḍuriba* is in the passive form, so no agent is mentioned, unlike in other places where the agent of striking a parable is stated, such as His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not hesitate to strike any parable﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah, and ﴿Allah strikes a parable: a slave owned﴾ [al-Naḥl: 75] in Surat al-Naḥl, and ﴿Allah strikes a parable: a man﴾ [al-Zumar: 29] in Surat al-Zumar, and ﴿Allah strikes a parable of two men﴾ [al-Naḥl: 76] in Surat al-Naḥl. In those places and others, the striking of a parable is attributed to Allah. Also His saying ﴿So do not strike for Allah parables﴾ [al-Naḥl: 74] in Surat al-Naḥl, and ﴿And he struck for Us a parable and forgot his own creation﴾ [Yā Sīn: 78] in Surat Yā Sīn, where the striking is attributed to the polytheists. Here the aim is to compose the expression concisely so that it can convey two possibilities.

The first: the agent is taken to be Allah, and the parable is a *tashbīh tamthīlī* (a comparison by means of an extended image), meaning that Allah has set forth a clarifying image that makes clear the state of the idols in their utter inability to create even the weakest of creatures, as is observed by everyone.

The second: the agent is taken to be the polytheists, and the parable carries the sense of "something similar" (*al-mithl*), meaning that they made their idols equal to Allah in divinity.

[Page 340]

The past form in *ḍuriba* is used, under the first possibility, to bring the time of the past close to the present, like His saying ﴿if they were to leave behind them weak offspring﴾ [al-Nisā': 9], meaning: if they were about to leave them, that is, after death.

The clause ﴿Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah﴾ to its end may be an explanation of the verb *ḍuriba* under the first possibility, meaning: a wondrous parable has been explained. It may also be an explanation of the word *mathal* under the second possibility, because of the phrase ﴿you call upon besides Allah﴾ within it. Following from this meaning of conciseness, His saying ﴿So listen to it﴾ is stated, to draw the ears' attention to the content of this parable, which nullifies the claim of partnership with Allah in divinity. That is, listen with contemplation. So the imperative form in ﴿so listen to it﴾ is used to urge attention under the first possibility, and to express wonder under the second. The pronoun in *lahu* ("to it") refers to the parable under the first possibility, since the parable in that sense belongs to the category of spoken words, and it refers to the striking derived from the verb *ḍuriba* under the second possibility, following the manner of ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 8]. That is, listen to the striking, meaning to what indicates the striking through words. Thus a noun is understood by the context of "listen," since what is heard can only be words, so the meaning is: listen to what indicates the striking of a parable that is marvelled at for the folly of those who strike it. The past form *ḍuriba* is used although it has not yet been spoken, to bring the past close to the present, as in His saying ﴿if they were to leave behind them weak offspring﴾ [al-Nisā': 9], meaning: if they were about to leave them. This is an alert to the listeners to prepare themselves to receive this parable, in keeping with what is known among eloquent speakers regarding their anticipation of parables and their proper places.

[Page 341]

The word *mathal* has come to mean the comparison of one state with another, as explained earlier at His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] in Surat al-Baqarah. So the comparison in this verse is implicit and hidden, indicated by His saying ﴿and even if they were to gather for it﴾ and His saying ﴿The seeker and the sought are both weak﴾. The many idols, scattered among the tribes of the Arabs and especially in Makkah, are likened to great persons in the eyes of their worshippers. Their condition of helplessness is likened to the condition of people who are unable to create even the weakest of creatures, which is the fly, let alone great creations such as the heavens and the earth. The attribution of the negation of creation to them indicates their likeness to beings endowed with will, because the negation of creating is by implication the negation of attempting to create, as in His saying ﴿They are dead, not alive﴾ [al-Naḥl: 21], as explained earlier in Surat al-Naḥl. And even if it were assumed that the fly took something from them, they would not be able to retrieve it from it, and the evidence for this is the observed fact that they do not move. Just as they are incapable of creating the weakest of creatures and of repelling the weakest of creatures from themselves, how then could they be described as divine? The image of the comparison (*al-hay'ah al-mushabbah bihā*) is alluded to by mentioning the necessary attributes of the components of the comparison, in His saying ﴿will not create﴾ and His saying ﴿And if the fly should snatch from them anything﴾ to its end. Therefore, the comparison of the idols' helplessness with a condition beneath that of the weakest creatures is effected, and so it is an *isti'ārah tamthīliyyah makniyyah* (an implicit metaphorical image). The author of *al-Kashshāf* explained the word *mathal* here as "a strange attribute," likening it to some well-known proverbs. This is an explanation without parallel and without any usage supporting it. He did so out of a limited delving into the meaning, not out of inability to extract the true sense of the parable, which is "its stump that is rubbed" and "its palm-trunk that is adorned." But I think he came upon it in a moment of haste in explanation, or busy with a weighty matter, and how often the first has left the last behind.

Following from the preparation to receive this parable is the command to listen to it, to direct the mind wholly to understand it, and to await the explanation of its generalities, in order to be alert to what is recited afterward.

[Page 342]

The clause ﴿Indeed, those you call upon﴾ and what follows is an explanation of the word *mathal* under both of the preceding possibilities in the sense of ﴿a parable has been struck﴾, since *mathal* has the sense of speech, and so its explanation by this statement is correct. The assertion is emphasized by the particle of affirmation, *inna*, and the negation within it is emphasized by the particle of negative emphasis, *lan*, in order to treat the addressees as those who deny the content of the statement, because their making the idols gods necessarily entails their affirming that the idols create, whereas creation has been negated of them in the future. This is more emphatic in bringing in those who ascribed divinity to them, since the negation of their creating in the future implies the negation of that in the past all the more, because one who does something will find doing it later easier.

Al-Jumhūr read *tad'ūna* with the second-person *tā'*, on the basis that the intended sense of "mankind" in "O mankind" is specifically the polytheists. Ya'qūb recited it with the third-person *yā'*, on the basis that "O mankind" addresses all people, and that they know of the condition of a group among them, namely the people of polytheism. The implied sense is: "Indeed, those who call upon [idols] are a group among you."

*Al-dhubāb* (the fly) is a collective noun whose singular is *dhubābah*, a well-known flying insect. Its plural is *dhibbān*, with a kasra on the *dhāl* and a shadda on the *nūn*. In Arabic, the singular is not called *dhibbānah*.

The fly is mentioned because it is among the most insignificant of living creatures that are visibly alive. As for what is related in the hadith about image-makers, that Allah says: "Then let them create a grain, or let them create an atom," it is in the context of challenging them, because a grain has no life in it while an atom has some weak life in it. The clause ﴿and even if they gathered for it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and the *wāw* is the *wāw* of circumstance, and *law* in it is *waṣliyyah* (a conjunctive particle meaning "even if"). Its reality was explained earlier at His saying ﴿never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold even if he offered it as ransom﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 91] in Surat Āl ʿImrān. That is: they will not be able to create it while they are scattered, and even if they gathered from the scattered tribes and cooperated to create the fly, they would not create it.

*Al-istinqādh* (rescuing) is an intensified form of *al-inqādh*, like *al-istiḥyā'* and *al-istijābah*.

The clause ﴿The seeker and the sought are both weak﴾ is a concluding statement and a summation of the purpose of the illustration, meaning: the one who calls and the one who is called upon are both weak. It alludes to His saying ﴿Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah will not create a fly﴾ and so on. That is: you are weak in calling upon them as gods, and the idols are weak in relation to the attributes of God. This clause is a statement sent forth as a proverb, and that is part of the eloquence of the speech.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 74:

﴿They have not esteemed God with the esteem due to Him. Indeed, God is All-Powerful, Almighty.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) appended to the parable, to the effect that their worship of idols alongside God is a belittling of the right of His divinity, exalted is He, since they associated with Him in the greatest of attributes the lowliest of the things described, and since they showed arrogance when His verses were recited to them, and when they intended to seize His Messenger.

Al-qadr (القدر) means greatness and magnificence. The verb qadara (قَدَرَ) implies that He is the one who acts according to His own measure. The meaning is: they did not magnify Him with the magnification due to Him, when they associated with Him the weak and powerless, while He is the Overcomer, the Mighty. Its interpretation has already been given earlier, in His words ﴿They have not esteemed God with the esteem due to Him when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon a human being."﴾ [al-An'am: 91], in Surat al-An'am.

The clause ﴿Indeed, God is All-Powerful, Almighty﴾ gives the reason for the content of the clause before it. For what they associated with God in worship is every weak and humiliated thing, so they did not esteem Him with the esteem due to Him; since He is All-Powerful and Almighty, how could the weak and humiliated share in His divinity? The shift away from saying "You have not esteemed God with the esteem due to Him" to the third-person form is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), serving as an implicit indication that they are not fit to be addressed directly, and as a rebuke to them. In this way, there is combined within His words ﴿Indeed, God is All-Powerful, Almighty﴾ a threat to them that He will take vengeance upon them for their audacity.

The emphasis of the clause by the particle of emphasis (inna) and the lam of initiation, although its content is something not disputed, is because their knowledge of this is treated as if it were denial, since they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires when they associated with the All-Powerful, the Almighty, weak and abased beings.

Al-Qawiyy (القوي, the All-Powerful) is among His names, exalted is He. It is used to mean the power to accomplish every will of His.

Al-'Aziz (العزيز, the Almighty) is among His names, and it means the Overcomer of every obstinate opponent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 75:

﴿Allah chooses messengers from the angels and from mankind. Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.﴾

When the preceding verses negated that the idols worshipped by the polytheists have any power to help them, saying ﴿And the wrongdoers have no helper﴾ [al-Hajj: 71], and ﴿The seeker and the sought are both weak﴾ [al-Hajj: 73], and when he censured the polytheists for their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), saying ﴿They almost attack those who recite Our verses to them﴾ [al-Hajj: 72], one of the motives for their denial was that they deemed it impossible for a messenger from among humans to come to them. ﴿They said, "Why was not an angel sent down to him?"﴾ [al-An'am: 8], meaning, to accompany him. ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Why were angels not sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 21]. After refuting their claims, it was followed by the statement that Allah chooses whomever He wills for election from among the angels and from among mankind, rather than stones, and that He chooses them in order to send them to people, that is, not to be partners (with Him). Therefore His saying ﴿Allah chooses messengers from the angels and from mankind﴾ decisively refuted all their claims about their idols. The sentence is thus a fresh, initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), and the connection (munasabah) is as you have understood.

[Page 344]

The fronting of the predicate's subject, which is the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalala, "Allah"), before the verbal predicate in His saying ﴿Allah chooses﴾, rather than saying "yastafi" (He chooses) alone, serves to express exclusivity (ikhtisas), meaning that Allah alone is the One who chooses, not you, who choose and attribute that choosing to Him.

The use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun here, where He did not say "He chooses messengers from the angels", is because the Name of Majesty is originally al-Ilah (the God), meaning the known God, besides whom there is no god. Its derivation indicates that its referent comprises all the supreme attributes, affirming complete power and overpowering might.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾ gives the reason for the content of the clause ﴿Allah chooses﴾, because the One whose knowledge encompasses all things is the One who is specially entitled to choose. No people of intellect, however keen their minds and however discerning their judgment, can perceive the hidden matters so as to choose for the lofty stations those whose faults may be concealed from them, let alone choose lifeless stones.

"All-Hearing, All-Seeing" is a metonymy (kinaya) for the comprehensiveness of knowledge of things, according to what is customary in regard to what is known, since known things do not exceed what is heard and what is seen.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 76:

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and to Allah all matters are returned.﴾

This sentence confirms the meaning of the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing﴾ [al-Hajj: 75]. Its benefit, beyond confirmation, is that it is an allusion (ta'ridh) to the obligation of their being mindful of their Lord in private and in public, because nothing hidden is concealed from Him.

As for ﴿what is before them﴾, it is a metaphor (isti'arah) for what they reveal, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ is what they conceal, because the thing a person displays places it before him, and the thing he hides places it behind him.

Page 345

It is also possible that ﴿what is before them﴾ is a metaphor for what will happen to them of their conditions, because these resemble the thing that is in front of a person as he walks toward it. And ﴿what is behind them﴾ is a metaphor for the past and bygone conditions of theirs, because these resemble what the traveler has left behind him and passed by. The pronoun in ﴿before them﴾ and ﴿behind them﴾ refers either to the polytheists to whom the pronoun in ﴿so let them not dispute with you about the matter﴾ [al-Hajj: 67] returns, or to the angels and people.

The "returning of matters" means the return of the judgment concerning their recompense, of reward and punishment, to Him on the Day of Resurrection. The verb ﴿is returned﴾ (turja'u) is put in the passive form with a deputy subject (na'ib al-fa'il) because the one who does the returning is evident, for it is fitting only for Allah, Exalted is He. He grants respite to people in this world, and He returns matters to Himself on the Day of Resurrection.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) serves to express a real restriction (al-hasr al-haqiqi), meaning: to Allah and not to other than Him are matters returned, because the recompense belongs to Him, since He is the King of the Day of Judgment. The definite article in ﴿the matters﴾ (al-umur) is for comprehensiveness (al-istighraq), meaning every matter. This combines glad tidings and warning, following what precedes it in His saying ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 22, verse 77:

﴿O you who have believed, bow down and prostrate yourselves, and worship your Lord, and do good, that you may succeed.﴾

Since the address to the polytheists (mushrikun) opened this surah and occupied most of it, what came as an interjection in the midst of that was set aside. The polytheists were addressed with "O mankind" four times. When the arguments, admonitions and warnings directed at the polytheists, and the rebuke of their evil deeds, had been fully delivered, the surah concluded by turning to address the believers with what would reform their deeds and raise their standing.

[Page 346]
In this ordering there is an indication that occupying oneself with reforming belief takes precedence over occupying oneself with reforming deeds.

By bowing (ruku') and prostration (sujud) is meant the prayers (salawat). They are singled out from among the acts of prayer because they are the greatest of the pillars of prayer, since through them the expression of humility and servitude is manifested. The singling out of prayer for mention before the command to the remaining acts of worship included in His words ﴿and worship your Lord﴾ is an alert that prayer is the pillar of the religion.

By worship ('ibadah) is meant what God commanded people to worship Him by, such as fasting and pilgrimage (hajj).

His words ﴿and do good﴾ are a command to confer good upon people, such as zakat and good treatment, like maintaining the ties of kinship, enjoining what is right (al-amr bil-ma'ruf), forbidding what is wrong (al-nahy 'an al-munkar), and all the noble qualities of character. This is a general statement (mujmal) which other proofs have clarified and whose degrees they have explained. The hope derived from ﴿that you may succeed﴾ is used in the sense of bringing success near to them when they reach, through their deeds, the limit that necessitates success in what God the Exalted has specified. This is the true meaning of hope. As for what hope entails of the hoper's uncertainty about attaining what is hoped for, that does not come to mind, because of the presence of the proofs that remove doubt concerning God the Exalted.

Know that the words of God the Exalted ﴿O you who have believed, bow down and prostrate yourselves﴾ up to ﴿that you may succeed﴾: the scholars (a'immah) differed over whether this is a place of prostration among the prostrations of the Qur'an (sujud al-tilawa, the prostration of recitation). The view adopted by the majority is that it is not a place of prostration, and this is the position of Malik in the Muwatta' and the Mudawwana, and of Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri.

A large group held that it is a place of prostration. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and the jurists of Medina (fuqaha' al-Madina) related this, and Ibn al-'Arabi attributed it to Malik in the transmission of the Medinese among his companions from him. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in al-Kafi: "Among the people of Medina, both in earlier and later times, there are those who hold that prostration is made in the second (verse) of the hajj." He said: "Ibn Wahb related it from Malik." The essence of his school is that the prostrations are eleven, none of which is in the mufassal (the final short surahs of the Qur'an). Therefore he did not attribute this to Malik except on the authority of Ibn Wahb. Likewise Ibn Rushd in al-Muqaddimat. Thus what Ibn al-'Arabi attributed to the Medinese among Malik's companions is strange.

[Page 347]
Al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn Lahi'ah, from Mishrah, from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir who said: "I said: O Messenger of God (ﷺ), has the surah of al-Hajj been given preference because it contains two prostrations? He said: 'Yes, and whoever does not prostrate in them should not recite them.'" (end of quotation). Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This hadith has an isnad that is not strong" (end of quotation), meaning because Ibn Lahi'ah was declared weak by Yahya ibn Ma'in. Muslim said: "Waki', al-Qattan and Ibn Mahdi abandoned him." Ahmad said: "His books were burned, so whoever related from him in earlier times, that is, before the burning of his books, is accepted."

**[p. 348]**

﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him.﴾
*Jihad* (striving; in its customary usage, fighting against the enemies of Islam in the cause of religion, to raise the word of Islam or to defend it), in the form *mufa'ala*, is a customary technical usage for fighting the enemies of the Muslims in religion, for the sake of raising the word of Islam or defending it, as the Prophet ﷺ explained: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the way of Allah." It is also narrated that the Prophet ﷺ, when he returned from the expedition of Tabuk, said to his companions: "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad." He explained the greater jihad to them as the servant's striving against his own desires. This is to be taken as a figure of speech (*mushakala*), by applying the term jihad to restraining the soul's urging toward disobedience.

The preposition *fi* (in) here expresses causation, meaning "for the sake of Allah," i.e., for the sake of supporting His religion. This is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat" (*fi hirra*), meaning for the sake of a cat, i.e., on account of an action connected with a cat, as he explained by saying: "She confined it, and did not feed it nor let it go to eat from the vermin of the earth, until it died of hunger."

The phrase ﴿*haqqa jihadihi*﴾ (with the striving due to Him) is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) specifying the type. The attribute has been added to the noun it qualifies; the original form is *jihadahu al-haqq* (His striving, the true one). The addition of *jihad* to the divine name is for the slightest connection, meaning "the true striving for His sake." The indication of this meaning is the prior mention of the preposition *fi*, as in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102].

*Al-haqq* here means "the pure," i.e., the striving that is not mixed with any shortcoming.

The verse is a command to strive. It is perhaps the first verse to come with a command to strive, since the surah is partly Meccan and partly Medinan, and because His saying preceded it: ﴿That, and whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with, then is wronged, Allah will surely help him﴾ [al-Hajj: 60]. So this now is a command to take up the means of victory. The verse was therefore revealed before the Battle of Badr, without doubt.

* * *

**[p. 349]**

﴿He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship — the creed of your father Abraham. He named you "Muslims" before, and in this [Qur'an], that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over the people.﴾

The clause ﴿He has chosen you﴾, if it is taken as standing in the position of a cause for what they were commanded at the outset from His saying: ﴿O you who believe, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77] and so on, then the meaning is: because He has chosen you, you are worthy of thanking Him through those qualities for which you were commanded.

*Al-ijtiba'* (choosing) means selecting and preferring, i.e., He has chosen you to receive His religion, to spread it, and to support it against its opponents. It appears that this is primarily addressed to the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that all who came after them share in it by the unity of the attribute across generations, as is the case in the addresses of legislation. If the words ﴿He has chosen you﴾ are taken to mean preference over the (other) nations, then what is intended is the preference of the whole community over all the previous nations, which returns to the preference of each class of this community over the corresponding class of the earlier nations.

Two such interpretations have already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

This is followed by the preference of this religion, which entails the preference of its adherents, in that He made it a religion without hardship, because that facilitates acting upon it while achieving the purpose of the Law through action, so its adherents are made happy by the ease of complying with it. Allah has favored by this meaning in many verses of the Qur'an, among them His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqara: 185]. Describing the religion as *hanif* (upright, inclining to the true faith), the Prophet ﷺ said: "I was sent with the tolerant *hanifiyya*."

*Al-haraj* (hardship) means constriction. It was applied to the difficulty of actions by analogy of the intelligible to the perceptible, and then this spread until it became a customary technical usage, as it is here.

*Al-milla* means religion and law. It was discussed previously at His saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the creed of Abraham, a *hanif*﴾ [al-Nahl: 123] in Surat al-Nahl, and at His saying: ﴿And I have followed the creed of my fathers﴾ [Yusuf: 38] in Surat Yusuf.

His saying ﴿the creed of your father Abraham﴾ is an addition to the honoring of this religion and an exhortation to adopt it, because it is distinguished by being a religion brought by two messengers, Abraham and Muhammad ﷺ, and this has not been established for any other religion. This is the meaning of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham," i.e., by His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 129]. Since this is the intended meaning, the sense of the statement is that this religion is the religion of Abraham, i.e., Islam encompasses the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him. It is known that Islam has many rulings, but it includes what the other laws do not include from the religion of Abraham, so it is treated as if it were the very creed of Abraham. On this consideration, the accusative of ﴿the creed of your father Abraham﴾ is a circumstantial state (*hal*) of "the religion," on the basis that Islam contains the creed of Abraham.

Then, if the address is directed to those who accompanied the Prophet ﷺ, the attribution of Abraham's fatherhood to them is by way of the majority of the community, since the majority of the community at that time were from the Mudar Arabs. As for the Ansar, their lineage does not trace back to Abraham, peace be upon him, since they are from the Qahtanite Arabs; moreover, most of them had Abraham as an ancestor through their mothers.

**[p. 351]**

If the address is to all Muslims in general, the attribution of Abraham's fatherhood to them is in the sense of comparison in sanctity and deserving of reverence, like His saying: ﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. It is also because he is the father of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and Muhammad holds the station of fatherhood for the Muslims. And His saying ﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6] has been recited with the addition: "and he is their father."

It is also possible that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ in the manner of honoring, as if He said: "the creed of your father Abraham."

The pronoun in ﴿He named you Muslims﴾ refers to the Divine Name, like the pronoun in ﴿He has chosen you﴾, so the clause is a second new sentence, meaning: He has chosen you and singled you out with this sublime name, so He did not give it to anyone other than you. It does not refer to Abraham. *Qabl* (before), when built on a *damma*, is on the presumption of a genitive noun that is understood in meaning but not in wording. The noun to which *qabl* is attached is omitted. *Qabl* was built on a *damma* to signal the omitted noun. The intended meaning is: "before the Qur'an." The indicator is His saying "and in this," i.e., and in this Qur'an.

The demonstrative in "and in this" refers to the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Bring me a Book from before this, or a trace of knowledge, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 4]; i.e., He named you Muslims in the Qur'an. This is like His saying: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: bear witness that we are Muslims﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64], and His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-Zumar: 12].

The *lam* in His saying ﴿that the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ is connected either to His saying ﴿bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], or to His saying "He has chosen you." That is: so that the Messenger, i.e., Muhammad ﷺ, may be a witness over the Muslim community that it believed in him; and the Muslim community will be witnesses over the people, i.e., over the nations, that

**[p. 352]**

their messengers conveyed the call to them, and the disbelievers rejected them. Among the people are the folk who disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ.

The testimony of the Messenger to the community is mentioned first here, while the testimony of the community is mentioned first in the verse of al-Baqara: ﴿And thus We have made you a median community, that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqara: 143]. This is because the verse of this surah is in the context of honoring the religion that the Messenger brought. So the Messenger is more immediately present here, and therefore mentioning his testimony is more important; while the verse of al-Baqara begins with praise of the community, so mentioning the testimony of the community is more important.

* * *

﴿So establish the prayer, give the zakat, and hold fast to Allah. He is your Protector — how excellent a Protector, and how excellent a Helper!﴾

This is a consequence (*tafri'*) of the clause ﴿He has chosen you﴾ and what follows it; i.e., thank Allah by persisting in establishing the prayer, giving zakat, and holding fast to Allah.

*Al-i'tisam* (holding fast) is a form of the root *'asm*, meaning protection from harm and deliverance. Allah said: ﴿He said: I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water. He said: There is no protector today from the command of Allah﴾ [Hud: 43]. And al-Nabigha said:

*He remains, out of fear, the sailor holding fast to the bamboo pole after exhaustion and distress.*

The meaning is: make Allah your refuge and your means of deliverance. The clause ﴿He is your Protector﴾ is a new sentence giving the reason for the command to hold fast to Allah, because the Protector is the one who is held fast to and returned to, for the greatness of His power and the wondrousness of His wisdom.

*Al-mawla* (protector): the master who looks after the welfare of his servant.

**[p. 353]**

Following from this is the expression of praise of Allah as the best Protector and the best Helper, i.e., the excellent manager of your affairs and the excellent helper for you. *Nasir* (helper) is an intensive form in support. That is: an excellent protector for you and an excellent helper for you. As for the disbelievers, His care does not take them as protégés, nor does He help them.

This expression includes the affirmation of the excellence of Allah's guardianship and the excellence of His support. On this basis, it is fitting that it follows from the command to hold fast to Him.

This is from the excellence of the conclusion, as is clear to people of understanding.

* * *

**[p. 5]**

In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Mu'minun.

It is also said: Surat al-Mu'minun (with the *nun* in the nominative).

The first (Surat al-Mu'minin) is based on the attribution of the surah to the believers, because it opens with informing about them that they have prevailed. This naming appears in what al-Nasa'i narrated: from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: "I attended the Messenger of Allah on the day of the Conquest; he prayed facing the Ka'ba, took off his sandals and placed them to his left, and began Surat al-Mu'minin. When the mention of Musa or Isa came, a cough seized him and he bowed."

The second (Surat al-Mu'minun) follows the quotation of the word *al-mu'minun* that occurs at its beginning in His saying: ﴿The believers have prevailed﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], so that word was made the designation of the surah.

This surah's name, Surat al-Mu'minun, is also attested in the Sunna. Abu Dawud narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: "The Messenger of Allah led us in the dawn prayer in Mecca, and began Surat al-Mu'minun. When he reached the mention of Musa and Harun, or the mention of Musa and Isa, a cough seized the Prophet, and he stopped and bowed."

What has become current on people's tongues is to call it Surat (Qad aflaha) (The Surah of "Has Prevailed"). This appears in the book *al-Jami'* of al-'Utbiyya, in the transmission of Ibn al-Qasim. Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik brought out for us a copy of the Qur'an belonging to his grandfather, and we discussed that he had written it in the time of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and its covering was from the kiswa of the Ka'ba; so we found... [the text continues] ... and in *Qad aflaha* all three [verses] are for Allah, i.e., contrary to the reading: "They will say: Allah." It is also called Surat al-Falah (The Surah of Prevailing).

It is Meccan by consensus. No weight is given to the objection of those who hesitated on the ground that the verse in which zakat is mentioned, His saying: ﴿And those who are active in zakat﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4], indicates that it is

**[p. 6]**

Medinan, because zakat was prescribed in Medina. The zakat mentioned in it is charity, not the zakat on specified amounts of wealth. The use of "zakat" for charity is well known in the Qur'an. Allah said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists who do not give zakat﴾ [Fussilat: 6], and that is from a surah that is Meccan by consensus; and He said: ﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il; he was truthful in promise and was a messenger and prophet﴾ [Maryam: 54], ﴿and he used to enjoin on his family the prayer and zakat﴾ [Maryam: 55], and the zakat on specified amounts was not legislated in the time of Isma'il.

It is the seventy-sixth surah in the order of revelation of the Qur'an's surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Tur and before Surat ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [al-Mulk: 1].

The number of its verses is 117 according to the majority count. The people of Kufa counted it as 118. The majority counted ﴿Those are the inheritors who will inherit Paradise; therein they will abide forever﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10] as one verse, whereas the people of Kufa counted ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10] as one verse and what follows it as another verse. This is what is understood from the words of Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi in al-'Aridah, in the hadith that we will mention after the commentary on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the inheritors who will inherit Paradise; therein they will abide forever﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10].

* * *

The verses of this surah revolve around the axis of affirming God's oneness, refuting polytheism and undermining its foundations, and emphasizing faith and its legislation.

Its opening was a good news to the believers of great success, for what they adorned themselves with of the foundational spiritual and practical virtues by which the soul is purified and conduct is made upright.

This was followed by a description of the creation of man, his origin and his progeny, which indicates God's exclusive divinity through His sole creation and origination of man, so that the observer begins with reflection on the formation of his own essence, then on his non-existence after life. It also indicates that this creation proves the resurrection after death, and that God did not create creation in vain or as play.

It then moved to reflection on the creation of the heavens and what it indicates of God's wisdom.

Page 7

And to reflection on, and the favour of, God's creatures whose origin is water, by which the life of animals and plants in this world exists, and the subtleties of craftsmanship in that, and the benefits in livestock, among them carrying loads.

And the subjugation of benefits for people, and what man has been given of the instruments of thought and contemplation.

Mention of being carried on ships occurred, and from it there was a transition to the sending of Noah and the event of the Flood.

It then moved to a reminder of the sending of the messengers for guidance and direction to monotheism and righteous action, and of what their peoples met them with of aversion, slander and division, and what was the punishment of the deniers. These are examples as an admonition for those who turn away from the call of Muhammad (ﷺ). This was followed by praise of those who believed and were mindful of God.

By alerting the polytheists that their situation is similar to the situations of past nations and that their word is one, so they are liable to have befallen them what befell the earlier denying nations.

God had shown them signs of punishment, perhaps they would desist from obstinacy, but they persisted in their polytheism because of what Satan cast into their minds.

They were reminded that when asked, they acknowledge that God alone is the Lord, yet they do not act upon the requirement of their acknowledgment, and that they will regret their disbelief when death comes to them and on the Day of Resurrection.

And that they knew the Messenger and had experienced his truthfulness, trustworthiness and sincere counsel, free of seeking any benefit for himself except God's reward. So there is no excuse for them in any way for their polytheism and their denial of the message, but they follow their desires and turn away from the truth.

Interspersed in all of this were comprehensive words.

The surah concludes with the command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to overlook their bad treatment of him, to repel it with what is better, and to ask forgiveness for the believers. That is the success with which the surah began.
